atacchabdasya tena śabdenābhidhānamiti, sahacaraṇāt--
'yaṣṭikāṃ bhojaya' iti yaṣṭikāsahacarito
brāhmaṇo 'bhidhīyate iti, sthānāt-- 'mañcāḥ
krāśantīti mañcasthāḥ puruṣā abhidhīyante,
tādarthyāt-- kaṭārtheṣu vīraṇeṣu
vyūhyamāneṣu 'kaṭaṃ karotīti bhavati,
vṛttāt-- 'yamo rājā' 'kubero rājā'
iti tadvadvartate iti, mānāt-- āḍhakena
mitāḥ saktavaḥ 'āḍhakaṃ saktavaḥ' iti, dhāraṇāt--
tulayā dhṛtaṃ candanam 'tulā candanam' iti,
sāmīpyāt-- 'gaṅgāyāṃ gāvaścarantīti
deśo 'bhidhīyate saṃnikṛṣṭaḥ, yogāt--
kṛṣṇena rāgeṇa yuktaḥ śākaṭaḥ 'kṛṣṇaḥ' ityabhidhīyate,
sādhanāt-- 'annaṃ prāṇāḥ' iti, ādhipatyāt--
'ayaṃ puruṣaḥ kulam' 'ayaṃ gotram' iti|

children.translated_text: In this regard,
the <s>jāti</s>-word (generic term) is applied to the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) through co-occurrence or connection
[End of NyS 2.2.63]

Even when [the thing denoted] is not of that nature, there is a metaphorical usage (<s>upacāra</s>) of that [word] for it — the designation of what is not [literally] that by that word. [This occurs] from co-occurrence — 'feed the staff' means the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> who accompanies the staff is designated. From location — 'the platforms are crying out' means the people standing on the platforms are designated. From purpose — when <s>vīraṇa</s> grasses meant for a mat are being arranged, 'he is making a mat' is said. From conduct — '<s>Yama</s> is king,' '<s>Kubera</s> is king' [means] he acts like one. From measure — barley-flour measured by the <s>āḍhaka</s> [vessel is called] 'an <s>āḍhaka</s> of barley-flour.' From holding — sandalwood weighed by a balance [is called] 'a balance of sandalwood.' From proximity — 'the cows are grazing on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>' means the nearby area is designated. From connection — a charioteer connected with the color black is called 'the black one.' From instrumentality — 'food is the vital breaths.' From lordship — 'this person is the family,' 'this is the lineage.'
[Section: NySBh 2.2.64]

children.text: yadi 'gauḥ' ityasya padasya na vyaktirarthaḥ ? astu tarhi---
children.translated_text: If the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) is not the meaning of the word 'cow'? Then let it be —
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.64: [Thesis:] <s>Ākṛti</s> (configuration) [is the word-meaning], because the determination of the being (<s>sattva</s>) depends on it.

children.text:
ākṛtiḥ padārthaḥ, kasmāt ?. padapekṣatvāt sattvavyavasthānasiddheḥ |
sattvāvayavānāṃ tadavayavānāṃ ca niyato vyūha ākṛtiḥ tasyāṃ gṛhyamāṇāyāṃ sattvavyavasthānaṃ sidhyati-- 'ayaṃ gauḥ' 'ayamaśvaḥ' iti. nāgṛhyamāṇāyām. yasya grahaṇāt sattvavyavasthānaṃ sidhyati taṃ śabdo 'bhidhātumarhati |
so 'syārtha iti // naitadupapadyate-- yasya jātyā yogastadatra jātiviśiṣṭamabhidhīyate-- 'gauḥ' iti. na cāvayavavyūhasya jātyā yogaḥ|
kasya tarhi ?. niyatāvayavavyūhasya dravyasya, tasmād nākṛtiḥ padārthaḥ // 64 //
children.translated_text: Of what then? Of the substance having a fixed arrangement of parts. Therefore, <s>ākṛti</s> is not the word-meaning. [End of NyS 2.2.64]

<s>Ākṛti</s> (configuration) is the word-meaning. Why? Because the determination of the being depends on the word, [i.e.,] depends on the <s>ākṛti</s>. The fixed arrangement of the parts of the being and of the sub-parts — that is <s>ākṛti</s>. When it is grasped, the determination of the being is established: 'this is a cow,' 'this is a horse.' Not when it is not grasped. That by the grasping of which the determination of the being is established — the word ought to designate that; that is its meaning. [Objection:] This is untenable — what has a connection with the universal (<s>jāti</s>) is designated here as qualified by the universal — 'cow.' And the arrangement of parts does not have a connection with the universal.
[Section: NySBh 2.2.65]
Then let the universal (<s>jāti</s>) be the word-meaning —

children.text: NyS_2,2.65: vyaktyākṛtiyukte 'py aprasaṃgāt prokṣaṇādīnāṃ mṛdgavake jātiḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 2.2.65: [Thesis:] Even when [something] possesses individual (<s>vyakti</s>) and configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>), because of the non-applicability of sprinkling and other [ritual acts] to a clay cow — [therefore] the universal (<s>jāti</s>) [is the word-meaning].

children.text:
jātiḥ
padārthaḥ, kasmāt ?. vyaktyākṛtiyuktepi mṛdgavake
prokṣaṇādīnāmaprasaṅgāditi = 'gāṃ prokṣaya' 'gāmānaya' 'gāṃ dehīti
naitāni mṛdgavake prayujyante, kasmāt ?

children.translated_text: Because of the absence of the universal (<s>jāti</s>). For there is the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) there, and there is
the configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>). That whose absence causes non-application there — that is the word-meaning
[End of NyS 2.2.65]

The universal (<s>jāti</s>) is the word-meaning. Why? Because even though the clay cow possesses individual and configuration, sprinkling and other [ritual acts applying to a cow] do not apply to it — 'sprinkle the cow,' 'bring the cow,' 'give the cow' — these are not applied to a clay cow. Why?
[Section: NySBh 2.2.66]
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.66: [Reply:] No, because the manifestation of the universal (<s>jāti</s>) depends on the configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>) and the individual (<s>vyakti</s>).
The manifestation of the universal depends on configuration and individual.
When the configuration and the individual are not grasped, the universal alone

children.text: śuddhaṃ gṛhyate tasmānna jātiḥ padārtha iti // 66 //
children.translated_text: in its pure [form] is not grasped. Therefore, the universal is not the word-meaning. [End of NyS 2.2.66]
[Section: NySBh 2.2.67]

children.text:
na vai padārthena na bhavituṃ
śakyam|
kaḥ khalvidānīṃ padārtha iti ?---
children.translated_text: It cannot be the case that none [of these three] is the word-meaning. Who then is the word-meaning? —
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.67: But the individual (<s>vyakti</s>), configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>), and universal (<s>jāti</s>) together are the word-meaning.

children.text:
tuśabdo viśeṣaṇārthaḥ, kiṃ
viśiṣyate ?. pradhānāṅgabhāvasyāniyamena
padārthatvamiti. yadā hi bhedavivakṣā viśeṣagatiśca
tadā vyaktiḥ pradhānamaṅgaṃ tu jātyākṛtī. yadā
tu bhedo 'vivakṣitaḥ sāmānyagatiśca tadā
jātiḥ pradhānamaṅgaṃ tu vyaktyākṛtī, tadetad

children.translated_text: is frequent in usage.
But the primary status of configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>)
is to be investigated. [End of NyS 2.2.67]

The word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) serves as a qualifier. What is qualified? That the word-meaning consists [of all three] without a fixed rule as to which is primary and which is subordinate. For when differentiation is intended and the particular is apprehended, then the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) is primary and the universal and configuration are subordinate. But when differentiation is not intended and the general is apprehended, then the universal (<s>jāti</s>) is primary and the individual and configuration are subordinate. This
[Section: NySBh 2.2.68]

children.text:
kathaṃ punarjñāyate nānā vyaktyākṛtijātaya iti ?. lakṣaṇabhedāt,
tatra tāvat---
children.translated_text: Now, how is it known that the individual, configuration, and universal are different? From the difference in their definitions. Therein, first —
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.68: The individual (<s>vyakti</s>) is what has form (<s>mūrti</s>), being the substrate of particular qualities.

children.text:
vyajyate iti vyaktiḥ |
indriyagrāhyeti. na sarvaṃ dravyaṃ vyaktiḥ, yo
guṇaviśeṣāṇāṃ sparśāntānāṃ gurutvadhanatvadravatvasaṃskārāṇām
avyāpinaḥ parimāṇasyāśrayo yathāsaṃbhavaṃ
taddravyaṃ mūrtiḥ-- mūrchitāvayavatvāditi
// 68 //
children.translated_text: What is manifested (<s>vyajyate</s>) is the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) — meaning it is graspable by the sense-organs. Not every substance is an individual. That substance which is the substrate of particular qualities ending with touch — heaviness, fluidity, viscosity, and <s>saṃskāras</s> (tendencies) — and of non-pervading magnitude, as applicable — that is <s>mūrti</s> (having form), because its parts are compacted (<s>mūrchita</s>). [End of NyS 2.2.68]
[Section: NySBh 2.2.69]
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.69: <s>Ākṛti</s> (configuration) is that by which the universal and the marks of the universal are made known.

children.text:
yayā jātirjātiliṅgāni ca prakhyāyante
tāmākṛtiṃ vidyāt. sā ca nānyā sattvāvayavānāṃ
tadavayavānāṃ ca niyatād vyūhāditi|
niyatāvayavavyūhāḥ
khalu sattvāvayavā jātiliṅgam-- śirasā
pādena gāmanuminvanti |
niyate ca sattvāvayavānāṃ vyūhe sati gotvaṃ
prakhyāyate iti|

children.translated_text: When the universal is not manifest through configuration —
[as in] 'clay,' 'gold,' 'silver,' and similar [substances] — configuration loses its role.
It abandons its word-meaning status. [End of NyS 2.2.69]

That by which the universal (<s>jāti</s>) and the marks of the universal are made manifest — that should be known as <s>ākṛti</s>. And it is nothing other than the fixed arrangement of the parts of the being and of their sub-parts. The fixed arrangement of the parts of a being is indeed the mark of the universal — by the head and the foot one infers a cow. And when the fixed arrangement of the being's parts is present, cow-ness (<s>gotva</s>) is made manifest.
[Section: NySBh 2.2.70]
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.70: The universal (<s>jāti</s>) is that whose nature produces cognition of sameness.

children.text:
yā samānāṃ buddhiṃ prasūte bhinneṣvadhikaraṇeṣu.
yayā bahūni itaretarato na vyāvatente.
yo 'rtho 'nekatra pratyayānuvṛttinimittaṃ tat sāmānyam, yacca keṣāṃ cidabhedaṃ keṣāñcid bhedaṃ karoti tat sāmānyaviśeṣo jātiriti
// 70 //
children.translated_text: That which produces the same cognition in different substrates; by which many [things] are not differentiated from one another; that object which is the cause of the continuity of cognition in many [things] — that is the general (<s>sāmānya</s>). And that which causes non-difference among some and difference from others — that general-particular is the universal (<s>jāti</s>). [End of NyS 2.2.70]

children.text: // iti vātsyāyanīye nyāyabhāṣye dvitīyādhyāyasya dvitīyamāhnikaṃ samāptam //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second lesson of the second chapter of <s>Vātsyāyana's</s> <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s>.
And the second chapter is complete.
Now the first lesson of the third chapter of the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> with sub-commentary.

children.text: parīkṣitāni pramāṇāni prameyamidānīṃ parīkṣyate-- taccātmādīti ātmā vivicyate-- kiṃ dehendriyamanobuddhivedanāsaṃghātamātramātmā ? āho svit tavdyatiriktaḥ ? iti|
children.translated_text: The <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) have been examined. Now the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) is examined — and that [begins with] the <s>Ātman</s> (self) and the rest. The <s>Ātman</s> is analyzed: Is the <s>Ātman</s> merely the aggregate of body, sense-organs, mind, cognition, and sensation? Or is it something distinct from them?

children.text: kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ ?, vyapadeśasyobhayathā siddheḥ, kriyākaraṇayoḥ kartrā saṃbandhasyābhidhānaṃ vyapadeśaḥ sa dvividhaḥ-- avayavena samudāyasya-- 'mūlairvṛkṣastiṣṭhati' 'stambhaiḥ prāsādo dhriyate' iti, anyenānyasya vyapadeśaḥ-- 'paraśunā vṛścati' 'pradīpena paśyati' (iti), asti cāyaṃ vyapadeśaḥ-- 'cakṣuṣā paśyati' 'manasā vijānāti' 'buddhyā vicārayati' 'śarīreṇa sukhaduḥkhamanubhavatīti, tatra nāvadhāryate-- kimavayavena samudāyasya |
children.translated_text: Whence the doubt? Because the designation (<s>vyapadeśa</s>) is established either way. A designation is the expression of the relation of an agent with its action and instrument. It is of two kinds: of the whole by a part — 'the tree stands by its roots,' 'the palace is supported by its pillars'; and the designation of one thing by another — 'he cuts with the axe,' 'he sees with the lamp.' And there is this designation: 'he sees with the eye,' 'he knows with the mind,' 'he deliberates with the intellect,' 'he experiences pleasure and pain with the body.' In this case, it is not determined — is this a designation of the whole by a part,
[that is,] of the body-aggregate? Or of one thing by another,
[that is,] of something distinct from it?
[Section: NySBh 3.1.1]
This is a designation of one thing by another. Why? —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.1: Because a single object is grasped by both sight and touch.

children.text: darśanena yāvadartho gṛhītaḥ sparśanenāpi so 'rtho gṛhyate-- 'yamahamadrākṣaṃ cakṣuṣā taṃ sparśanenāpi spṛśāmi, iti. 'yaṃ cāspārkṣaṃ sparśanena taṃ cakṣuṣā paśyāmīti ekaviṣayau cermā pratyayau ekakartṛkau pratisaṃdhīyete. na ca saṃghātakartṛkau. na (vā) indriyeṇaikakartṛkau, tad yo 'sau cakṣuṣā tvagindriyeṇa caikārthasya grahītā bhinnanimittau ananyakartṛkau pratyayau samānaviṣayau pratisaṃdadhāti so 'rthāntarabhūta ātmā|
children.translated_text: The same object that is grasped by sight is also grasped by touch — 'what I saw with my eyes, I also touch with the sense of touch'; 'and what I touched with the sense of touch, I see with my eyes.' These two cognitions with a single object are recognized as having a single agent. They do not have the aggregate as their agent; nor do they have a [single] sense-organ as their single agent. Therefore, the one who grasps a single object through the eye and the tactile sense-organ — who connects two cognitions that have different causes but are not of different agency and have the same object — that is the <s>Ātman</s>, which is a different entity.

children.text: kathaṃ punarnendriyeṇaikakartṛkau ?. indriyaṃ khalu svaṃ svaṃ viṣayagrahaṇam ananyakartṛkaṃ pratisaṃdhātumarhati nendriyāntarasya viṣayāntaragrahaṇamiti|
children.translated_text: But how are they not of a single agency with a sense-organ? A sense-organ can indeed connect its own particular object-apprehension as being of a single agency, [but] not the apprehension of a different object by a different sense-organ.

children.text: kathaṃ na saṃghātakartṛkau ?. ekaḥ khalvayaṃ bhinnanimittau svātmakartṛkau pratyayau pratisaṃhitau vedayate na saṃghātaḥ, kasmāt ?. anivṛttaṃ hi saṃghāte pratyekaṃ viṣayāntaragrahaṇasyāpratisaṃdhānam indriyāntareṇeveti // 1 //
children.translated_text: How are they not of the agency of the aggregate? This single [self] experiences [the fact that] two cognitions of its own agency, with different causes, are connected — not the aggregate. Why? Because in the aggregate, the non-connection of the apprehension of a different object by each [component] individually is not eliminated — just as with a different sense-organ. [End of NyS 3.1.1]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.2]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.2: [Objection:] No, because of the fixed restriction of objects [to sense-organs].

children.text:
na dehādisaṃghātādanyaścetanaḥ, kasmāt ?. viṣayavyavasthānāt |
vyavasthitaviṣayāṇīndriyāṇi-- cakṣuṣy asati rūpaṃ na gṛhyate sati ca gṛhyate. yacca yasminn asati na bhavati sati ( ca ) bhavati tasya taditi vijñāyate, tasmād rūpagrahaṇaṃ cakṣuṣaḥ cakṣū rūpaṃ paśyati, evaṃ ghrāṇādiṣvapīti|
tānīndriyāṇīmāni svasvaviṣayagrahaṇāt cetanāni-- indriyāṇāṃ bhāvābhāvayorviṣayagrahaṇasya tathābhāvāt, evaṃ sati kimanyena cetanena //. saṃdigdhatvādahetuḥ|

yo 'yamindriyāṇāṃ bhāvābhāvayorviṣayagrahaṇasya tathāl̃āvaḥ sa kiṃ cetanatvāt ? āhosvit cetanopakaraṇānāṃ grahaṇanimittatvāt ? iti saṃdihyate, cetanopakaraṇatve 'pīndriyāṇāṃ grahaṇanimittatvād bhavitumarhati // 2 //
children.translated_text: This correspondence of object-apprehension with the presence and absence of the sense-organs — is it because [the senses] are conscious? Or is it because, as instruments of a conscious being, they are the occasion for apprehension? This is doubtful. Even if the sense-organs are instruments of a conscious being, because they are the occasion for apprehension, [this correspondence] is possible. [End of NyS 3.1.2]

There is no conscious entity other than the body-aggregate. Why? Because of the fixed restriction of objects. The sense-organs have restricted objects — when the eye is absent, form is not grasped; when present, it is grasped. And what does not exist when something is absent and exists when it is present — it is known as belonging to that. Therefore, the apprehension of form belongs to the eye; the eye sees form. Similarly for the organ of smell and the rest. These sense-organs are conscious because of their apprehension of their respective objects — since the apprehension of objects corresponds to the presence and absence of the sense-organs, this being so, what need is there for another conscious entity? [Reply:] This is an inconclusive reason (<s>ahetu</s>), because of being doubtful.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.3]
And as for what was said — 'because of the fixed restriction of objects' —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.3: Because the existence of the <s>Ātman</s> [follows] from that very restriction, [the objection] is not a refutation.

children.text:
yadi khalvekamindriyamavyavasthitaviṣayaṃ sarvajñam |
sarvaviṣayagrāhi cetanaṃ syāt kastato 'nyaṃ cetanamanumātuṃ śaknuyāt, yasmāttu vyavasthitaviṣayāṇīndrinayāṇi tasmāt tebhyo 'nyaścetanaḥ sarvajñaḥ |

sarvaviṣayagrāhī viṣayavyavasthitim atīto 'numīyate, tatredaṃ pratyabhijñānam apratyākhyeyaṃ cetanavṛttamudāhriyate-- rūpadarśī khalvayaṃ rasaṃ gandhaṃ vā pūrvagṛhītamanuminoti. gandhaprativedī ca rūparasāv anuminoti. evaṃ viṣayaśeṣepi vācyam|
children.translated_text: apprehending all objects, transcending the restriction of objects — is inferred from them. Here, this recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>) is undeniable and is cited as evidence of the activity of a conscious being: this seer of form infers a previously grasped taste or smell; this perceiver of smell infers form and taste. The same should be said for the remaining objects.

children.text: rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā gandhaṃ jighrati. ghrātvā ca gandha rūpaṃ paśyati. tadevamaniyataparyāyaṃ sarvaviṣayagrahaṇam ekacetanādhikaraṇam ananyakartṛkaṃ pratisaṃdhatte, pratyakṣānumānāgamasaṃśayān pratyayāṃśca nānāviṣayān svātmakartṛkān pratisaṃdadhāti pratisaṃdhāya vedayate, sarvārthaviṣayaṃ ca śāstraṃ pratipadyate. arthamaviṣayabhūtaṃ śrotrasya, kramabhāvino varṇān śrutvā padavākayabhāvaṃ pratisaṃdhāya śabdārthavyavasthāṃ ca budhyamāno 'nekaviṣayamarthajātamagrahaṇīyamekaikenendriyeṇa gṛhṇāti, seyaṃ sarvajñasya jñeyāvyavasthānupadaṃ na śakyā parikramitum|
children.translated_text: Having seen form, one smells a smell; having smelled a smell, one sees form. Thus, the apprehension of all objects, in an unfixed sequence, belonging to a single locus of consciousness, having a single agency, is connected [through recognition]; one connects cognitions of perception, inference, scripture, and doubt — which have diverse objects and one's own agency — and having connected them, experiences them; and one comprehends the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise), which has all things as its object — an object that is not within the domain of the ear [alone], hearing phonemes that occur in sequence, connecting them into words and sentences, and understanding the determination of word-meanings — one apprehends a class of objects pertaining to many domains that cannot be grasped by any single sense-organ. This [capacity] of the omniscient [self], following the non-restriction of objects to be known, cannot be fully traversed.

children.text: ākṛtimātraṃ tūhāhṛtam, tatra yaduktam-- 'indriyacaitanye sati kimanyena cetanena' ( iti ) tadayuktaṃ bhavati // 3 //
children.translated_text: Only a sketch has been presented here. Therefore, what was said — 'given the consciousness of the sense-organs, what need is there for another conscious entity?' — is unjustified. [End of NyS 3.1.3]

If there were a single sense-organ with unrestricted objects — omniscient, apprehending all objects, conscious — who could then infer another conscious entity? But because the sense-organs have restricted objects, a different conscious entity — omniscient,
[Section: NySBh 3.1.4]
And for another reason, the <s>Ātman</s> is distinct from the body and the rest — it is not merely the body-aggregate —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.4: Because of the absence of sin (<s>pātaka</s>) in the burning of a body.

children.text: śarīragrahaṇena śarīrendriyabuddhivedanāsaṃghātaḥ prāṇibhūto gṛhyate, prāṇibhūtaṃ śarīraṃ dahataḥ prāṇihiṃsākṛtapāpaṃ pātakamityucyate. tasyābhāvaḥ-- tatphalena karturasaṃbandhāt akartuśca saṃbandhāt |
children.translated_text: By the word 'body,' the aggregate of body, sense-organs, cognition, and sensation as a living being is meant. The sin (<s>pātaka</s>) incurred from harming a living being by burning a body that is a living being — its absence [when burning a dead body proves the ātman is distinct from the body]. Because the doer [of the burning] has no connection with that result [of sin], and because one who is not the doer [the dead person] does have the connection [with the body].

children.text: śarīrendriyabuddhivedanāprabandhe khalvanyaḥ saṃghāta utpadyate 'nyo nirudhyate. utpādanirodhasaṃtatibhūtaḥ prabandho nānyatvaṃ bādhate-- dehādisaṃghātasyānyatvādhiṣṭhānatvāt. anyatvādhiṣṭhāno hyasau prakhyāyate iti, evaṃ sati yo dehādisaṃghātaḥ prāṇibhūto hiṃsā karoti nāsau hiṃsāphalena saṃbadhyate. yaśca saṃbadhyate na tena hiṃsā kṛtā, tadevaṃ sattvabhede kṛtahānamakṛtābhyāgamaḥ prasajyate, sati ca sattvotpāde. sattvanirodhe cākarmanimittaḥ sattvasargaḥ prāpnoti tatra muktyartho brahmacaryavāso na syāt|
children.translated_text: In the continuum of body, sense-organs, intellect, and sensation, indeed one aggregate arises and another ceases. The continuum, which consists of a succession of arising and ceasing, does not invalidate otherness — because the body-aggregate and so forth is the substrate of otherness. For that [aggregate] is manifested as the substrate of otherness. This being so, the body-aggregate that, being a living being, commits hiṃsā (violence) is not connected with the fruit of that violence. And the one who is connected [with the fruit] did not commit the violence. Thus, when there is a difference of beings, the loss of what was done and the accrual of what was not done would follow, and upon the arising of a being, upon the cessation of a being, the creation of beings would occur without karma as its cause. In that case, celibate studentship for the purpose of liberation would be pointless.

children.translated_text: If, therefore, the being were merely the body-aggregate and so forth, then in the burning of the body there would be no sin. But this is undesirable. Therefore, the <s>ātman</s> (self), distinct from the body-aggregate and so forth, is eternal. [End of NyS 3.1.4]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.5]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.5: The absence of that [sin] even in the burning of what possesses a self, because of its eternality.

children.translated_text: Even for one whose body, possessing an eternal <s>ātman</s>, is burned — for him too, there would be no sin in the burning of the body for the burner. Why? Because of the eternality of the <s>ātman</s>. No one can ever harm what is eternal. But if it is harmed? Then its eternality would not hold. Thus, on one view, <s>hiṃsā</s> (violence) is fruitless; on the other, it is untenable. [End of NyS 3.1.5]

Regarding what was stated —
'The absence of that [sin] even in the burning of what possesses a self, because of its eternality' — that is unjustified. [End of NyS 3.1.6]

We do not say that the killing of an eternal being is <s>hiṃsā</s> (violence); rather, for a being that is subject to destruction, the injury to the body — which is the substrate of effects — and to the sense-organs — which are the agents of apprehending their respective objects — affliction characterized by distress and disability, or the severance of the continuum characterized by slaying, constitutes <s>hiṃsā</s>. The effect is the experience of pleasure and pain; its receptacle, its substrate, is the body. The destruction of the body — the substrate of effects — and of the sense-organs — the agents of apprehending their respective objects — is <s>hiṃsā</s>, not [the destruction] of the eternal <s>ātman</s>. Regarding what was stated — 'The absence of that [sin] even in the burning of what possesses a self, because of its eternality' (3.1.5) — that is unjustified. For one whose position is that <s>hiṃsā</s> is the annihilation of the being, the fault of loss of what was done and accrual of what was not done [follows]. And this much is the case: either <s>hiṃsā</s> is the annihilation of the being, or it is the destruction of the substrate of effects and the agents of a being subject to non-annihilation. There is no third alternative. And the annihilation of beings has been refuted; so what else remains? The matter stands as stated. Alternatively, 'because of the destruction of the substrate of effects and the agents' — the substrate of effects is the aggregate of body, sense-organs, and intellect of the eternal <s>ātman</s>; therein, the experience of pleasure and pain, and its substrate, its receptacle — that exists and is nothing other than it; and that same is the agent — for the occurrence of the experience of pleasure and pain is caused by it and does not happen without it. Its destruction means injury,
[Section: NySBh 3.1.7]
And furthermore, the <s>ātman</s> is distinct from the body and so forth —

When that [memory] is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>, because of its existence, there is no refutation of the <s>ātman</s> — if memory is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>, then in that case memory is tenable — one [organ] does not remember what was perceived by another. Or if there were connecting, the determination of objects would be untenable. But one conscious entity, perceiving many objects, remembers — from different causes — what was previously perceived. Because of the connecting of perceptions by a single perceiver of many objects, when memory is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>, its existence [is established]; in the contrary case, it is untenable. All activities of living beings are grounded in memory. The modification of another sense-organ is merely an illustration, an indicator of the <s>ātman</s>.

Without fully enumerating the object of memory, this is stated — 'No, because memory has its content as its object' (3.1.13). This memory, when the object is not being perceived — 'I knew this object' — the object of this [memory] is the previously known object qualified by the knower and the knowledge, not the mere object. 'I have known this object,' 'this object was known by me,' 'my knowledge of this object occurred' — this fourfold statement, conveying the same meaning, indicates the object of memory. In every case, the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable are grasped. Now, the memory that occurs when the object is present — by that, three cognitions are connected regarding a single object, having the same agent, not having different agents, not being without an agent, but rather having a single agent. 'I saw this very object that I now see' — 'I saw' is the seeing and the awareness of the seeing — for without being aware of one's own seeing, one would not say 'I saw.' These indeed are two cognitions. 'That which I now see' is the third cognition. Thus, a single object, being connected with three cognitions, is not without an agent, not with different agents, but rather with a single agent. This object of memory, not being fully enumerated though it exists and is known, is denied — 'the <s>ātman</s> does not exist — because memory has its content as its object.' But this is not mere memory with merely its content as object; rather, this is a connecting of memory, like the connecting of knowledge. Because of the all-objectness of one — this one knower, having all [things] as objects, connects his own cognitions — 'I shall know this object,' 'I know this object,' 'I knew this object.' Having desired to know an object and having not known it for a long time, he determines — 'I knew it.' Thus, he connects memory too, qualified by the three times and qualified by the desire to remember. But if the being were merely a continuum of impressions, impressions would arise and disappear in succession, and there would be no single impression that could experience knowledge and memory qualified by the three times. And without experience, there is no connecting of knowledge and memory. And 'I' and 'mine' arise as in other bodies. Therefore it is inferred —
[Section: NySBh 3.1.16]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.16: Because the grounds for apprehending the self are possible in the mind, [the self is not distinct from the body-aggregate].

This being so, the designation '<s>ātman</s>' (self) for the knower is not accepted, but the designation '<s>manas</s>' (mind) is accepted. And for <s>manas</s>, the designation 'mind' is not accepted, but the designation 'instrument of thought' is accepted. This is merely a difference of designation, not a dispute about the thing itself. Or, if [the mind] is rejected, there follows the absurdity of the destruction of all sense-organs. This restriction that is accepted — 'the instruments for apprehending form and the rest exist for it, but an instrument of thought encompassing all objects does not exist' — this restriction is without inferential basis; there is no inference here by which we could establish the restriction. And from form and the rest, pleasure and the like are different objects; for the apprehension of those, there must be another instrument. Just as odor is not grasped by the eye, hence the nose is another instrument; just as taste is not grasped by the eye and nose, hence the tongue is another instrument — similarly for the remaining [senses] as well. Likewise, since pleasure and the like are not grasped by the eye and the rest, there must be another instrument. And that is indicated by the non-simultaneity of cognitions, and that which serves as the instrument for the apprehension of pleasure and the like, that too is indicated by the non-simultaneity of cognitions. Because of the proximity and non-proximity of that instrument (<s>indriya</s>) to each sense-organ,
[Section: NySBh 3.1.19]

children.text:
kiṃ punarayaṃ dehādisaṃghātādanyo nityaḥ ? utānityaḥ ? / kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ ?, ubhayathā dṛṣṭatvāt saṃśayaḥ--
vidyamānamubhayathā bhavati nityamanityaṃ ca,
pratipādite cātmasadbhāve saṃśayānivṛtteriti/
ātmasadbhāvahetubhirevāsya prāgdehabhedādavasthānaṃ
siddham ūrdhvamapi dehabhedādavatiṣṭhate/
kutaḥ ?---
children.translated_text: But is this [self], which is different from the aggregate of body and the rest, permanent? Or impermanent? Whence the doubt? The doubt arises because both are observed — what exists can be either permanent or impermanent, and because doubt is not removed even when the existence of the <s>ātman</s> has been demonstrated. By the very reasons proving the existence of <s>ātman</s>, its persistence prior to the dissolution of the body is established; and it persists even after the dissolution of the body. How so? —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.19: Because of the apprehension of joy, fear, and sorrow in a newborn, arising from the continuation of memory of what was previously practiced.

children.text:
jātaḥ khalvayaṃ
kumāro 'smin janmany agṛhīteṣu
harṣabhayaśokahetuṣu harṣabhayaśokān
pratipadyate liṅgānumeyān, te ca smṛtyanubandhādutpadyante
nānyathā. smṛtyanubandhaśca pūrvābhyāsamantareṇa

children.translated_text: does not occur without prior practice. And prior practice is possible only if there was a previous birth
and not otherwise — thus it is established: this [self] persists after
(and before) the dissolution of the body. [End of NyS 3.1.19]

Indeed, this newborn child, even though the causes of joy, fear, and sorrow have not been experienced in this birth, experiences joy, fear, and sorrow — which are to be inferred from signs. And these arise from the continuation of memory and not otherwise. And the continuation of memory
[Section: NySBh 3.1.20]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.20: Just as there is modification of blooming and closing in lotuses and the like, so would be its modification.
Just as in lotuses and the like, which are impermanent,
there occurs modification consisting of blooming and closing,
so too, the apprehension of joy, fear, and sorrow would be a modification of the impermanent <s>ātman</s>.

children.text:
hetvabhāvādayuktam |
anena hetunā padmādiṣu prabodhasaṃmīlanavikāravad
anityasyātmano harṣādisaṃpratipattiriti
nātrodāharaṇasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanaṃ
heturna vaidharmyādasti, hetvabhāvāt--
asaṃbaddhārthakamapārthakamucyate
iti|
dṛṣṭāntācca harṣādinimittasyānivṛttiḥ |
yā ceyamāseviteṣu viṣayeṣu
harṣādisaṃpratipattiḥ smṛtyanubandhakṛtā pratyātmaṃ
gṛhyate seyaṃ padmādisaṃmīlanadṛṣṭāntena
na nivartate. yathā ceyaṃ na nivartate tathā
jātamātrasyāpīti|

children.translated_text: And the action consisting of the separation and conjunction of petals
constitutes the blooming and closing. And the cause of action is to be inferred from action.
This being so, what is negated by the example? [End of NyS 3.1.20]

This is unjustified because of the absence of a valid reason. By this reasoning — 'just as there is modification of blooming and closing in lotuses and the like, so the apprehension of joy and the rest belongs to the impermanent <s>ātman</s>' — here neither from the similarity of the example is there proof of the thesis, nor is there a reason from dissimilarity; because of the absence of a reason, what is said is incoherent and meaningless. And from the example, the cause of joy and the rest is not negated. This apprehension of joy and the rest regarding experienced objects, produced by the continuation of memory, is grasped in each individual self — this is not negated by the example of the closing of lotuses and the like. Just as this is not negated, so too for the newborn.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.21]

children.text:
atha nirnimittaḥ padmādiṣu
prabodhasaṃmīlanavikāra iti matam evamātmanopi
harṣādisaṃpratipattiriti ? tacca---
children.translated_text: Now, if it is held that the modification of blooming and closing in lotuses and the like is without cause, then the apprehension of joy and the rest for <s>ātman</s> too [would be without cause]? To that —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.21: No, because the modifications of things composed of the five [elements] are caused by heat, cold, and rain seasons.

children.text:
uṣṇādiṣu satsu bhāvād asatsvabhāvād tannimittāḥ pañcabhūtānugraheṇa
nirvṛttānāṃ padmādīnāṃ prabodhasaṃmīlanavikārā
iti narnimittāḥ, evaṃ harṣādayopi vikārā
nimittād bhavitumarhanti na nimittamantareṇa.
na cānyat pūrvābhyastasmṛtyanubandhād nimittamastīti/
na cotpattinirodhakāraṇānumānamātmanaḥ--
adṛṣṭāntāt|

children.translated_text: Joy and the rest do not arise without a cause.
Nor is another cause besides [the above] to be adduced
for joy and the rest; therefore this is unjustified. [End of NyS 3.1.21]

Because they occur when heat and the rest are present, and do not occur in their absence, the modifications of blooming and closing of lotuses and the like — which are produced with the assistance of the five elements — are caused by those [conditions] and are not without cause. Similarly, the modifications of joy and the rest too must arise from a cause, not without a cause. And there is no cause other than the continuation of memory of what was previously practiced. And there is no inference of <s>ātman</s>'s origination and destruction — because of the absence of an example.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.22]
And for this further reason <s>ātman</s> is permanent —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.22: Because of the desire for milk, produced by the practice of eating after death [in a previous life].

children.text:
jātamātrasya vatsasya pravṛttiliṅgaḥ stanyābhilāṣo gṛhyate sa ca nāntareṇāhārābhyāsam|
kayā yuktyā ?, dṛśyate hi śarīriṇāṃ kṣudhā pīḍyamānānāmāhārābhyāṃsakṛtāt
smaraṇānubandhādāhārābhilāṣaḥ, na ca pūrvaśarīrābhyāsamantareṇāsau
jātamātrasyopapadyate, tenānumīyatebhūtapūrvaṃ
śarīram yatrānenāhāro 'bhyasya iti,
sa khalvayamātmā pūrvaśarīrāt pretya śarīrāntaramāpannaḥ
kṣutpīḍitaḥ pūrvābhyastamāhāramanusmaran

children.translated_text: desires milk. Therefore <s>ātman</s> is not destroyed upon the dissolution of the body,
but
continues to exist after the dissolution of the body. [End of NyS 3.1.22]

In the newborn calf, a desire for milk is observed, indicated by its activity, and this is not possible without the practice of eating. By what reasoning? For it is seen that in embodied beings afflicted by hunger, from the continuation of memory produced by the practice of eating, there arises a desire for food. And this is not possible for a newborn without practice in a previous body. Therefore it is inferred — 'there was a previous body in which it practiced eating.' Indeed, this <s>ātman</s>, having departed from the previous body and obtained another body, being afflicted by hunger and remembering the previously practiced food,
[Section: NySBh 3.1.23]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.23: That approaching is like the approach of iron to a magnet, without [prior] practice.
Just as iron approaches a magnet without practice, so too a child desires milk without the practice of eating. [End of NyS 3.1.23]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.24]

children.text: kimidamayaso 'yaskāntābhigamanaṃ nirnimittam ? artha nimittāt ? iti, nirnimittaṃ tāvat--
children.translated_text: Is this approach of iron to a magnet without cause? Or is it from a cause? First, [consider] without cause —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.24: No, because of the absence of activity toward other things.

children.text:
yadi nirnimittam ? loṣṭādayopyayaskāntamupasarpayeyuḥ--
na jātu niyame kāraṇamastīti|
atha nimittāt ?. tat kenopalabhyate ? iti, kriyāliṅgaḥ
kriyāhetuḥ kriyāniyamaliṅgaśca kriyāniyamahetuḥ

kriyopalabhyate. na ca stanyābhilāṣaliṅgam

kasya cidutpattiḥ, na dṛṣṭānto dṛṣṭamabhilāṣahetuṃ

iti|

na jātvayo loṣṭamupasarpati|
kiṅkṛtosya
niyamaḥ ? iti, yadi kāraṇaniyamāt sa ca
kriyāniyamaliṅgaḥ, evaṃ bālasyāpi niyataviṣayo 'bhilāṣaḥ

children.translated_text: must be due to the restriction of causes; and that cause is the memory of past practice,
which is distinguished from the other by what is observed.
For in embodied beings, the desire for food arises from the memory of past practice —
this is observed. [End of NyS 3.1.24]

If it were without cause, then clods of earth and the like too should approach a magnet — for there is never no reason for a restriction. Or if it is from a cause — by what is that apprehended? The cause of action is indicated by action, and the cause of the restriction of action is indicated by the restriction of action. Hence the absence of activity toward other things. For the child too, a definite approaching activity is observed. And there is no other cause for the sign of milk-desire besides the continuation of memory produced by the practice of eating. The cause is demonstrated by the example. And without a cause, nothing arises. The example does not negate the observed cause of desire. Therefore, the approach of iron to a magnet is not a [valid] counter-example. For iron too, there is no activity toward other things — iron never approaches a clod of earth. What is the reason for this restriction? If it is due to the restriction of causes — and that is indicated by the restriction of action — then for the child too, the desire directed toward a specific object
[Section: NySBh 3.1.25]
And for this further reason <s>ātman</s> is permanent — why? —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.25: Because one without attachment (<s>vītarāga</s>) is not observed at birth.

children.text:
sarāgo jāyate ityarthādāpadyate, ayaṃ jāyamāno

yoniḥ. pūrvānubhavaśca viṣayāṇāṃ pūrvasmin
janmani śarīramantareṇa nopapadyate. soyamātmā
pūrvaśarīrānubhūtān viṣayān anusmaran
teṣu teṣu rajyate. tathā cāyaṃ dvayorjanmanoḥ
pratisandhiḥ, evaṃ pūrvaśarīrasya pūrvatareṇa

children.translated_text: the earlier body with one still earlier — and so the conjunction of the conscious being with bodies is beginningless,
and the continuation of attachment is beginningless —
thus the permanence [of <s>ātman</s>] is established. [End of NyS 3.1.25]

That [every being] is born with attachment follows by implication — this one, being born, is born pervaded by attachment. The source of attachment is the recollection of previously experienced objects. And the previous experience of objects is not possible without a body in a previous birth. This <s>ātman</s>, remembering the objects experienced in the previous body, becomes attached to each of them. And thus there is the connection between two births; similarly, the previous body [is connected] with an earlier one,
[Section: NySBh 3.1.26]

children.text:
kathaṃ punarjñāyate-- pūrvaviṣayānucintanajanito
jātasya rāgaḥ na punaḥ---
children.translated_text: But how is it known that the attachment of the newborn is produced by the recollection of previously experienced objects, and not rather —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.26: Its origination is like the origination of a substance with qualities?
Just as qualities of a substance that has the nature of origination
arise from a cause, so too the attachment of <s>ātman</s>, which has the nature of origination, arises from some cause.
Here, this restatement of what has been said is for the purpose of illustration. [End of NyS 3.1.26]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.27]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.27: No, because attachment and the rest are caused by volition (<s>saṃkalpa</s>).

children.text:
na khalu saguṇadravyotpattivad utpattirātmano
rāgasya ca|
kasmāt ?. saṃkalpanimittatvādrāgādīnām |
ayaṃ khalu prāṇināṃ viṣayān āsevamānānāṃ
saṃkalpajanito rogo gṛhyate. saṃkalpaśca
pūrvānubhūtaviṣayānucintanayoniḥ tenānumīyate--
jātasyāpi pūrvānubhūtārthacintanakṛto rāga iti|
ātmotpādādhikaraṇāttu rāgotpattirbhavantī
saṃkalpādanyasmin rāgakāraṇe sati vācyā
kāryadravyaguṇavat, na cātmotpādaḥ siddhaḥ nāpi
saṃkalpādanyad rāgakāraṇamasti, tasmādayuktam--
'saguṇadravyotpattivattayorutpattiḥ' iti|
athāpi

children.translated_text: an unseen [force] (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) characterized as <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) is adduced as another cause of attachment besides <s>saṃkalpa</s>,
even so, the conjunction with a previous body is not to be rejected —
for its [i.e., the unseen force's] production was in a previous life, not in this birth.

The origination of <s>ātman</s> and of its attachment is indeed not like the origination of a substance with qualities. Why? Because attachment and the rest are caused by <s>saṃkalpa</s> (volition/intention). Indeed, in living beings who are experiencing objects, attachment produced by volition is observed. And volition has as its source the recollection of previously experienced objects. Therefore it is inferred — the attachment of the newborn too is produced by the contemplation of previously experienced objects. But the origination of attachment from the origination of <s>ātman</s> — if there were another cause of attachment besides <s>saṃkalpa</s>, it could be stated as [analogous to] the quality of a product-substance. But neither is the origination of <s>ātman</s> established, nor is there another cause of attachment besides <s>saṃkalpa</s>. Therefore it is unjustified [to say] 'the origination of both is like the origination of a substance with qualities.' Even if

children.text:
tanmayatvādrāga iti|
viṣayābhyāsaḥ khalvayaṃ
bhāvanāhetustanmayatvamucyate iti|
jātiviśeṣācca
rāgaviśeṣa iti|

children.translated_text: This <s>karma</s> (action) indeed produces the specific birth-type,
and because of identity [with it], the designation is understood. Therefore it is untenable —
that there is another cause of attachment besides <s>saṃkalpa</s>. [End of NyS 3.1.27]

Because of being pervaded by that, there is attachment. This practice regarding objects is the cause of <s>bhāvanā</s> (mental cultivation); that state of being pervaded is what is called [attachment]. And from the specific birth-type, there is a specific attachment.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.28]

children.text:
anādiścetanasya śarīrayoga ityuktam. svakṛtakarmanimittaṃ
cāsyaṃ śarīraṃ sukhaduḥkhādhiṣṭhāna tatṛ parīkṣyate--
kiṃ ghrāṇādivadekaprakṛtikam ? uta nānāprakṛtikam ? iti|
kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ ?, vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ--
pṛthivyādīni bhūtāni saṃkhyāvikalpena śarīraprakṛtiriti pratijānata iti|
kiṃ tatra
tattvam ?---
children.translated_text: It was stated that the conjunction of the conscious being with bodies is beginningless. And this body, whose ground is pleasure and pain, is caused by one's own <s>karma</s>. Regarding that, it is examined — is [the body] of a single nature, like the nose and the rest? Or of a multiple nature? Whence the doubt? The doubt arises from conflicting views — those who assert that the elements beginning with earth constitute the material cause of the body differ in their enumeration. What is the truth there? —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.28: [The body] is made of earth, because qualities different [from earth] are apprehended.

children.text:
tatra mānuṣaṃ śarīraṃ pārthivam, kasmāt ?
guṇāntaropalabdheḥ = gandhavatī pṛthivī gandhavacca śarīram, abādīnām agandhatvāt
tatprakṛti agandhaṃ syāt|
na tvidamabādibhirasaṃpṛktayā
pṛthivyārabdhaṃ ceṣṭendriyārthāśrayabhāvena
kalpate ityataḥ pañcānāṃ bhūtānāṃ saṃyoge
sati śarīraṃ bhavati, bhūtasaṃyogo hi
mithaḥ pañcānāṃ na niṣiddha iti|
āpyataijasavāyavyāni
lokāntare śarīrāṇi teṣvapi bhūtasaṃyogaḥ
pūruṣārthatantra iti|
athālyādidravyaniṣpattāvapi
niḥsaṃśayaḥ-- nābādisaṃyogamantareṇa niṣpattiriti/
'pārthivāpyataijasam-- tadguṇolabdheḥ' 'niḥśvāsocchvāsopalabdheścāturbhauntikam'
'gandhakledapākavyūhāvakāśadānebhyaḥ pāñcabhautikam'
te ime saṃdigdhā hetava ityupekṣitavān
sūtrakāraḥ|
kathaṃ saṃdigdhāḥ ?, sati ca prakṛtibhāve
bhūtānāṃ dharmopalabdhiḥ asati ca saṃyogāpratiṣedhāt
saṃnihitānāmiti. yathā sthālyāmudakatejovāyvākāśānāmiti/
tadidamanekabhūtaprakṛti ( sat ) śarīram agandham arasam arūpam asparśaṃ ca prakṛtyanuvidhānāt syāt.
children.translated_text: This [body], being of multiple elemental origin, would be odorless, tasteless, formless, and touchless, following the nature of its material causes.
But it is not of such nature; therefore it is earthen,
because of the apprehension of other qualities. [End of NyS 3.1.28]

In this regard, the human body is earthen (<s>pārthiva</s>). Why? Because of the apprehension of other qualities — earth possesses odor, and the body also possesses odor; since water and the other [elements] are odorless, if [the body] were made of them, it would be odorless. But this [body], made of earth not mixed with water and the rest, does not function as the locus of effort, sense-organs, and objects — therefore the body exists when the five elements (<s>bhūtas</s>) are in conjunction, for the conjunction of the five elements with one another is not prohibited. Watery, fiery, and airy bodies in other worlds — in those too, the conjunction of elements is subservient to human purpose. And in the production of pots and other objects, there is no doubt — production does not occur without the conjunction of water and the rest. [The arguments] 'earthen, watery, and fiery — because of the apprehension of their qualities,' 'four-elemental, because of the apprehension of inhalation and exhalation,' 'five-elemental, from odor, moisture, heat, arrangement, and space-giving' — these are doubtful reasons, and so the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (aphorist) has disregarded them. How are they doubtful? Because when the material cause [of the body] is [one element], the qualities of [other] elements are apprehended [due to conjunction], and when [the material cause] is absent, [there is] no refutation of the conjunction of nearby [elements] — as water, fire, air, and space [are present] in a pot.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.29]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.29: And because of the authority of scripture (<s>śruti</s>).

children.text:
"sūryaṃ te cakṣurgacchatām" ityatra mantre "pṛthivīṃ te śarīram"
iti śrūyate tadidaṃ prakṛtau vikārasya pralayābhidhānamiti/
"sūryaṃ te cakṣuḥ spṛṇomi" ityatra mantrāntare "pṛthivīṃ te śarīraṃ spṛṇomi" iti śrūyate seyaṃ kāraṇād vikārasya spṛttirabhidhīyate iti|
sthālyādiṣu ca
tulyajātīyānāmekakāryārambhadarśanād
bhinnajātīyānāmekakāryārambhānupapattiḥ
// 29 //
children.translated_text: In the <s>mantra</s> 'May your eye go to the sun' — it is heard: 'your body to the earth.' This is the statement of the dissolution of the effect into its material cause. In the other <s>mantra</s> 'I restore your eye to the sun' — it is heard: 'I restore your body to the earth.' This states the completion of the effect from its cause. And in pots and the like, since the production of a single effect from things of the same class is observed, the production of a single effect from things of different classes is untenable. [End of NyS 3.1.29]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.30]

children.text:
athedānīmindriyāṇi
prameyakrameṇa vicāryante-- kimāvyaktikāni ? āhosvid bhautikāni ? iti|
kṛtaḥ saṃśayaḥ ?
children.translated_text: Now the sense-organs are examined in the order of <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge) — are they non-manifest (<s>āvyaktika</s>)? Or elemental (<s>bhautika</s>)? The doubt has been raised —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.30: The doubt [arises] because of apprehension when the pupil (<s>kṛṣṇasāra</s>) is intact, and apprehension [of objects] apart from it.

children.text: kṛṣṇasāraṃ bhautikaṃ tasminn anupahate rūpopalabdhiḥ upahate cānupalabdhiriti,

children.translated_text: But there is apprehension of an object that exists apart from the pupil, [even of objects] not reached by the pupil.

And the sense-organs do not operate without reaching [their objects] — this [non-contact apprehension] is possible if [the sense-organs] are non-elemental, because of being all-pervading (<s>vibhu</s>).
Thus, because properties of both [alternatives] are apprehended, there is doubt. [End of NyS 3.1.30]
The pupil is elemental; when it is unimpaired, there is apprehension of form; when impaired, non-apprehension.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.31]
[Thesis:] They are non-elemental, he says. Why? —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.31: Because of the apprehension of the large and the small.

children.text:
mahaditi--
mahattaraṃ mahattamaṃ copalabhyate yathā nyagrodhaparvatādi |
aṇviti-- aṇutaramaṇutamaṃ ca gṛhyate yathā
nyagrodhadhānādi, tadubhayamupalabhyamānaṃ cakṣuṣo

children.translated_text: being elemental — for what is elemental
pervades only as much [as its size], but what is non-elemental,
being all-pervading, pervades everything. [End of NyS 3.1.31]

'Large' — what is larger and largest is apprehended, such as a banyan tree, a mountain, and so on. 'Small' — what is smaller and smallest is grasped, such as a banyan seed and so on. Both being apprehended, [this] contradicts the eye's
[Section: NySBh 3.1.32]

children.text:
na mahadaṇugrahaṇamātrādabhautikatvaṃ vibhutvaṃ
cendriyāṇāṃ śakyaṃ pratipattam. idaṃ khalu--
children.translated_text: But the non-elemental nature and all-pervasiveness of the sense-organs cannot be established merely from the apprehension of the large and the small. For indeed —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.32: [Reply:] The apprehension of those [large and small] is due to the particular contact of the [eye-]ray and the object.

children.text:
tayormahadaṇvorgrahaṇaṃ cakṣūraśmerarthasya

// 47 //
children.translated_text: 'The sun's ray is not obstructed' — 'even when behind crystal, it is not obstructed' — 'the combustible [object] is not obstructed' — due to the word-connection with 'non-obstruction,' there are different readings of the sentence. And according to each reading, there is a difference of meaning. The sun's ray is not obstructed in pots and the like — due to non-obstruction, it heats water in a pot; for when there is contact, the quality of heat (<s>uṣṇa sparśa</s>) belonging to another substance is grasped, and by that, cold touch is overpowered. [Reading] 1: Even when something to be illuminated is behind crystal, the lamp's rays are not obstructed — due to non-obstruction, what has reached [the object] is grasped. [Reading] 2: A substance placed on a roasting pan and the like is burned by fiery <s>tejas</s> — there, because of non-obstruction, there is contact; and upon contact, burning [occurs] — thus fire does not act without reaching. [Reading] 3: The word 'non-obstruction' is taken independently — what is this non-obstruction? It is the non-displacement of a substance in all directions by an obstructing substance whose parts are not displaced; the non-prevention of the cause of action; the non-negation of contact. For it is observed that the cold touch of water clinging to a pot is grasped from outside. And without [being] in the manner of the sense-organ, there is no apprehension of touch of a substance not in contact. And trembling and oozing are observed [as signs of contact]. Therefore, because the eye-ray is not obstructed by glass, mica sheets, and the like, apprehension is established through contact with the object, having penetrated [the transparent medium]. [End of NyS 3.1.47]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.48]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.48: Because there would be the undesirable consequence of the interchange of properties.

// 49 //
children.translated_text: Mirrors and water possess transparency (<s>prasāda</s>). A particular form is their own property — because a fixed rule is observed. Or, the apprehension of form is the own property of transparency. Just as the eye-ray, reflected back after striking a mirror, comes into contact with one's own face, and the apprehension of one's own face — called the grasping of a reflection — occurs due to the aid of the mirror's form, having that as its cause — because in the absence of the mirror's form, it does not occur. And in walls and the like, the grasping of a reflection does not occur. Thus, the eye-ray is not obstructed by glass, mica sheets, and the like, but is obstructed by walls — due to the fixed rule regarding the nature of substances. [End of NyS 3.1.49]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.50]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.50: There is no tenability of either enjoining or prohibiting what is observed and inferred.

children.translated_text: Apprehension and non-apprehension serve to establish [these properties] — from non-apprehension of what is obstructed, it is inferred that
there is obstruction by walls and the like; from apprehension of what is obstructed [i.e., behind a transparent medium], it is inferred that
there is non-obstruction by glass, mica sheets, and the like. [End of NyS 3.1.50]

Because a means of knowledge has reality as its object — indeed, one who examines cannot enjoin observed and inferred things [saying] 'let them be thus,' nor prohibit [them saying] 'let them not be thus.' For this is untenable — 'let smell too be visual like form,' or 'let form not be visual like smell,' or 'let there be knowledge of water from smoke as there is knowledge of fire,' or 'let there not be knowledge of fire from smoke as there is no knowledge of water [from smoke].' Why? Because things exist as they are. Their own nature, their own property — they are apprehended by a means of knowledge as having that nature — for a means of knowledge has things of that nature as its object. Now, these enjoining and prohibiting have been taught by you — 'let there be non-obstruction by walls, just as by glass and mica sheets,' or 'let there not be non-obstruction by glass and mica sheets, just as by walls.' But no — these properties of substances are indeed observed and inferred.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.51]

satyāṃ tvaci gṛhyamāṇe ( ca ) tvagindriyeṇe
sparśe indriyāntarārthā rūpādayo na gṛhyante

children.translated_text: by the blind and others. There is no sense-organ other than the touch-grasping sense, [for if there were,]
form and the rest should be grasped by the blind and others just as touch [is grasped]. But
they are not grasped. Therefore, skin is not the one sense-organ.

[Objection:] Because of the non-apprehension of objects belonging to other sense-organs — when skin exists with the characteristic of touch-apprehension, and when the skin-sense grasps touch, the objects of other sense-organs such as form and the rest are not grasped
located at the eye grasps the touch of smoke,
but another [part] does not — similarly, particular parts of skin that grasp form and the rest, when those are damaged, form and the rest are not grasped
by the blind and others.
[Reply:] That apprehension is like the apprehension of smoke through a particular part of skin. Just as a particular part of skin

children.text:
vyāhatatvādahetuḥ/
'tvagavyatirekādekamindriyam' ityuktvā
'tvagakyavaviśeṣeṇa dhūmopalabdhivad rūpādyupalabdhiḥ'
ityucyate. evaṃ ca sati nānābhūtāni
viṣayagrāhakāṇi-- viṣayavyavasthānāt |

children.translated_text: Because in the presence of that [particular part], there is apprehension of the [corresponding] object,

children.text: cābhāvāt. tathā ca pūrvo vāda uttareṇa vādena
children.translated_text: and in its destruction, there is non-apprehension. And thus the former position is contradicted
by the latter position.

[Counter-reply:] This is a non-reason because of self-contradiction. Having said 'because of the non-difference from skin, there is one sense-organ,' it is [then] said 'the apprehension of form and the rest is through a particular part of skin, like the apprehension of smoke.' And in that case, the sense-faculties grasping [different] objects are of different natures — because of the fixed assignment of objects.
And when those are absent, apprehension of objects
does not occur. Therefore, neither skin nor anything else
is a single sense-organ for all objects. [End of NyS 3.1.52]
[Further objection:] And the non-difference is doubtful. The seats of sense-organs are also pervaded by elements such as earth and the rest.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.53]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.53: Because of the non-apprehension of objects simultaneously.

// 53 //
children.translated_text: The self (<s>ātman</s>) is connected with the mind (<s>manas</s>), the mind with the sense-organ, and the sense-organ is in contact with all objects — thus from the contacts of self, sense-organ, mind, and object, there should be simultaneous apprehensions. But form and the rest are not grasped simultaneously; therefore, there is no single sense-organ for all objects. And because the apprehensions of objects are not co-occurring, there is no single sense-organ for all objects — for if they were co-occurring, the condition of the blind and others would be untenable. [End of NyS 3.1.53]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.54]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.54: And because of contradiction, skin is not the one [sense-organ].

children.text:
na khalu tvagekamindriyam-- vyāghātāt,
tvacā rūpāṇy aprāptāni gṛhyante iti aprāpyakāritve

āvaraṇānupapatteśca rūpamātrasya grahaṇaṃ
vyavahitasya cāvyahitasya ceti|

children.translated_text: And the conformity to distance and proximity
in the apprehension and non-apprehension of form would not obtain —

children.text: aprāptaṃ tvacā gṛhyate rūpamiti dūre rūpasyāgrahaṇamantike
children.translated_text: if form is grasped by skin without being reached, then the non-grasping of form at a distance
and grasping at proximity would not hold. [End of NyS 3.1.54]

Indeed, skin is not the one sense-organ — because of contradiction. If forms that are not reached by skin are grasped, then the implication of non-contact-based action (<s>aprāpyakāritva</s>) would extend to touch and the rest as well. And since touch and the rest are grasped [only] when reached, form and the rest too should be grasped [only] when reached. [Objection:] What if [skin] acts both by reaching and without reaching? [Reply:] Because obstruction would be untenable, there would be apprehension of form alone [without restriction] — or rather, should one think that touch and the rest are grasped by skin when reached, but forms without being reached — in that case, there would be no obstruction. And because obstruction would be untenable, there would be apprehension of form alone, whether obstructed or unobstructed.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.55]
And since the oneness [of sense-organ] has been refuted, in establishing multiplicity, the reason of location is also adduced —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.55: Because the purposes of the sense-organs are five.

children.text:
arthaḥ prayojanaṃ tat pañcavidhamindriyāṇām
usparśanenendriyeṇa sparśagrahaṇe sati na
tenaiva rūpaṃ gṛhyate iti rūpagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ
cakṣuranumīyate, sparśarūpagrahaṇe ca tābhyāmeva
na gandho gṛhyate iti gandhagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ ghrāṇamanumīyate,
trayāṇāṃ grahaṇe na taireva raso gṛhyate
iti rasagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ rasanamanumīyate,
na caturṇāṃ grahaṇe taireva śabdaḥ śrūyate iti
children.translated_text: When four [qualities] are grasped, sound is not heard by those very [organs] — thus
the ear (<s>śrotra</s>) is inferred as having the purpose of grasping sound. Thus, because the purpose of sense-organs is not mutually achievable,
there are exactly five sense-organs. [End of NyS 3.1.55]

The purpose (<s>artha</s>) is the function, and that is fivefold for the sense-organs. When touch is grasped by the tactile sense-organ, form is not grasped by that same [organ] — thus the eye is inferred as having the purpose of grasping form. And when touch and form are grasped by those two, smell is not grasped by those very [organs] — thus the nose (<s>ghrāṇa</s>) is inferred as having the purpose of grasping smell. When three [qualities] are grasped, taste is not grasped by those very [organs] — thus the tongue (<s>rasana</s>) is inferred as having the purpose of grasping taste.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.56]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.56: [Objection:] No, because of the multiplicity of those objects.

children.text:
na khalu 'indriyārthapañcatvāt pañcendriyāṇīti sidhyati, kasmāt ?
teṣāmarthānāṃ bahutvāt |
bahavaḥ khalvime indriyārthāḥ |
sparśāstāvat śītoṣṇānuṣṇāśītā iti.
rūpāṇi śuklaharitādīni. gandhā iṣṭāniṣṭopekṣaṇīyāḥ.
rasāḥ kaṭukādayaḥ, śabdā varṇātmano dhvanimātrāśca

children.translated_text: and are differentiated. Thus, for one who [holds] that 'because the purposes of the sense-organs are five, the sense-organs are five,'
because of the multiplicity of the objects of the sense-organs, the consequence would be that the sense-organs are many
[i.e., more than five]. [End of NyS 3.1.56]

Indeed, it is not established that 'because the purposes of the sense-organs are five, the sense-organs are five.' Why? Because of the multiplicity of those objects. For these objects of the sense-organs are many. Touches, for instance, are cold, hot, and neither cold nor hot. Forms are white, green, and so forth. Smells are pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral. Tastes are pungent and so forth. Sounds are of the nature of phonemes and mere sounds,
[Section: NySBh 3.1.57]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.57: Because there is no deviation from smell-ness and the rest, there is no negation of smell and the rest [as distinct categories].

children.text:
gandhatvādibhiḥ svasamānyaiḥ kṛtavyavasthānāṃ gandhādīnāṃ
yāni gandhādigrahaṇāni tāny asamānasādhanasādhyatvād

bhavān pratiṣedhati. tasmādayuktoyaṃ pratiṣedha

trividhaḥ--- śīta uṣṇo 'nuṣṇāśītaśca sparśatvena
svasāmānyena saṃgṛhītaḥ, gṛhyamāṇe ca śītasparśe
noṣṇasyānuṣṇāśītasya vā sparśasya grahaṇaṃ

uyenaiva śītasparśo gṛhyate tenaivetarāvapīti/
evaṃ gandhatvena gandhānām. rūpatvena rūpāṇām.
rasatvena rasānām. śabdatvena śabdānāmiti/

children.translated_text: But the apprehensions of smell and the rest, because they are not accomplishable by the same means, do not serve as [grounds for postulating] separate sense-organs.
Therefore it is established that because of the fivefold nature of sense-objects,
there are five sense-organs. [End of NyS 3.1.57]

Of smell and the rest, whose classification has been made by their own universals such as smell-ness (<s>gandhatva</s>) and so on, the apprehensions of smell and so forth — because they are accomplished by different means — do not necessitate separate sense-organs. The aggregate of objects is free from inference, not a part of the object; and relying on a part of the object, you negate only the fivefold nature of objects. Therefore this negation is unjustified. But how are smell and the rest classified by their own universals such as smell-ness? Touch (<s>sparśa</s>) indeed is threefold — cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold — comprehended by its own universal, touch-ness (<s>sparśatva</s>). And when cold touch is being grasped, neither the hot nor the neither-hot-nor-cold touch necessitates a separate sense-organ — because the varieties of touch are accomplishable by the same means; by whatever [organ] cold touch is grasped, by that same [organ] the other two are also [grasped]. Similarly, smells by smell-ness (<s>gandhatva</s>), forms by form-ness (<s>rūpatva</s>), tastes by taste-ness (<s>rasatva</s>), sounds by sound-ness (<s>śabdatva</s>).
[Section: NySBh 3.1.58] If the universal is what comprehends? Then it follows for the sense-organs —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.58: Because there is no deviation from the property of being an object, [there would be] unity.
[there would be only one sense-organ]. [End of NyS 3.1.58]
Because smell and the rest are comprehended by the universal of 'being an object' (<s>viṣayatva</s>),
[Section: NySBh 3.1.59]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.59: [This is] not [so], because of the fivefold nature of cognition-characteristics, substrates, movements, forms, and origins.

children.translated_text: The sources of the five sense-organs are the five elements (<s>bhūta</s>s) beginning with earth.
Therefore, because of the fivefold nature of their material cause (<s>prakṛti</s>) also, there are five sense-organs.
This is established. [End of NyS 3.1.59]

Objects whose classification has been made by the universal of 'being an object' are not independent of separate sense-organs; [they] are inferred as graspable by one means. And the five [objects] — smell and the rest — classified by their own universals such as smell-ness, are graspable by different sense-organs. Therefore this [objection] is disconnected. And this very meaning is restated — 'because of the fivefold nature of cognition-characteristics.' Cognitions themselves are the characteristics — the marks of sense-organs consisting of the apprehension of objects, and so forth. This has been commented upon in the sūtra 'because of the fivefold nature of sense-objects [NyS 3.1.55]'; therefore, because of the fivefold nature of cognition-characteristics, there are five sense-organs. The substrates (<s>adhiṣṭhāna</s>) of the sense-organs are also five — the organ of touch (<s>sparśana</s>), marked by the apprehension of touch, has the entire body as its substrate; the eye (<s>cakṣus</s>), marked by the apprehension of form, has the pupil (<s>kṛṣṇatārā</s>) as its substrate and extends outward; smell (<s>ghrāṇa</s>) has the nose as its substrate; taste (<s>rasana</s>) has the tongue as its substrate; hearing (<s>śrotra</s>) has the ear-cavity as its substrate — because they are marked by the apprehension of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound respectively. Sense-differentiation is also [known] from movement (<s>gati</s>) — the eye, bound to the pupil, extends outward and reaches the substances that are the substrata of form; but the sense-organs beginning with touch — the objects themselves approach through the coming near of their substrate; and in the case of sound, [there is] proximity to the ear through a continuous series. Form (<s>ākṛti</s>) indeed is magnitude — that extent is fivefold: smell, taste, and touch [organs] are confined to their own location, non-pervading of objects, and inferred; the eye, based on the pupil, extends outward and pervades its objects; hearing is nothing other than space (<s>ākāśa</s>), and that is all-pervading, inferred from the experience of sound alone, and because of the appropriation of the individual's dispositions, it manifests sound with restriction to the substrate. Origin (<s>jāti</s>) refers to the source —
[Section: NySBh 3.1.60]
But how is it known that the sense-organs have elements (<s>bhūta</s>s) as their material cause and not the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>)?
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.60: Because of the apprehension of specific elemental qualities, [there is] identity [of sense-organs with elements].

children.text:

is the manifester of smell of some substance. And there is this fixed rule of the apprehension of specific elemental qualities by the sense-organs; therefore, from the apprehension of specific elemental qualities, we consider that the sense-organs have elements as their material cause,
not the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>). [End of NyS 3.1.60]
For a fixed rule of the manifestation of specific qualities of elements beginning with wind (<s>vāyu</s>) is observed — wind is the manifester of touch, water the manifester of taste,
[Section: NySBh 3.1.61]
Now the examination of objects.

children.translated_text: It has been stated that smell and the rest are qualities of earth and the rest. And the enumeration is the same whether earth and the rest have one quality or many qualities. Therefore [the sūtra] says —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.61: Of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound — earth [has qualities] up to and including touch.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.62]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.62: For water, fire, and wind, [remove] the preceding one by one; and of space (<s>ākāśa</s>), the last [i.e., sound alone].

uśabdaḥ sparśaparyantebhya iti|

tarapnirdeśaḥ ?. svatantraviniyogasāmarthyāt

children.translated_text: For in the enumeration-sūtra, sound is beyond [i.e., after] those up to and including touch.
Or it is a single statement — because touch is what is intended to be expressed.
When [qualities] up to and including touch have been assigned, what is other [than these] is the 'last' —
namely sound. [End of NyS 3.1.62]

'Up to and including touch' — this is a transformation of case-ending. 'The last of space' means sound, which is beyond those up to and including touch. But how then is the comparative [suffix] to be explained? By the force of independent application, thereby the word 'last' (<s>uttara</s>) is understood as denoting something relative —
[Section: NySBh 3.1.63]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.63: [This is] not [so], because not all qualities are apprehended.

children.text: yasya bhūtasya ye guṇā na te tadātmakenendriyeṇa
children.translated_text: Because the qualities that belong to a given element are not all apprehended
by the sense-organ that is of the same nature as that [element].

children.text: pārthivena hi ghrāṇena sparśaparyantā na gṛhyante
children.translated_text: For by the earthy (<s>pārthiva</s>) organ of smell, [qualities] up to and including touch are not grasped;
only smell alone is grasped. Similarly for the rest also. [End of NyS 3.1.63]
This assignment of qualities is not correct. Why?
[Section: NySBh 3.1.64]
How then should these qualities be assigned?
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.64: Because of the existence of successively higher qualities one by one, there is non-apprehension of those [lower qualities] by the subsequent [elements].
is a quality of each one of earth and the rest; therefore there is non-apprehension of those [other qualities].
There is non-apprehension of those, of those two, and of that one [respectively].
By the organ of smell — of taste, form, and touch; by the organ of taste — of form and touch;
by the eye — of touch. [End of NyS 3.1.64]
Of smell and the rest, one by one in order,
[Section: NySBh 3.1.65]
How then are elements with multiple qualities grasped?
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.65: And the apprehension of multiple qualities is due to combination (<s>saṃsarga</s>).
And because of combination with water and the rest,
taste and the other [qualities] are grasped in earth. Similarly
for the rest also. [End of NyS 3.1.65]

[Section: NySBh 3.1.66] Then a fixed rule would not obtain — because combination has no fixed rule — [that] 'earth has four qualities,' 'water has three qualities,' 'fire has two qualities,' 'wind has one quality.' But a fixed rule does obtain. How?

children.translated_text: Because combination has no fixed rule — [that] 'earth has four qualities,' 'water has three qualities,' 'fire has two qualities,' 'wind has one quality.' But a fixed rule does obtain. How?

Of earth and the rest, each prior [element] is pervaded by each subsequent one.

is to be understood in the context of the creation of elements, not at present. [End of NyS 3.1.66]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.67]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.67: [This is] not [so], because earthy and watery [substances] are perceptible.

dṛṣṭaśca vivekaḥ-- pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt |

children.translated_text: 'Not' — this refutes the three sūtras. Why? Because earthy substances and watery substances are perceptible. [One might say:] 'Apprehension is due to largeness, consisting of many substances, and having form' — [if so,] only fiery (<s>taijasa</s>) substances alone should be perceptible, not earthy or watery — because of the absence of form [in them]. But just as fiery [substances are perceptible], so too earthy and watery substances are perceptible; therefore the apprehension of multiple qualities of elements is not due to combination. And for one who says that the perceptibility of earthy and watery [substances] is caused by the form of another element, it would follow that wind is perceptible. Or let a reason for the restriction be stated. Or, because of the perceptibility of the tastes of earthy and watery [substances] — the earthy taste is sixfold, the watery [taste] is sweet alone — and this cannot be due to combination. Or, because of the perceptibility of the forms of earthy and watery [substances] — when aided by the form of fire in combination, only the manifesting form exists, not the manifested one. And because of the perceptibility of forms of earthy and watery [substances] that are of one and many kinds — earthy form is manifold — green, red, yellow, etc.; but watery [form] is white and non-luminous — and this is not apprehended when there is combination with single-quality [elements]. And this is merely an illustration. Beyond this is elaboration: or, because of the perceptibility of the touches of earthy and fiery [substances] — earthy touch is neither-hot-nor-cold, fiery [touch] is hot and perceptible; and this is not tenable through combination with wind, which has neither-hot-nor-cold touch and is single-qualitied. Or, because of the perceptibility of earthy and watery substances whose qualities are fixed — an earthy substance has four qualities, a watery one has three — they are perceptible, and thereby their cause is inferred — 'it is of such a nature.' The effect is the mark — because from the existence of the cause, the existence of the effect [follows]. Similarly, from the perceptibility of fiery and airy substances, the inference of the arrangement of qualities in their causal substance [is established]. And differentiation is observed — from the perceptibility of earthy and watery [substances]: an earthy substance, separated from water and the rest, is perceptibly grasped, and a watery one [is separated] from the other two, and a fiery one from wind; and none is grasped as having only a single quality. But without inference,

children.translated_text: And it is observed that from the overpowering of the airy touch
by the fiery touch, [the airy touch] is not grasped; but not conversely
is there overpowering of that [fiery touch] by that [airy touch]. [End of NyS 3.1.67]

'for the prior is pervaded by the subsequent [NyS 3.1.66]' — this [claim remains unsupported]. No inferential mark that would make us accept this is grasped here. And what was said — 'for the prior is pervaded by the subsequent — this is to be understood in the context of element-creation, not at present' — is unjustified, because of the absence of a reason for the restriction. And it is observed at present — 'the prior is pervaded by the subsequent.' And fire is pervaded by wind. [Now regarding] pervadedness — [it means] conjunction, and that is the same for both; and because fire is pervaded by wind, fire has touch; but it does not follow that because fire pervades wind, wind has form — there is no reason for the restriction.
[Section: NySBh 3.1.68]

children.translated_text: Thus, having refuted the doctrine that does not conflict with reasoning — as raised in 'not, because not all qualities are apprehended [NyS 3.1.63]' — [the sūtra] resolves [the matter]:
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.68: Because of the predominance of each preceding quality, each [sense-organ] has that [quality] as its chief [object].

children.text:

children.translated_text: the organ of smell is the grasper of smell because it has the quality of smell; similarly
for the tongue and the rest as well — the consequence would be that it grasps qualities corresponding to each quality through the nose and the rest.
[End of NyS 3.1.68]

Therefore the sense-organs beginning with smell do not apprehend all qualities. Because of the predominance of each preceding quality beginning with smell, each [sense-organ] has that as its chief [function]. What is the predominance? The capacity to grasp the object. What is the predominance of quality? The capacity for manifestation. Just as external earthy, watery, and fiery substances — having four, three, and two qualities respectively — do not manifest all qualities, but because of the predominance of smell, taste, and form respectively, they manifest smell, taste, and form in order; so too the organs of smell, taste, and the eye — having four, three, and two qualities respectively — do not grasp all qualities, but because of the predominance of smell, taste, and form respectively, they grasp smell, taste, and form in order. Therefore, the sense-organs beginning with smell do not apprehend all qualities. But one who maintains —
[Section: NySBh 3.1.69]

children.text:
kiṅkṛtaṃ punarvyavasthānaṃ kiñcit pārthivamindriyaṃ na sarvāṇi ?. kānicit āpyataijasavāyavyāni

children.translated_text: What then determines the arrangement — that some sense-organ is earthy and not all? That some are watery, fiery, or airy, and not all? —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.69: But that arrangement is due to predominance (<s>bhūyastva</s>).

children.text:
arthanirvṛttisamarthasya pravibhaktasya dravyasya saṃsargaḥ puruṣasaṃskārakārito bhūyastvam,
dṛṣṭo hi prakarṣe bhūyastvaśabdaḥ--
prakṛṣṭo yathā viṣayaḥ 'bhūyān' ityucyate,
yathā pṛthagarthakriyāsamarthāni puruṣasaṃskāravaśād
viṣauṣadhimaṇiprabhṛtīni dravyāṇi nirvartyante
na sarvaṃ sarvārtham evaṃ pṛthagviṣayagrahaṇasamarthāni
ghrāṇādīni nirvartyante na sarvaviṣayagrahaṇasamarthānīti
// 69 //
children.translated_text: The combination of a substance that is differentiated and capable of accomplishing its purpose — that combination, produced by the dispositions of a person (<s>puruṣasaṃskāra</s>), is predominance (<s>bhūyastva</s>). For the word 'predominance' is seen [used] in the sense of excellence — just as an excellent object is called 'predominant.' Just as substances such as poisons, herbs, and gems, each capable of different functions, are produced by the force of personal dispositions — not everything serves every purpose — so too the sense-organs beginning with the nose are produced [each] capable of grasping different objects, not capable of grasping all objects. [End of NyS 3.1.69]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.70]
The sense-organs do not apprehend their own qualities — why? —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.70: Because things possessing [those] qualities function as sense-organs.

children.text:

The sense-organs beginning with the nose do not apprehend their own qualities such as smell and the rest. For what reason? Because the nose and the rest function as sense-organs together with their own qualities. The nose, together with its own smell which cooperates in the same function,
[Section: NySBh 3.1.71]

<s>NyS</s> 3.1.71: And because of its non-apprehension by that very [sense-organ].

children.text:
na guṇopalabdhirindriyāṇām/
