for in both cases there is an equal absence of a cause of cognition. [End of NyS 3.1.71]
There is no apprehension of [their own] qualities by the sense-organs. One who says — 'just as an external substance
[Section: NySBh 3.1.72]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.72: [Objection:] No, because the quality of sound is apprehended [by its own sense-organ].
'The sense-organs do not apprehend their own qualities' — this is not so, for the own quality, sound, is apprehended by the ear. [End of NyS 3.1.72]
[Section: NySBh 3.1.73]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.73: [Reply:] That apprehension is because of the dissimilarity of the qualities of the two substances.

children.text:

// 73 //
children.translated_text: Space (<s>ākāśa</s>), possessing the quality of sound, does not become a sense-organ [merely] by having sound as its quality. Sound is not the manifester of sound. And the apprehension of their own qualities by the nose and the rest is neither perceived directly nor inferred; but it is inferred that the ear, being space, grasps sound, and that sound is the quality of space. And this elimination (<s>pariśeṣa</s>) should be understood as inference — the self (<s>ātman</s>) is the hearer, not the instrument; if the mind were the ear, there would be no deafness; earth and the rest have the capacity for being the nose and the rest, but not the capacity for being the ear; and there exists this ear, and space remains [as the only candidate] — by elimination, space is the ear. [End of NyS 3.1.73]
Thus ends the first section (<s>āhnika</s>) of the third chapter of the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> composed by <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
Now the second section of the third chapter of the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s>.
[Section: NySBh 3.2.1]

children.text:
parīkṣitānīndriyāṇi arthāśca, buddheridānīṃ parīkṣākramaḥ-- sā kimanityā nityā vā ? iti|
kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ ?---
children.translated_text: The sense-organs and objects have been examined. Now is the turn of the examination of cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) — is it non-eternal or eternal? Whence the doubt? —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.1: The doubt [arises] because of the similarity with <s>karma</s> (action) and <s>ākāśa</s> (space).

children.text: asparśavattvaṃ tābhyāṃ samāno dharma upalabhyate buddhau. viśeṣaścopajanāpāyadharmavattvam, viparyayaśca yathāsvamanityanityayostasyāṃ buddhau nopalabhyate tena saṃśaya iti //
children.translated_text: Intangibility (<s>asparśavatva</s>) is a common property observed in cognition [shared] with both of those. And the distinguishing [property] is being subject to origination and destruction; and the contrary [i.e., eternality], each pertaining respectively to the non-eternal and the eternal, is not observed in cognition — hence the doubt.

children.text: anupapannaḥ khalvayaṃ saṃśayaḥ-- sarvaśarīriṇāṃ hi pratyātmavedanīyānityā buddhiḥ sukhādivat. bhavati ca saṃvittiḥ-- 'jñāsyāmi' 'jānāmi' 'ajñāsiṣam' iti, na copajanāpāyāvantareṇa traikālyavyaktistataśca traikālyavyakteḥ 'anityā buddhiḥ' ityetat siddham, pramāṇasiddhaṃ cedaṃ śāstrepyuktam--
children.translated_text: But this doubt is untenable — for cognition is non-eternal, known to each individual self of all embodied beings, like pleasure and the rest. And there is awareness: 'I will know,' 'I know,' 'I knew.' And without origination and destruction, temporal distinction [past, present, future] would not be manifest. And from that temporal distinction, 'cognition is non-eternal' — this is established. And this, being established by a means of knowledge, is also stated in the śāstra —
"The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind [NyS 1.1.16]"
— and so forth. Therefore, the procedure of doubt is untenable.

children.text: dṛṣṭipravādopālambhārthaṃ tu prakaraṇam. evaṃ hi paśyantaḥ pravadanti sāṃkhyāḥ-- 'puruṣasyāntaḥkaraṇabhūtā nityā buddhiḥ' iti // 1 //
children.translated_text: But the section is for the purpose of criticizing the view of those who hold [otherwise]. For the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, seeing thus, declare — 'Cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), which is the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) of <s>puruṣa</s> (the conscious being), is eternal.' [End of NyS 3.2.1]
"Born from the contact of the sense-organ and the object [NyS 1.1.4]"
[Section: NySBh 3.2.2]
And they put forward a proof —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.2: Because of the recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>) of objects.

children.text: kiṃ punaridaṃ pratyabhijñānam ? 'pūrvamajñāsiṣamarthaṃ tamimaṃ jānāmītijñānayoḥ samāne 'rthe pratisandhijñānaṃ pratyabhijñānam etaccāvasthitāyā buddherupapannam. nānātve tu buddhibhedeṣūtpannāpavargiṣu pratyabhijñānānupapattiḥ-- nānyajñātamanyaḥ pratyabhijānātīti // 2 //
children.translated_text: What then is this recognition? 'I previously knew this object, and now I know this same [object]' — the connecting knowledge (<s>pratisandhijñāna</s>) regarding the same object between two cognitions is recognition. And this is tenable when cognition is stable [i.e., persistent]. But if cognitions are different [i.e., arising and perishing], recognition would be untenable among cognitions that arise and cease — for what is known by one [cognition] is not recognized by another. [End of NyS 3.2.2]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.3]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.3: [This] is a non-reason, because of being equal to what is to be proved.

children.text: yathā khalu nityatvaṃ buddheḥ sādhyam evaṃ pratyabhijñānamapīti|

kiṃ kāraṇam ?. cetanadharmasya karaṇe 'nupapattiḥ-- puruṣadharmaḥ khalvayaṃ jñānaṃ darśanamupalabdhirbodhaḥ pratyayo 'dhyavasāya iti-- cetano hi pūrvajñātamarthaṃ pratyabhijānāti tasyaitasmād hetornityatvaṃ yuktamiti|
children.translated_text: Why? Because [recognition as] a property of the conscious [being] is untenable in an instrument — this [capacity of] knowing, seeing, apprehending, understanding, cognizing, determining is a property of the conscious being (<s>puruṣa</s>). For the conscious being recognizes a previously known object; its eternality is appropriate for this reason.

children.text: karaṇacaitanyābhyupagame tu cetanasvarūpaṃ vacanīyam-- nānirdiṣṭasvarūpamātmāntaraṃ śakyamastīti pratipattum|
children.translated_text: But if one accepts consciousness in the instrument, then the nature of the conscious [being] must be stated — for without specifying its nature, another self cannot be accepted as existing.

children.text: jñānaṃ ced buddherantaḥkaraṇasyābhyupagamyate cetanasyedānīṃ kiṃ svarūpaṃ ko dharmaḥ kiṃ tattvam, jñānena ca buddhau vartamānenāyaṃ cetanaḥ kiṃ karorīti //
children.translated_text: If knowledge is accepted as belonging to the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), that is, <s>buddhi</s> — then what is the nature of the conscious [being]? What is its property? What is its essence? And what does this conscious [being] do when knowledge exists in <s>buddhi</s>?
Just as the eternality of cognition is what is to be proved, so too is recognition.
If [one says] 'it is conscious' (<s>cetayate</s>) — that is not something different from knowing.

children.text: puruṣaścetayate buddhirjānātīti. nedaṃ jñānādarthāntaramucyate-- yetayate jānīte paśyati upalabhate ityekoyamartha iti|
children.translated_text: <s>Puruṣa</s> is conscious and <s>buddhi</s> knows — this is not stated as something different from knowing. 'Is conscious,' 'knows,' 'sees,' 'apprehends' — this is one and the same meaning.

children.text: buddhirjñāpayatīti cet ?. addhā jānīte puruṣo buddhirjñāpayatīti satyametat. evaṃ cābhyupagame 'jñānaṃ puruṣasya' iti siddhaṃ bhavati na buddherantaḥkaraṇasyeti //
children.translated_text: If [one says] '<s>buddhi</s> causes knowing' — truly, <s>puruṣa</s> knows and <s>buddhi</s> causes knowing — this is correct. But with such acceptance, 'knowledge belongs to <s>puruṣa</s>' is established, not to the inner instrument <s>buddhi</s>.
And the assertion that different words designate [different entities] for each person — and the statement of a reason for negation —

children.text: yaśca pratijānīte-- kaścit puruṣaścetayate kaścid budhyate kaścidupalabhate kaścit paśyati iti puruṣānatarāṇi khalvimāni|
children.translated_text: One who asserts — 'one <s>puruṣa</s> is conscious, another cognizes, another apprehends, another sees' — these are indeed different <s>puruṣas</s>.

children.text: cetano boddhā upalabdhā draṣṭeti naikasyeti dharmā iti, atra kaḥ pratiṣedhaheturiti //
children.translated_text: 'The conscious one, the cognizer, the apprehender, the seer' — these are not properties of one [entity] — what is the reason for negating [this]?

children.text:
arthasyābheda iticet ?. samānam|
abhinnārthā ete śabdā iti tatra vyavasthānupapattirityevaṃ cet manyase ?. samānaṃ bhavati |
puruṣaścetayate buddhirjānīte ityatatrāpyartho na bhidyate, tatrobhayoścetanatvādanyataralopa iti|
yadi punarbudhyate 'nayeti bodhanaṃ buddhirmana evocyate tacca nityam ? astvetadevaṃ na tu manaso viṣayapratyabhijñānād nityatvam. dṛṣṭaṃ hi karaṇabhede jñāturekatvāt pratyabhijñānam-- savyadṛṣṭasyetareṇa pratyabhijñānāditi cakṣurvat. pradīpavacca |
pradīpāntaradṛṣṭasya pradīpāntareṇa pratyabhijñānamiti, tasmād jñāturayaṃ nityatve heturiti// 3 //
children.translated_text: If [one says] 'because of non-difference of meaning' — it is the same [argument]. These words have undifferentiated meaning — if you think the arrangement is untenable therefore — [the reply is:] it is the same. '<s>Puruṣa</s> is conscious, <s>buddhi</s> knows' — here too the meaning is not different, and of the two, because both are conscious, one is redundant. But if [<s>buddhi</s>] 'cognizes another [i.e., illuminates for another],' then <s>buddhi</s> is illumination, and that is just the mind (<s>manas</s>), and that is eternal. Let this be so — but the eternality of the mind is not [established] from the recognition of objects. For recognition is observed when there is a difference of instrument but identity of the knower — from the recognition by one eye of what was seen by the other. Like a lamp — what was seen by one lamp is recognized by another lamp. Therefore this [recognition] is a reason for the eternality of the knower. [End of NyS 3.2.3]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.4]

children.text:
yacca manyate-- buddher avasthitāyā yathāviṣayaṃ vṛttayaḥ |
jñānāni niścaranti vṛttiśca vṛttimato nānyeti. tacca---
children.translated_text: And one who thinks — the modifications (<s>vṛtti</s>) of <s>buddhi</s>, which is stable, are cognitions arising according to objects; and a modification is not different from that which has modifications — against that —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.4: [This is refuted] because of the non-simultaneous grasping.

children.text: vṛttivṛttimatorananyatve vṛttimato 'vasthānād vṛttīnāmavasthānamiti yānīmāni viṣayagrahaṇāni tānyavatiṣṭhante iti yugapad viṣayāṇāṃ grahaṇaṃ prasajyate iti // 4 //
children.translated_text: If the modification and what has modifications are not different, then from the persistence of what has modifications, the modifications persist — and thus the grasping of objects, which are these [modifications], would persist, and the consequence would be simultaneous grasping of objects. [End of NyS 3.2.4]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.5]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.5: And when there is no recognition, there would be the undesirable consequence of destruction.

children.text: atīte ca pratyabhijñāne vṛttimānapyatīta ityantaḥkaraṇasya vināśaḥ prasajyate, viparyaye na nānātvamiti // 5 //
children.translated_text: And when recognition has passed, what has modifications has also passed — thus the destruction of the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) would follow. In the contrary case [i.e., if it persists], there would be no plurality [of cognitions]. [End of NyS 3.2.5]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.6]

children.text: avibhu caikraṃ manaḥ paryāyeṇendriyaiḥ saṃyujyate iti---
children.translated_text: And the mind (<s>manas</s>), being non-pervasive and singular, successively conjoins with the sense-organs — thus —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.6: The non-simultaneous grasping is because of successive functioning.
The modification and what has modifications are different. And if they were one, the appearance and disappearance [of cognitions] would not occur. [End of NyS 3.2.6]
Of the sense-organs and objects.
[Section: NySBh 3.2.7]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.7: And non-recognition is because of engagement with another object.
Non-recognition,

The sense-organs have [already] reached the inner instrument — thus there is no movement for the purpose of reaching. Therefore, because there is no successive functioning, non-simultaneous grasping is untenable. And because of the absence of movement, simultaneous grasping of a pervasive inner instrument, being negated, is not inferred by another mark. Just as movement of the eye is negated — because of the equal-time grasping of the near and the distant; but through the obstruction [of vision] by the interposition of hand and moon, [movement] is inferred. This dispute is not about the inner instrument nor about its eternality — for it is established that the mind is the inner instrument and is eternal. Where then is the dispute? About its pervasiveness. And that, being not apprehended by a means of knowledge, is negated. And the inner instrument is one, but the cognitive modifications (<s>vṛtti</s>) are many — visual cognition, olfactory cognition,

This property belonging to specific particular instances is to be understood as applying to particular instances in general.
[End of NyS 3.2.10]

The thesis that 'the notion of plurality in crystal, which remains undifferentiated, is due to differences in the substrate' — this is a thesis without a valid reason. Why? Because even in crystal there is successive arising — in crystal too, different particular instances arise and different ones cease. How? Because of the momentariness of particular instances; a moment (<s>kṣaṇa</s>) is a very brief time; those that last for a moment are momentary. But how is it understood that particular instances are momentary? Because of the observation of a continuous series of increase and decrease in bodies and the like — the nutriment produced from the ripening of food undergoes increase in the body in the form of blood and the like, and decrease proceeds in a continuous series; from increase there is the arising of particular instances, from decrease there is the cessation of particular instances; and when this is so, through the differentiation of the transformation of parts,
[Section: NySBh 3.2.11]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.11: Because of the absence of a reason for the restriction, acknowledgment should be in accordance with observation.

That there is a continuous series of increase and decrease in all particular instances as in the body — this is not a fixed rule. Why? Because of the absence of a reason — there is neither perception nor inference to establish this. Therefore, acknowledgment should be in accordance with observation. Where a continuous series of increase and decrease is observed, there the successive arising of particular instances is acknowledged on the basis of the observation of the continuous series of increase and decrease, as in bodies and the like. The inferential mark of the destruction of milk is the cause of the destruction of milk, and the inferential mark of the arising of curds is the cause of the arising of curds — [the cause] is grasped [through these marks]; therefore there is no non-apprehension.
[Section: NySBh 3.2.15]

One says: 'There is transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) of milk, not destruction.' Transformation is the arising of a different property upon the cessation of the prior property of an enduring substance. Another says: 'There is the manifestation of a different quality' — upon the cessation of the prior quality of an existing substance, a different quality arises.
[Section: NySBh 3.2.16] But here is the refutation —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.16: From [the fact that] the arising of a different substance from a different arrangement [of parts] is observed, the cessation of the prior substance is inferred.

When a different substance — curds — is observed to arise from a different arrangement of parts characterized by coagulation, the prior substance of milk is inferred to have ceased from its parts' separation. // 17 //
children.translated_text: And having acknowledged origination and destruction in crystal — [the argument of] one who proves this, because of whose acknowledgment there is no refutation — the example 'the destruction and arising of crystal and the like are not without cause, like a pot' should be acknowledged — because it cannot be refuted. But that 'destruction and arising are without cause, like milk and curds' — this can be refuted, because destruction and arising are observed to have causes. One who observes the destruction and arising of milk and curds should infer their cause — for cause is [inferred through] the mark of effect. Thus it is established — cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) is non-eternal. [End of NyS 3.2.17]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.18]

children.translated_text: But this is to be considered — whose quality is this cognition? It is a quality of the <s>ātman</s> (self), the sense-organs, and the mind (<s>manas</s>) with their objects. Though this matter is well-known, it is taken up [here] with the thought 'I shall set forth the remainder of the investigation.' This is the doubt about cognition — from the contact [of various factors] its arising [is questioned] — 'because of the non-apprehension of the specific [substrate].' Here the specific consideration is —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.18: [Cognition] is not [a quality] of the sense-organs or objects, because cognition persists even when they are destroyed.

children.text:
nendriyāṇāmarthānāṃ

bhāvāt, bhavati khalvidamindriye 'rthe ca
vinaṣṭe jñānam 'adrākṣam' iti. na ca jñātari

indriyārthavināśe na bhavati, idamanyadātmamanaḥsaṃnikarṣajaṃ
tasya yukto bhāva iti

yuktam-- na cānyadṛṣṭamanyaḥ smarati, na ca manasi
children.translated_text: — and what one person has seen, another does not remember; and when the mind
is accepted as the knower, it is not possible to establish that the sense-organs and objects are the knower.
[End of NyS 3.2.18]

Cognition is not a quality of the sense-organs or of the objects — because cognition exists even when they are destroyed. For indeed, when the sense-organ and the object have been destroyed, the cognition 'I perceived' exists. And cognition cannot exist when the knower has been destroyed. That cognition born from the contact of sense-organ and object which does not exist upon the destruction of sense-organ and object is one thing; this is another — born from the contact of the <s>ātman</s> (self) and <s>manas</s> (mind), the existence of which is justified. This is indeed <s>smṛti</s> (memory) — 'I perceived' — having as its object what was previously seen. And memory of what was previously perceived is not justified when the cognizer has perished
[Section: NySBh 3.2.19]
Let cognition then be a quality of the mind —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.19: And because of the non-apprehension of simultaneous objects, [cognition is] not [a quality] of the mind.

children.text:

manaḥ sa ātmā. yattu sukhādyupalabdhisādhanamantaḥkaraṇaṃ
manastaditi saṃjñābhedamātraṃ nārthabheda iti/
yugapajjñeyānupalabdheścāyogina iti
cārthaḥ, yogī khalu ṛddhau prādurbhūtāyāṃ
vikaraṇadharmā nirmāya sendriyāṇi śarīrāntarāṇi
teṣu teṣu yugapaj jñeyānyupalabhate taccaitad
vibhau jñātaryupapadyate nāṇau manasīti/
vibhutve vā manaso jñānasya nātmaguṇatvapratiṣedhaḥ--
vibhu ca manastadantaḥkaraṇabhūtamiti tasya sarvendriyairyugapat
saṃyogāt yugapaj jñānānyutpadyeranniti
// 19 //
children.translated_text: The non-apprehension of simultaneous objects is the inferential mark of the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>). Therein, what is inferred through the non-apprehension of simultaneous objects as the internal organ — cognition is not a quality of that. Of what then? Of the knower (<s>jña</s>) — because of [its] sovereignty; the knower is the sovereign, the instrument is the governed. Or, if [cognition were] a quality of the instrument, the status of being an instrument would be negated. And since the knower who uses smell and the other [sense-organs] as instruments has cognition of smell and the rest, it is inferred — the knower who uses the internal organ as an instrument has cognition of pleasure and the like, and also memory. Therein, if the mind whose quality is cognition is the <s>ātman</s> (self), and if the internal organ that is the instrument of apprehending pleasure and the like is the mind — that is merely a difference in name, not a difference in meaning. And 'because of the non-apprehension of simultaneous objects' [applies to] one who is not a <s>yogin</s> — this is the meaning. For a <s>yogin</s> indeed, when supernatural powers have manifested, having the attribute of acting without instruments, having created other bodies with sense-organs, apprehends simultaneous objects in each of those [bodies]. And this is tenable for a knower that is all-pervading (<s>vibhu</s>), not for an atomic mind. Or, if the mind is all-pervading, there is no negation of cognition being a quality of the <s>ātman</s> — and if the mind is all-pervading and serves as the internal organ, then from its simultaneous conjunction with all sense-organs, simultaneous cognitions would arise. [End of NyS 3.2.19]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.20]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.20: Even if [cognition] is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>, the same [objection applies].
therefore the consequence of simultaneous cognitions arising [would follow]. [End of NyS 3.2.20]
The <s>ātman</s> is all-pervading and is conjoined with all sense-organs —
[Section: NySBh 3.2.21]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.21: Because of the absence of contact of the mind with the sense-organs, there is no arising of those [simultaneous cognitions].

Just as contact of the sense-organs with their objects is a cause for the apprehension of smell and the rest, so too the contact of the sense-organs with the mind is a cause [of cognition]; and the non-simultaneity of that [contact] — because of the atomicity of the mind — the non-simultaneity [of contact explains] the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions, even though [cognition] is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>. [End of NyS 3.2.21]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.22] But what if cognition of smell and the rest arises merely from the contact of the <s>ātman</s> with the sense-organs and objects? —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.22: Because no cause of origination is indicated.
That cognition of smell and the rest arises merely from the contact of the <s>ātman</s> with the sense-organs —
no cause of origination is indicated here by which
we would accept this. [End of NyS 3.2.22]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.23]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.23: And because the cause of destruction is not apprehended, if [cognition] persists, there would be the consequence of its eternality.

[End of NyS 3.2.34]

And this is the second refutation — for one whose body is stationary, because of the inherence of many cognitions, there would be simultaneous remembering of many objects at a single location. For a knower with a body stationed at some place, cognition, through the sequence of sense-object contacts, inheres in a single region of <s>ātman</s>. When <s>manas</s> is conjoined with that [region], simultaneous remembering of many previously known [objects] would follow — because of the absence of a succession of regional contacts. And because the regions of <s>ātman</s> are not different substances, there being no distinction in the inherence of a single object, the refutation of the simultaneity of memories is untenable. But in a series of sounds, just as hearing of sound [occurs] due to the proximity of the auditory organ's seat, so too, due to the proximity of <s>saṃskāra</s>, the arising of memory from <s>manas</s> [occurs], so there is no absurdity of simultaneous arising.

children.translated_text: Indeed, this [person] first knows — 'this is the means of my pleasure, this is the means of my pain.' Having known what is the means of one's own pleasure, one desires to obtain it; having known the means of pain, one desires to avoid it. For one who desires to obtain, the particular endeavor to acquire the means of pleasure is undertaking; for one impelled by the desire to avoid, the avoidance of the means of pain is cessation. Thus cognition, desire, effort, aversion, pleasure, and pain all belong to a single [entity]. There is a single agent of cognition, desire, and activity, and a common substrate. Therefore desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain are properties of the knower, not of something non-conscious. And because undertaking and cessation are observed in one's own inner self, inference regarding others is to be understood. [End of NyS 3.2.35]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.36]

Of those two — desire and aversion — restriction and non-restriction are the differentiators, the distinguishers. For a sentient being, activity and cessation caused by desire and aversion [occur] not in its own substrate, but rather in the substrate of what is impelled. There, activity and cessation in the elements being impelled do not [occur] in all — thus the tenability of non-restriction [is explained]. But for one who [maintains] that, because of the sentience of elements, construction and cessation caused by desire and aversion [occur] in their own substrate — for him there would be no restriction. Just as the activity of elements caused by other qualities, and the cessation due to the obstruction of qualities, invariably occurs in every element, so too activity and cessation caused by knowledge, desire, and aversion would invariably occur in their own substrate in every element — but this does not happen. Therefore, knowledge, desire-and-aversion, and effort reside in the impeller, while activity and cessation [reside] in the substrate of the impelled — this is established. The plurality of knowers in one body is without inferential support. For the proponent of elemental sentience, since there are many elements in one body possessing the qualities of knowledge, desire, aversion, and effort, the plurality of knowers

'Because of the apprehension of the same object by sight and touch [NyS 3.1.1]' — because such reasons for the ascertainment of the self are not refuted. The statement about the tenability of the reasons as stated is for the purpose of establishing [the self] by elimination and for the purpose of knowing the establishment of the topic. Or, 'and because of tenability' is itself another reason — this self is indeed eternal, because having practiced <s>dharma</s> (merit) in one body, after the dissolution of the body, one is born (<s>upapadyate</s>) among the gods in heaven; and having practiced <s>adharma</s> (demerit), after the dissolution of the body, one is born in the hells — this is birth (<s>upapatti</s>), characterized by the attainment of another body. That [birth], being possessed of a substrate, [occurs] when the entity exists and is eternal. But in the case of a mere continuum of cognitions without a self, being without a substrate, [birth] is not tenable. And <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) — the connection with multiple bodies based on one entity — is tenable; and <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), release from the continuum of bodies, is tenable. But in the case of a mere continuum of cognitions, because one entity is not tenable, no one traverses the long path, no one is released from the continuum of bodies — thus <s>saṃsāra</s> and <s>apavarga</s> are untenable. And in the case of a mere continuum of cognitions, because of the difference of entities, all these dealings pertaining to living beings would be unaccounted for, undifferentiated, and unsettled. Then because of the absence of memory — one does not remember what was seen by another — and memory indeed is the grasping by the same knower of what was previously known — 'I knew this object that is to be known.' children.translated_text: Attention (<s>praṇidhāna</s>) is the fixing of the mind with the desire to remember — the contemplation of the mark of what one desires to remember is the cause of the memory of the object (1). Association (<s>nibandha</s>) is indeed the binding together of objects — objects that are bound together become causes of each other's memory, in sequence or otherwise; or the placement of things to be remembered among known objects, made by the science of memory-retention, is association (2). Repetition (<s>abhyāsa</s>) is the recurrence of cognitions regarding the same object — the disposition (<s>saṃskāra</s>) born of repetition, which is a quality of the self, is denoted by the word 'repetition,' and that is the cause of memory of the same [object] (3). Inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is what is conjoined, what inheres, what co-inheres in the same object, and what is opposed — conjoined, for example: smoke of fire, horn of a cow, hand of a foot, form of touch, the non-existent of the existent (4). Characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>) — such as a particular feature of a family (<s>gotra</s>) is the cause of memory — 'this belongs to the <s>Vidā</s>s, this to the <s>Gargā</s>s' (5). Similarity (<s>sādṛśya</s>) — a likeness in a picture is [the cause of memory] of <s>Devadatta</s>, and so forth (6). From ownership (<s>parigraha</s>) — by property, the owner is remembered, or by the owner, the property is remembered (7). From the substrate (<s>āśraya</s>) — the village headman remembers what is dependent on him (8). From the dependent (<s>āśrita</s>) — by what is dependent, the headman is [remembered] (9). From relation (<s>saṃbandha</s>) — by a student, the connected teacher is remembered; by a priest, the sacrificer (10). From succession (<s>ānantarya</s>) — in objects to be learned in sequence (11). From separation (<s>viyoga</s>) — one who is separated from someone, experiencing the separation, intensely remembers [that person] (12). From common effect (<s>ekakārya</s>) — from seeing one agent, memory of another agent [arises] (13). From opposition (<s>virodha</s>) — of two who wish to conquer, from seeing one, the other is remembered (14). From excellence (<s>atiśaya</s>) — one by whom distinction was produced [is remembered] (15). From attainment (<s>prāpti</s>) — from whom or by whom something has been or is to be obtained, him one frequently remembers (16). From interposition (<s>vyavadhāna</s>) — by sheaths and the like, swords and such are remembered (17). From pleasure and pain — their cause is remembered (19). From desire and aversion — whom one desires or whom one hates, that one remembers (21). From fear — that from which one fears [is remembered] (22). From need (<s>arthitva</s>) — that which one needs, whether food or clothing (23). From action (<s>kriyā</s>) — by a chariot, the chariot-maker is remembered (24). From attachment (<s>rāga</s>) — the woman to whom one is attached, her one frequently remembers (25). From <s>dharma</s> (merit) — memory of other births, and here the retention of what has been studied and heard (26). From <s>adharma</s> (demerit) — one remembers means of suffering previously experienced (27). And since there are no simultaneous cognitions of these causes, there is no simultaneous memory. And this is [merely] an illustration of the causes of memory, not an exhaustive enumeration. [End of NyS 3.2.43]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.44]

Why? Because an impression born from cognition
is a different quality, the cause of memory — not the cognition [itself].

Because of the apprehension of action that does not persist — from the falling of a shot arrow, a continuum of action is grasped, and because cognitions are restricted to their objects, like the continuum of action, the tenability of a continuum of cognitions [follows]. And when a persisting [object] is grasped, perception ceases when [the object] is obstructed. And when a persisting pot is being grasped, cognition proceeds by way of a continuum until the obstruction. Therefore, when it is obstructed, perceptual knowledge ceases; but if cognition were to persist over an interval of time, even when the visible [object] is obstructed, perception should persist. And memory is not an indicator of the persistence of cognition — because an impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) born from cognition is the cause of memory. And should one think — cognition persists, for memory is seen regarding the object of cognition, and if cognition were non-persistent,
If [one objects:] it is unjustified because the reason is absent — if perception [holds] because cognition persists, then memory would be absent.
As long as
cognition persists, so long the object to be known is perceptual; and when [something is] perceptual,
memory is untenable. [End of NyS 3.2.44]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.45]

children.translated_text: the tenability of distinct and indistinct apprehension [is established]. And
this indistinct apprehension is not tenable due to the non-persistence of either cognition or the object to be known.
[End of NyS 3.2.46]

Where there is indistinct apprehension, there cognition arises and ceases — the distinction in apprehension is due to the distinction in the cause of apprehension, not due to the distinction in cognition. This distinction — that in some cases apprehension is indistinct and in others distinct — is due to the distinction in the cause of apprehension: where the cause of apprehension does not persist, there apprehension is indistinct; where it persists, there it is distinct — but not due to the persistence or non-persistence of cognition. Why? Because cognition is the apprehension of an object. That apprehension of the object — whether it is indistinct or distinct — that is cognition. And when specific [features] are not grasped, the grasping of the general is indistinct apprehension; in that case, cognition of another object does not arise, due to the absence of a cause. Where the property-bearer is grasped as possessing both common and specific properties — that is distinct apprehension. But where, when the specific is not grasped, there is merely the grasping of the general — that is indistinct apprehension. And because of the connection with common properties, connection with specific properties is a different object; the cognition that does not arise regarding that [different object] is due to the absence of a cause for apprehension, not due to the non-persistence of cognition. And apprehension, corresponding to its object, is always distinct — because cognitions are restricted to each object. The apprehension of the general regarding its own object is distinct, and the apprehension of the specific regarding its own object is distinct — for cognitions are restricted to each object. Thus, indistinct apprehension has been explained — in what domain would non-persistence of cognition produce it? But the tenability of distinct and indistinct apprehension with reference to the property-bearer is through the presence and absence of the difference of properties. For the property-bearer, i.e., the object, has both common and specific properties; regarding these, cognitions — restricted to each object — are multiple. If both [common and specific properties] are present in the property-bearer, then apprehension is distinct with reference to the property-bearer. But when there is merely the grasping of the general, then apprehension is indistinct. Thus, with reference to the property-bearer,

children.translated_text: And there is no doubt-free simultaneous arising of cognitions
by which the plurality of minds in a single body could be inferred.
[End of NyS 3.2.60]

Due to rapid movement, the existing succession in a whirling firebrand-circle is not grasped. Because the succession is not grasped, there arises the cognition of a circle due to the notion of continuity. Similarly, because of the rapid functioning of cognitions and actions, the existing succession is not grasped. Because the succession is not grasped, there arises the notion that actions occur simultaneously. But is the notion of simultaneous actions due to the non-grasping of succession? Or is the apprehension of multiple actions simultaneously due to actual simultaneity? No reason for a distinction is stated here. It has been said — cognitions of different sense-organs regarding different objects occur successively — and that cannot be refuted, because it is self-evident. Moreover, when one deliberates on things seen and heard, cognitions proceed in succession, not simultaneously — this should be inferred. The non-grasping of succession is due to the rapid functioning of cognitions of phonemes, words, sentences, and their meanings. How? When phonemes in a sentence are being uttered, there is hearing of each phoneme. Having heard one or more phonemes, one connects them as a word. Having connected, one determines the word. By determining the word, one apprehends the meaning of the word through memory. And from the connection of a group of words, one determines the sentence. And having grasped the connected word-meanings, one apprehends the sentence-meaning. And the succession of these cognitions, which proceed in order, is not grasped due to their rapid functioning. This is the inference against the notion of simultaneity of cognitions and actions.
[Section: NySBh 3.2.61]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.61: And [the mind is] atomic, because of the aforementioned reason.

The continuity of that fruit is its persistence as inherent in the self. From elements impelled by that, there is the production of that body, not from independent [elements]. That in which this self is established, thinking 'this is I,' where it is engaged, where it experiences objects through the thirst for enjoyment, and where it generates <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — that is its body. na

children.translated_text: And this [process] is not possible for food and drink placed in a pot and the like.
For this reason, it is understood that the body is caused by <s>karma</s>.
[End of NyS 3.2.66]

'Because it is the cause of production' — this is what is presupposed. Food that is eaten and drunk — the nutrient substance produced by its digestion accumulates in the mother's body. When the seed is in the womb, the accumulation in the seed is of the same digestion as the mother's, until the accumulation is sufficient for the formation [of the body]. And the accumulated [substance] is organized into the form of embryo, flesh-mass, lump, along with tendons, head, hands, and the rest, with the division of sense-organ seats. And in the formed [body], nutrient substance conveyed through the umbilical cord accumulates until [the fetus is] ready for birth.
[Section: NySBh 3.2.67]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.67: And because there is no fixed rule when contact [of parents] occurs.

children.text:
na sarvo dampatyoḥ saṃyogo garbhādhānaheturdṛśyate.
tatrāsati karmaṇi na bhavati sati ca bhavatītyupapanno
niyamābhāva iti|

children.translated_text: If elements independent of <s>karma</s>
were the causes of body-production, there would be a fixed rule —
for there would be no absence of the cause here. [End of NyS 3.2.67]

Not every union of a married couple is observed to be the cause of conception. When <s>karma</s> is absent, it does not occur; when it is present, it occurs — thus the absence of a fixed rule is tenable.
[Section: NySBh 3.2.68]
And furthermore —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.68: <s>Karma</s> is the cause of the production of the conjunction [of self and body], just as it is the cause of body-production.

children.translated_text: The establishment [of the body] for each individual self —
that we call the conjunction of the body with the self.
[End of NyS 3.2.68]

Just as this body — composed of channels (<s>nāḍīs</s>) carrying vital fluids and <s>prāṇa</s>, bodily constituents ending with semen, sinews, skin, bones, veins, muscles, embryonic membranes, tendons, and [limbs such as] head, arms, abdomen, and thighs, and the internal [organs] — bile, phlegm, and wind — and the passages of mouth, throat, heart, stomach, intestines, and lower outlets — is organized with an arrangement that produces extreme suffering and cannot be produced by earth and the rest without dependence on <s>karma</s> — therefore, body-production is understood to be caused by <s>karma</s>. And thus, because of the absence of a cause specific to each individual self, because of the connection with selves that have no [inherent] distinction, and because of the absence of a cause for distinction in earth and the rest which are common to all selves — the same body should result for all selves. But what is established for each individual self — there, <s>karma</s> as the cause of body-production is understood as the cause of the arrangement. For the store of <s>karma</s> (<s>karmāśaya</s>) specific to each individual self, ripening in the self in which it exists, produces and establishes the body as the seat of experience for that self alone. Thus, just as <s>karma</s> is the cause of body-production, so too is it understood as the cause of the production of the conjunction [of self and body].
[Section: NySBh 3.2.69]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.69: By this, the [question of] fixed rule is answered.

// 69 //
children.translated_text: What is called 'the fixed rule when body-production is without <s>karma</s> as cause' — this is answered by '<s>karma</s> is the cause of the production of the conjunction, just as it is the cause of body-production [NyS 3.2.68].' What then is this fixed rule? That all selves should have a body just like one self — this is the fixed rule. That one has it one way and another differently — this is the absence of fixed rule, that is, differentiation, that is, distinction. And differentiation of birth is observed — one of noble birth and one of low birth; one praiseworthy and one censured; one prone to disease and one healthy; one complete and one impaired; one prone to suffering and one prone to happiness; one endowed with marks of personal excellence and one the opposite; one with praiseworthy marks and one with censured marks; one with sharp sense-organs and one with dull sense-organs. And the subtle differentiation is immeasurable. This differentiation of birth is tenable because of the differentiation of <s>karma</s> specific to each self. In the absence of <s>karma</s>-differentiation specific to each self, because of the non-distinction of selves and the sameness of earth and the rest, and because of the absence of a cause for distinction in earth and the rest — everything would result for all selves [equally]. But this birth is not of such a [uniform] kind. Therefore, body-production is not without <s>karma</s> as its cause. [End of NyS 3.2.69]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.70]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.70: And the separation from that [body] is tenable, because of the tenability of the exhaustion of <s>karma</s>.

// 70 //
children.translated_text: When body-production is caused by <s>karma</s>, the separation of the self from that body is tenable. Why? Because of the tenability of the exhaustion of <s>karma</s>. For the exhaustion of <s>karma</s> is tenable through right knowledge (<s>samyagdarśana</s>). When delusion is destroyed, one who is free from attachment does not perform <s>karma</s> that causes rebirth through body, speech, and mind — thus there is no further accumulation. And through experiencing the ripening of what was previously accumulated, there is exhaustion. Thus, because of the absence of a cause of rebirth, when this body falls, there is no production of another body, and hence no reconnection [with a new birth]. But if body-production is without <s>karma</s> as cause, because of the impossibility of the destruction of elements, the separation from that [body] would be impossible. [End of NyS 3.2.70]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.71]

<s>NyS</s> 3.2.71: If [one says] 'that [body-production] is caused by the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>),' [we reply:] then there would again be the undesirable consequence of that [i.e., rebirth] and [no] cessation.

children.translated_text: and that non-arising of seeing upon the cessation of the body in liberation — which constitutes 'non-seeing' —
there is no specific difference between these two [types of] non-seeing; therefore, because non-seeing does not cease in liberation,
the recurrence of the body's origination would follow.

Non-seeing is indeed called the 'unseen' (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>). The origination of the body from the elements is brought about by the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>). When the body has not yet arisen, the seer, without a basis, never sees the visible. And that visible [object] of his is twofold — the object and the distinction between the unmanifest and the self. The creation of the body is for that purpose. When that [purpose] has been accomplished, the elements, having served their purpose, do not produce a body — thus the separation from the body is justified. If you think so? [Then] in liberation (<s>apavarga</s>), there would be the recurrence of that [embodiment]. The origination of the body would recur again. That non-arising of seeing when the body has not arisen — which is considered as 'non-seeing' —

// 71 //
children.translated_text: The specific difference is that the elements, having served their purpose with the cessation of seeing, do not undertake another body. If this is said? No — because activity is observed in both doing and not-doing. The repeated origination of the body by the elements that have served their purpose is observed — because of their bringing about the apprehension of objects. The purposeless origination of the body is repeatedly observed — because the seeing of the distinction between <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) and <s>puruṣa</s> (self) does not take place. Therefore, when the creation of beings is not caused by <s>karma</s> (action), the origination of the body for the purpose of seeing is not justified. But the origination of the body for the purpose of seeing is justified when creation is caused by <s>karma</s>. Seeing means the experience of the fruits of <s>karma</s> — and some hold that this is caused by the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>). The unseen is a specific quality of atoms, a cause of activity; impelled by it, atoms coalesce and produce the body. And that [<s>adṛṣṭa</s>] enters the mind, impelled by its own quality, the unseen. When there is a body endowed with mind, the seer has apprehension. And in this view, because of the non-destruction of the quality, the recurrence of that [embodiment follows] — in liberation, in liberation, the body arises — because the unseen quality of atoms is not annihilated. [End of NyS 3.2.71]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.72]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.72: And because of the mind's [connection with the body being] caused by <s>karma</s>, the conjunction is not annihilated.

children.translated_text: And if this were so, a single unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>)
would be the cause of both living and dying — this would follow,
and this is untenable. [End of NyS 3.2.72]

When the mind has been made to enter [the body] by the unseen, which is a quality of the mind, the severance of conjunction would not occur. Then what causes the mind's departure from the body? Upon the exhaustion of a store of <s>karma</s>, the departure [of the mind] is justified because of a different store of <s>karma</s> ripening. If one says the departure is also due to the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) — the same unseen that is the cause of the mind's approach to the body would also be the cause of departure — no, because it is untenable that a single thing is the cause of both living and dying.
[Section: NySBh 3.2.73]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.73: And the consequence of eternality [of the body], because death (<s>prāyaṇa</s>) would be untenable.

children.text:
vipākasaṃvedanāt karmāśayakṣaye śarīrapātaḥ
prāyaṇam. karmāśayāntarācca punarjanma|
bhūtamātrāttu karmanirapekṣāt śarīrotpattau kasya kṣayāt śarīrapātaḥ |

children.translated_text: Death — thus, because death is untenable,
we understand the consequence of eternality [of the body]. And if death were accidental,
the differentiation of deaths would be untenable. [End of NyS 3.2.73]

Death (<s>prāyaṇa</s>) is the fall of the body upon the exhaustion of the store of <s>karma</s> through the experience of its fruits. And rebirth is from another store of <s>karma</s>. But if the origination of the body is merely from the elements, independent of <s>karma</s>, from whose exhaustion would the body fall?
[Section: NySBh 3.2.74]
Wishing to establish 'the recurrence of that [embodiment] in liberation [NyS 3.2.71],' [the opponent] says —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.74: This would be like the eternality of blackness in an atom.
Just as the blackness of an atom, being eternal, when obstructed by conjunction with fire,
does not arise again — so too the body brought about by the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>)
does not arise again in liberation. [End of NyS 3.2.74]
[Section: NySBh 3.2.75]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.75: No, because of the consequence of obtaining what was not done.

children.translated_text: and because of the manifold and uniform nature of actions, the differentiation of pleasure and pain is justified.
This observed differentiation of pleasure and pain, in the absence of a differentiation of causes,
would not exist — and this is the contradiction with perception.

This example is not [valid]. Why? Because of the consequence of <s>akṛtābhyāgama</s> (obtaining what was not done). What is 'not done' — that which is not established by any <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge). Its acceptance and determination — this must be accepted by one who has faith [in it] as something not established by <s>pramāṇa</s>. Therefore this example is not [valid] — neither perception nor inference is cited [in support]. And this is said to be the defect of the example being equal to the thesis to be proved. Alternatively — no, because of the consequence of obtaining what was not done. For one who, by the example of the blackness of an atom, establishes the origination of the body as not caused by <s>karma</s>, there would follow the consequence of <s>akṛtābhyāgama</s> — that pleasure and pain would accrue to a person without the <s>karma</s> that is the cause of pleasure and pain. 'Yes' — [but] this contradicts perception, inference, and scripture in many respects. First, the contradiction with perception — this pleasure and pain, being directly experienced by each self, is perceptible to all embodied beings. What is the differentiation? Intense, mild, long-lasting, swift, of many kinds, of one kind — such and similar specific differences. And there is no specific cause of pleasure and pain that is fixed for each self; and where there is no specific difference of cause, no specific difference of result is observed. But when pleasure and pain are connected with <s>karma</s>, because of the intensity and mildness of actions, and because of the increase and decrease in the accumulations of <s>karma</s>,

itiviruddhyate, seyaṃ pāpiṣṭhānāṃ

children.translated_text: false view (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>) — 'the creation of the body is not caused by <s>karma</s>;
the connection with pleasure and pain is not caused by <s>karma</s>.'
[End of NyS 3.2.75]

Similarly, the contradiction with inference — for it is observed that from the arrangement of qualities in a person, the arrangement of pleasure and pain [follows]. That conscious being who, having understood that pleasure is to be accomplished by certain means, desires it and strives for the attainment of those means — he is endowed with pleasure, not the reverse. And that [conscious being] who, having understood that pain is to be produced by certain means, wishes to avoid it and strives for the avoidance of those means — he is abandoned by pain, not the reverse. And this arrangement of pleasure and pain for conscious beings does not exist without effort; therefore it must be inferred that it is brought about by the arrangement of another quality of conscious beings. This is contradicted when pleasure and pain are not connected with <s>karma</s>. And that other quality, being not directly experienced, is the 'unseen' (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), and because the time of its ripening is not fixed, it is indeterminate. But cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) and the like are directly experienced and lead to liberation. Now, the contradiction with scripture (<s>āgama</s>) — much indeed is this spoken by the <s>Ṛṣis</s> (sages). The body of the teachings of the sages is based on performance and avoidance. And the fruit of these teachings is the activity characterized by performance according to the division of <s>varṇas</s> (classes) and <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life), and the cessation characterized by avoidance, for all embodied beings. And both of these, in this [opposing] view — 'there is no good or bad <s>karma</s>; the connection of persons with pleasure and pain is not caused by <s>karma</s>' — are contradicted. This is the wicked
Thus ends the second section of the third chapter in the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> of <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
And the third chapter is concluded.
Now begins the first section of the fourth chapter of the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> with commentary.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.1]

children.text: manaso 'nantaraṃ pravṛttiḥ parīkṣitavyā, tatra khalu yāvad dharmādharmāśrayaśarīrādi parīkṣitaṃ sarvā sā pravṛtteḥ parīkṣetyāha---
children.translated_text: After the mind, activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>) is to be examined. Therein, since everything related to the body and the rest, which is the substrate of <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), has been examined — all that is the examination of activity — [the sūtra] says:
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.1: Activity is as stated.
It has been thus examined. [End of NyS 4.1.1]
If activity has [already been examined], then let the defects (<s>doṣas</s>) be examined next — therefore [the sūtra] says:
[Section: NySBh 4.1.2]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.2: Likewise the defects (<s>doṣas</s>).

children.text: parīkṣitā iti, buddhisamānāśrayatvādātmaguṇāḥ. pravṛttihetutvāt punarbhavapratisaṃdhānasāmarthyācca saṃsārahetavaḥ. saṃsārasyānāditvādanādinā prabandhena pravartante|
children.translated_text: [They have been] examined — because they share the same substrate as cognition, they are qualities of the <s>ātman</s> (self). Because they are causes of activity and because of their capacity to connect one with further existence, they are causes of <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of rebirth). Because <s>saṃsāra</s> is beginningless, they operate in a beginningless series.

The cessation of false knowledge arises from true knowledge (<s>tattvajñāna</s>); upon the cessation of that [false knowledge], with the severing of the series of attachment and aversion, there is liberation (<s>apavarga</s>).
That they have the nature of manifestation and concealment — and so forth has been stated about the defects. [End of NyS 4.1.2]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.3]

children.text:
"pravartanālakṣaṇā doṣāḥ 1-1-18"
ityuktaṃ tathā ceme mānerṣyāsūyāvicikitsāmatsarādayaḥ te kasmānnopasaṃkhyāyante ? ityata āha---
children.translated_text: It has been said that 'defects are characterized by impelling [NyS 1.1.18].' Then why are pride, jealousy, envy, suspicion, conceit, and the like not additionally enumerated? Therefore [the sūtra] says:
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.3: Their grouping into three [is] because attachment (<s>rāga</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>) are of distinct natures.

children.text:
teṣāṃ doṣāṇāṃ trayo rāśayaḥ |
trayaḥ pakṣāḥ-- rāgapakṣaḥ-- kāmo matsaraḥ spṛhā tṛṣṇā lobha iti. dveṣapakṣaḥ-- krodha īrṣyāsūyā droho 'marṣa iti, mohapakṣaḥ-- mithyājñānaṃ vicikitsā mānaḥ pramāda iti. trairāśyānnopasaṃkhyāyante iti|
lakṣaṇasya tarhy abhedāt tritvamanupapannam ?. nānupapannam-- rāgadveṣamohārthāntarabhāvāt |
children.translated_text: But because there is no difference in the definition, the threefold [division] would be unjustified? No, it is not unjustified — because attachment, aversion, and delusion are of distinct natures.

children.text: āsaktilakṣaṇo rāgaḥ. amarṣalakṣaṇo dveṣaḥ. mithyāpratipattilakṣaṇo moha iti, etat pratayātmavedanīyaṃ sarvaśarīriṇām |
children.translated_text: Attachment is characterized by clinging. Aversion is characterized by intolerance. Delusion is characterized by false apprehension — this is directly experienced by each self, for all embodied beings.

children.text: vijānātyayaṃ śarīrī rāgamutpannam-- 'asti me 'dhyātmaṃ rāgadharmaḥ' iti, virāgaṃ ca vijānāti-- 'nāsti me 'dhyātmaṃ rāgadharmaḥ' iti. evamitarayorapīti|
children.translated_text: This embodied being recognizes attachment when it has arisen — 'There is the nature of attachment within me' — and recognizes dispassion — 'There is no nature of attachment within me.' Similarly for the other two also.
But pride, jealousy, envy, and the rest have fallen within the threefold grouping and therefore are not additionally enumerated. [End of NyS 4.1.3]

Of those defects there are three groups, three classes — the class of attachment: desire, envy, craving, thirst, greed. The class of aversion: anger, jealousy, spite, malice, intolerance. The class of delusion: false knowledge, suspicion, pride, negligence. Because of the three groups, they are not additionally enumerated.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.4]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.4: Not [so], because they have a single antidote.
True knowledge (<s>tattvajñāna</s>),
right understanding (<s>samyaṅmati</s>),
noble wisdom (<s>āryaprajñā</s>),
awakening (<s>saṃbodha</s>) — this single [thing] is the antidote of [all] three. [End of NyS 4.1.4]
Attachment and the rest are not of distinct natures. Why? Because they have a single antidote.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.5]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.5: Because of deviation, it is not a [valid] reason.

children.text: ekapratyanīkāḥ pṛthivyāṃ śyāmādayo 'gnisaṃyogenaikena. ekayonayaśca pākajā iti // 5 //
children.translated_text: Things having a single antidote [can still be distinct] — blackness and the like in earth [are destroyed] by conjunction with a single fire. And heat-produced [qualities] are of a single origin. [End of NyS 4.1.5]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.6]
And if they are indeed of distinct natures —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.6: Among them, delusion (<s>moha</s>) is the worst, because the other two do not arise for one who is not deluded.

children.text:
mohaḥ pāpaḥ pāpataro vā dvāvabhipretyoktam, kasmāt ?. nāmūḍhasyetarotpatteḥ |
amūḍhasya rāgadveṣau notpadyete, mūḍhasya tu yathāsaṃkalpamutpattiḥ |

viṣayeṣu rañjanīyāḥ saṃkalpā rāgahetavaḥ kopanīyāḥ saṃkalpā dveṣahetavaḥ ubhaye ca saṃkalpā na mithyāpratipattilakṣaṇatvād mohādanye, tāvimau mohayonī rāgadveṣāviti, tattvajñānācca mohanivṛttau rāgadveṣānutpattirityekapratyanīkabhāvopapattiḥ, evaṃ ca kṛtvā tattvajñānāt"
children.translated_text: Among objects, the conceptions that produce delight are causes of attachment; the conceptions that produce anger are causes of aversion; and both types of conceptions are not other than delusion, because they are characterized by false apprehension. Thus these two — attachment and aversion — originate from delusion. And upon the cessation of delusion through true knowledge (<s>tattvajñāna</s>), the non-arising of attachment and aversion [follows] — thus the justification of a single antidote [is established]. And having done so, from true knowledge,
'through the successive removal of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there is liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) [NyS 1.1.2]'
— this has been explained. [End of NyS 4.1.6]

Delusion is bad or worse than the others — this is said with reference to both [interpretations]. Why? Because the other two do not arise for one who is not deluded. For one who is not deluded, attachment and aversion do not arise; but for one who is deluded, they arise according to [his] conceptions.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.7]
Then it follows —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.7: Because of the relation of cause and effect, [delusion] is of a distinct nature from the [other] defects.

children.text: anyaddhi nimittam anyacca naimittakamiti doṣanimittatvādadoṣo moha iti // 7 //
children.translated_text: For the cause is one thing and the effect is another — therefore, since the defects are the effect and delusion is their cause, delusion is not a defect [in the same category]. [End of NyS 4.1.7]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.8]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.8: No, because of the inclusion within the definition of defect.
— by this definition of <s>doṣa</s>, delusion (<s>moha</s>) is included among the faults. [End of NyS 4.1.8]
'Activity is the defining characteristic of <s>doṣa</s> (fault) [NyS 1.1.18]'
[Section: NySBh 4.1.9]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.9: And because of the tenability of the cause-and-effect relation, there is no preclusion of those of the same class.

children.text: dravyāṇāṃ guṇānāṃ vānekavidhavikalpo nimittanaimittakabhāvo tulyajātīyānāṃ dṛṣṭa iti // 9 //
children.translated_text: The manifold varieties of substances and qualities — the cause-and-effect relation among those of the same class is observed. [End of NyS 4.1.9]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.10]

children.text:
doṣānantaraṃ pretyabhāvaḥ, tasyāsiddhiḥ-- ātmano nityatvāt |
na khalu nityaṃ kiñcit jāyate mriyate vā iti. janmamaraṇayornityatvādātmano 'nupapattiḥ ubhayaṃ ca pretyabhāva iti / tatrāyaṃ siddhānuvādaḥ---
children.translated_text: After the faults [comes] rebirth (<s>pretyabhāva</s>). Its non-establishment [is objected] — because of the eternality of the self. Nothing eternal is ever born or dies. Because of the eternality of the self, birth and death are untenable; and both [birth and death] constitute rebirth. Regarding this, the following is a restatement of the established [position] —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.10: When the self is eternal, rebirth is established.

children.text:
nityoyamātmā praiti |
pūrvaśarīraṃ jahāti |
mriyate iti. pretya ca |
pūrvaśarīraṃ hitvā bhavati |

children.translated_text: it is born —
it assumes another body. And both of these —

children.text: punarutpattiḥ pretyabhāva iti. taccaitat nityatve saṃbhavatīti|
children.translated_text: re-birth — constitute rebirth (<s>pretyabhāva</s>). And this is possible [only] when [the self] is eternal.

children.text: yasya tu sattvotpādaḥ sattvanirodhaḥ pretyabhāvastasya kṛtahānamakṛtābhyāgamaśca doṣaḥ, ucchedahetuvāde ṛṣyupadeśāścānarthakā iti // 10 //
children.translated_text: But for one whose [view of] rebirth is the arising and cessation of an entity, there is the fault of loss of what has been done and the approach of what has not been done; and in the doctrine of annihilation, the teachings of the sages would be purposeless. [End of NyS 4.1.10]
This self is eternal and departs — it leaves the former body — it dies. And after departing — having left the former body, it comes into being —
[Section: NySBh 4.1.11]
If [one asks] how does birth [occur]?
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.11: Because of the perceptual validity of [the origin of] manifest [things] from the manifest.

children.text:
kena prakāreṇa kindharmakāt kāraṇād vyaktaṃ śarīramutpadyate iti ?, vyaktāt |
bhūtasamākhyātāt pṛthivyāditaḥ paramasūkṣmād nityāt vyaktam |
śarīrendriyaviṣayopakaraṇādhāraṃ prajñātaṃ dravyamutpadyate, vyaktaṃ ca khalvindriyagrāhyaṃ tatsāmānyāt kāraṇamapi vyaktam|

children.translated_text: What is the analogy? The possession of qualities such as form and the rest.

children.text: rūpādiguṇayuktebhyaḥ pṛthivyādibhyo nityebhyo rūpādiguṇayuktaṃ śarīrādi utpadyate-- pratyakṣaprāmāṇyāt |
children.translated_text: From earth and the rest, which are eternal and possess qualities such as form, body and the rest possessing qualities such as form arise — because of perceptual validity.

children.text: dṛṣṭo hi rūpādiguṇayuktebhyo mṛtprabhṛtibhyastathābhūtasya dravyasyotpādaḥ tena cādṛṣṭasyānumānamiti |
children.translated_text: For the arising of such a substance from [things] such as clay possessing qualities such as form is observed; and by that, inference of the unobserved [is established].

children.text: rūpādīnāmanvayadarśanāt prakṛtivikārayoḥ pṛthivyādīnāṃ nityānāmatīndriyāṇāṃ kāraṇabhāvo 'numīyate iti // 11 //
children.translated_text: From the observation of the continuity of form and the rest in the material cause and its transformation, the causal nature of earth and the rest — which are eternal and beyond the senses — is inferred. [End of NyS 4.1.11]

By what process, from what kind of cause does the manifest body arise? From the manifest — from what is designated as an element (<s>bhūta</s>), from earth and the rest, from what is supremely subtle and eternal, manifest — a substance known as the substrate of body, sense-organs, objects, and instruments arises. And since what is manifest is indeed graspable by the sense-organs, by analogy the cause too is manifest.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.12]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.12: Because a pot is not produced from [another] pot.

children.text: idamapi pratyakṣam-- na khalu vyaktād ghaṭād vyakto ghaṭa utpadyamāno dṛśyate iti. vyaktād vyaktasyānutpattidarśanānna vyaktaṃ kāraṇamiti // 12 //
children.translated_text: This too is perceptual — a manifest pot is not observed being produced from a manifest pot. Because of the observation that the manifest is not produced from the manifest, the manifest is not the cause. [End of NyS 4.1.12]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.13]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.13: There is no preclusion of the production of a pot from the manifest.

children.text: na brūmaḥ sarvaṃ sarvasya kāraṇamiti kiṃ tu yadutpadyate vyaktaṃ dravyaṃ tat tathābhūtādevotpadyate iti, vyaktaṃ ca tad mṛddravyaṃ kapālasaṃjñakaṃ yato ghaṭa utpadyate na caitad nihnuvānaḥ kvacidabhyanujñāṃ labdhumarhatīti|

children.translated_text: This is the truth of the matter. [End of NyS 4.1.13]

We do not say that everything is the cause of everything; rather, whatever manifest substance is produced, that is produced from [a cause] of the same nature. And that manifest clay-substance called a potsherd, from which the pot is produced — one who denies this is not entitled to gain acceptance anywhere.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.14]
Hereafter, the views of the debaters are presented —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.14: [The thesis:] Being arises from non-being — because of emergence through destruction.

children.text: asataḥ sadutpadyate ityayaṃ pakṣaḥ, kasmāt ?, upamṛdya prādurbhāvāt |
children.translated_text: The existent arises from the non-existent — this is the thesis. Why? Because of emergence through destruction.

children.text: upamṛdya bījamaṅkura utpadyate nānupamṛdya, na ced bījopamarde 'ṅkurakāraṇam ? anupamardepi bījasyāṅkurotpattiḥ syāditi // 14 //
children.translated_text: The sprout arises by destroying the seed, not without destroying [it]. If the destruction of the seed were not the cause of the sprout, then the sprout should arise even without the destruction of the seed. [End of NyS 4.1.14]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.15]
To this it is replied —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.15: Because of self-contradiction, [this] reasoning is inapplicable.
'Because of emergence through destruction' — this reasoning is unjustified, because of self-contradiction.

children.text: yadupamṛdnāti na tadupamṛdya prādurbhavitumarhati-- vidyamānatvāt. yacca prādurbhavati na tenāprādurbhūtena |
children.translated_text: What destroys cannot, after destroying, come into being — because it [already] exists. And what comes into being — by that, which has not [yet] come into being,
which is non-existent, destruction [cannot be effected]. [End of NyS 4.1.15]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.16]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.16: Because of the usage of causal terms for the past and the future, [it is] not [so].

children.text: atīti cānāgate cāvidyamāne kārakaśabdaḥ prayujyante-- putro janiṣyate janiṣyamāṇaṃ putramabhinandati, putrasya janiṣyamāṇasya nāma karoti, abhūt kumbho bhinnaṃ kumbhamanuśocati-- bhinnasya kumbhasya kapālāni, ajātāḥ putrāḥ pitaraṃ tāpayanti iti bahulaṃ bhāktāḥ prayogā dṛśyante|
children.translated_text: Regarding the past and the future, which are non-existent, causal terms are used — 'a son will be born,' one rejoices at the son who will be born; one names the son who will be born; 'the pot existed,' one grieves over the broken pot — the potsherds of the broken pot; 'unborn sons torment the father' — thus many figurative usages are seen.
But what is this figurativeness? Figurativeness based on succession.
By the force of succession, [it has] the meaning of emergence through destruction.
The sprout that is about to emerge will destroy [the seed] — thus the agency is figurative. [End of NyS 4.1.16]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.17] <s>NyS</s> 4.1.17: Because there is no production from what has been destroyed, [it is] not [so].

children.text: na vinaṣṭād bījādaṅkura utpadyate iti tasmānnābhāvād bhāvotpattiriti // 17 //
children.translated_text: The sprout is not produced from a destroyed seed; therefore being does not arise from non-being. [End of NyS 4.1.17]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.18]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.18: Because of the indication of sequence, there is no preclusion.

children.text: uṣamardaprādurbhāvayoḥ paurvāparyaniyamaḥ kramaḥ sa khalvabhāvād bhāvotpatterheturnirdiśyate sa ca na pratiṣidhyate iti //
children.translated_text: The fixed order of priority between destruction and emergence is the sequence — that is indeed indicated as the reason for the arising of being from non-being, and that is not refuted.
When the previous arrangement of the parts whose arrangement has been disrupted ceases, the production of a substance from a different arrangement [occurs] — not from non-being.

children.text: bījāvayavāḥ kutaścinnimittāt prādurbhūtākriyāḥ pūrvavyūhaṃ jahati vyūhāntaraṃ cāpadyante vyūhāntarādaṅkura utpadyate-- dṛśyante khalu avayavāstatsaṃyogāścāṅkurotpattihetavaḥ, na cānivṛtte pūrvavyūhe bījāvayavānāṃ śakyaṃ vyūhāntareṇa bhavitumiti upamardaprādurbhāvayoḥ paurvāparyaniyamaḥ kramaḥ tasmānnābhāvād bhāvotpattiriti, na cānyad bījāvayavebhyo 'ṅkurotpattikāraṇamityupapadyate bījopādānaniyama iti // 18 //
children.translated_text: The parts of the seed, having activities that have arisen from some cause, abandon the previous arrangement and assume a different arrangement; from the different arrangement the sprout is produced — for the parts and their conjunctions are observed as the causes of the production of the sprout. And it is not possible for the parts of the seed to have a different arrangement without the cessation of the previous arrangement — thus the fixed order of priority between destruction and emergence is the sequence. Therefore, being does not arise from non-being. And no other cause of the production of the sprout besides the parts of the seed is tenable — thus the restriction to the seed as the material cause [is established]. [End of NyS 4.1.18]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.19] Now another says —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.19: <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is the cause — because of the observation that human action does not [always] bear fruit.

children.text: puruṣoyaṃ samīhamāno nāvaśyaṃ samīhāphalaṃ prāpnoti tenānumīyate-- parādhīnāṃ puruṣasya karmaphalārādhanamiti. yadadhīnaṃ sa īśvaraḥ tasmādīśvaraḥ kāraṇamiti // 19 //
children.translated_text: This person, striving, does not necessarily obtain the fruit of his striving; thereby it is inferred — the attainment of the fruit of human action is dependent on another. That on which [it is] dependent is <s>Īśvara</s>; therefore <s>Īśvara</s> is the cause. [End of NyS 4.1.19]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.20]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.20: Because without human action, fruit is not produced, [it is] not [so].

children.text: īśvarādhīnā cet phalaniṣpattiḥ syād api tarhi puruṣasya samīhāmantareṇa phalaṃ niṣpadyeteti // 20 //
children.translated_text: If the production of fruit were dependent on <s>Īśvara</s>, then fruit should be produced even without the person's striving. [End of NyS 4.1.20]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.21]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.21: Because [fruit] is caused by that [human action], [this objection] is not a valid reason.

children.text:
puruṣakāramīśvaro 'nugṛhṇāti |
phalāya puruṣasya yatamānasyeśvaraḥ phalaṃ saṃpādayatīti. yadā na saṃpādayati tadā puruṣakarmāphalaṃ bhavatīti. tasmād īśvarakāritatvād ahetuḥ--
"puruṣakarmābhāve phalāniṣpatteḥ" iti|
guṇaviśiṣṭamātmāntaramīśvaraḥ tasyātmakalpāt
kalpāntarānupapattiḥ, adharmamithyājñānapramādahānyā
dharmajñānasamādhisaṃpadā ca viśiṣṭamātmāntaramīśvaraḥ
tasya ca dharmasamādhiphalam aṇimādyaṣṭavidhamaiśvaryam,
saṃkalpānuvidhāyī cāsya dharmaḥ pratyātmavṛttīn
dharmādharmasaṃcayān pṛthivyādīni ca bhūtāni
pravartayati, evaṃ ca svakṛtābhyāgamasyālopena
nirmāṇaprākāmbhamīśvarasya svakṛtakarmaphalaṃ veditavyam|
āptakalpaścāyam uyathā pitāpatyānāṃ tathā pitṛbhūta īśvaro
bhūtānām, na cātmakalpādanyaḥ kalpaḥ saṃbhavati |
na tāvadasya buddhiṃ vinā kaścid dharmo liṅgabhūtaḥ
śakya upapādayitum. āgamācca draṣṭā boddhā
sarvajñātā īśvara iti |
buddhyādibhiścātmaliṅgairnirupākhyamīśvaraṃ
pratyakṣānumānāgamaviṣayātītaṃ kaḥ rakta upapādayitum |

children.translated_text: And for this one who operates without violation of [the principle of receiving the fruit of] one's own actions,
whatever collection of objections has been stated regarding the creation of the body without [personal] action —
all of that would follow. [End of NyS 4.1.21]

<s>Īśvara</s> favors human effort — for a person who strives toward a fruit, <s>Īśvara</s> brings about the fruit. When he does not bring it about, then human action becomes fruitless. Therefore, because [it is] caused by <s>Īśvara</s>, [the objection] is not a valid reason — 'because without human action, fruit is not produced.' <s>Īśvara</s> is another self distinguished by [particular] qualities; the impossibility of any other nature than that of a self [applies to him]. Distinguished by the absence of <s>adharma</s> (demerit), false knowledge, negligence, and lassitude, and by the possession of <s>dharma</s> (merit), knowledge, and <s>samādhi</s> (concentration) — [such] another self is <s>Īśvara</s>. And the eightfold sovereignty beginning with <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness) is the fruit of his <s>dharma</s> and <s>samādhi</s>. And his <s>dharma</s>, which conforms to his will, sets in motion the individual courses of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, and the elements beginning with earth. And thus, without violation of [the principle of] the approach of what has been done by oneself, the fruit of <s>Īśvara</s>'s own <s>karma</s> — his creative activity — is to be understood. And he is like a trustworthy authority (<s>āpta</s>) — just as a father [is] to his children, so <s>Īśvara</s>, having become like a father, [is] to beings. And no nature other than that of a self is possible [for him]. Indeed, no property that serves as a mark [of his existence] can be established without [accepting] his cognition. And from scripture — <s>Īśvara</s> is the seer, the knower, the omniscient. But who is capable of establishing an <s>Īśvara</s> who is without designation, beyond the scope of perception, inference, and scripture, [solely] through the marks of the self such as cognition and the rest?
[Section: NySBh 4.1.22]
Now another says —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.22: Being arises without a cause — because of the observation of the sharpness of thorns and the like.
because of the observation of the sharpness of thorns and the like — the sharpness of thorns, the variegation of mountain minerals,
the smoothness of stones. And causeless origination is observed;
similarly the creation of the body also. [End of NyS 4.1.22]
The arising of the body and the rest is without cause —
[Section: NySBh 4.1.23]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.23: Because of the causality of what is [claimed to be] without a cause, not from [what is] without a cause.

children.text: ityucyate. yataścotpadyate tannimittam, animittasya nimittatvād nānimittā bhāvotpattiriti // 23 //
children.translated_text: — it is said. But that from which [something] arises is the cause; because of the causality of what is [claimed to be] without a cause, the arising of being is not without a cause. [End of NyS 4.1.23]
'Being arises without a cause'
[Section: NySBh 4.1.24]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.24: Because of the difference between cause and non-cause, there is no preclusion.
For the cause is one thing, and the denial of a cause is another.
And the denial itself is not what is denied — just as 'a waterless
water-pot' — the negation of water does not become water.
This argument — 'the creation of the body and the rest is without <s>karma</s> as cause' —
does not differ from that; because of non-difference, it should be understood
as refuted by the very refutation of that. [End of NyS 4.1.24]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.25] Others think —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.25: Everything is impermanent, because of having the nature of arising and perishing.

children.text: kimanityaṃ nāma ?, yasya kadācid bhāvastadanityam = utpattidharmakamanutpannaṃ nāsti. vināśadharmakaṃ
children.translated_text: What is 'impermanent'? That whose existence is at some time — that is impermanent; having the nature of arising — what has not arisen does not exist; having the nature of perishing —
what has not perished does not exist.

children.text: kiṃ punaḥ ?, sarvaṃ bhautikaṃ ca śarīrādi abhautikaṃ ca buddhyādi tadubhayamutpattivināśadharmakaṃ vijñāyate tasmāttatsarvamanityamiti // 25 //
children.translated_text: What then? Everything — both the material such as the body and the rest, and the non-material such as cognition and the rest — both of these are known to have the nature of arising and perishing; therefore all that is impermanent. [End of NyS 4.1.25]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.26]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.26: Not [so], because of the impermanence of impermanence itself.

children.text: yadi tāvat sarvasyānityatā nityā ? tannityatvād na sarvamanityam|

children.translated_text: But if [impermanence itself] is impermanent, then in its absence, everything would be permanent. [End of NyS 4.1.26]
If the impermanence of everything is permanent, then because of that permanence, not everything is impermanent.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.27]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.27: The impermanence of that [impermanence] is like fire perishing along with what is to be burned.
Even the impermanence of that impermanence [is accepted].
How? Just as fire perishes along with what is to be burned,
so too the impermanence of everything perishes along with everything. [End of NyS 4.1.27]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.28]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.28: The non-rejection of the permanent, because of determination according to apprehension.

children.text:
ayaṃ khalu vādo nityaṃ pratyācaṣṭe nityasya ca pratyākhyānamanupapannam |
