children.translated_text: and for some of their qualities, and for <s>sāmānya</s> (universals), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularities), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) —
the nature of having origination and destruction is not apprehended through valid means of knowledge.
Therefore, these are permanent. [End of NyS 4.1.28]

This doctrine indeed affirms the permanent, and the rejection of the permanent is untenable. Why? Because of determination according to apprehension. That whose nature of having origination and destruction is apprehended through valid means of knowledge — that is impermanent. That for which [such nature] is not apprehended — that is the contrary. And for the supremely subtle elements, <s>ākāśa</s> (space), <s>kāla</s> (time), <s>dik</s> (direction), <s>ātman</s> (self), and <s>manas</s> (mind),
[Section: NySBh 4.1.29]
This is another extreme view —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.29: Everything is permanent, because of the permanence of the five elements.

children.text: bhūtamātram idaṃ sarvaṃ. tāni ca nityāni--

children.translated_text: because the destruction of elements is untenable. [End of NyS 4.1.29]
All this is nothing but elements. And they are permanent —
[Section: NySBh 4.1.30]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.30: No, because causes of origination and destruction are apprehended.
this contradicts the permanence of everything. [End of NyS 4.1.30]
Both a cause of origination and a cause of destruction are apprehended;
[Section: NySBh 4.1.31]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.31: Because [what is apprehended] is included within the characteristics of those [elements], there is no refutation.
that is not grasped as something different, lacking the characteristics of elements.
Because of inclusion within the characteristics of elements, all this is nothing but elements —
therefore this refutation is unjustified. [End of NyS 4.1.31]
That for which you think a cause of origination and destruction is apprehended —
[Section: NySBh 4.1.32]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.32: No, because origination and its cause are apprehended.

children.translated_text: [the argument] 'because of the permanence of the five elements' and 'because of the inclusion within the characteristics of those' —
does not cover sound, action, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort.
Therefore [this view] is inconclusive.

Origination is [the arising] of [an effect] having qualities similar to [its] cause, and the cause is apprehended. Neither of these two pertains to permanent [entities]. Nor can the apprehension of origination and its cause be rejected — for there is no apprehension that lacks an object. By the power of apprehension, it is inferred that an effect having qualities similar to the cause originates — that indeed is the object of apprehension. And thus the inclusion within the characteristics of those [elements] is tenable. The effort of the knower, prompted by the causes of origination and destruction, is observed. And the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) with those properties is well-established. And the composite whole having the property of origination and destruction is established. And there is non-pervasion regarding sound, action, cognition, and the rest —
[Objection:] If [one says] the apprehension is false, like the assumption of objects in a dream? [Reply:] The same [would apply] to the apprehension of elements.
Just as in a dream there is merely the assumption of objects, so too [you say] the assumption of causes of origination [is false].

children.text: iti, evaṃ ca etad bhūtopalabdhau tulyam
children.translated_text: But this same [argument] applies equally to the apprehension of elements —
the apprehension of earth and the rest too would follow as being like the assumption of objects in a dream.
[Objection:] If, in the absence of earth and the rest, all practical activity would be destroyed? [Reply:] The same [applies] to the other.
In the absence of what is the object of the apprehension of causes of origination and destruction too,
all practical activity would be destroyed. This [argument] 'like the assumption of objects in a dream' is not a valid reason, because permanent [entities] are beyond the senses
and because origination and destruction are not objects [of direct perception]. [End of NyS 4.1.32]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.33]

children.text:

And what arises also exists even before its arising, and what ceases also exists even after ceasing — and thus everything is permanent. [Reply:] —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.33: No, because determination is untenable.

children.translated_text: is arising; the losing of being by what is existent is ceasing — when this [is accepted],
these defects do not apply. Therefore, what was said — 'even before arising it exists,
and what has ceased also exists' — that is unjustified. [End of NyS 4.1.33]

The determination 'this is an arising, this is a cessation' is untenable — because both the arisen and the ceased are existent. 'This property has arisen, this has ceased' — because there is no distinction in their existence, there is no determination. 'Now there is arising and ceasing, not at other times' — temporal determination is untenable, because [they] exist at all times. 'There is arising and ceasing of this property but not of that one' — such determination is untenable, because there is no distinction between the two. And the temporal determination 'future' and 'past' is untenable — because the present is characterized by existence. The gaining of being by what is non-existent
[Section: NySBh 4.1.34]
This is another extreme view —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.34: Everything is separate, because of the separateness of the defining characteristics of entities.

children.translated_text: The naming word '<s>kumbha</s>' (pot) applies to the aggregate of smell, taste, form, and touch,
and to the aggregate of bottom, sides, neck, and the rest — this is merely an illustration.
[End of NyS 4.1.34]

Everything is diverse. There is no single entity. Why? Because of the separateness of the defining characteristics of entities. The characteristic of an entity is its designation — the naming word by which an entity is characterized; because of the distinct objects [of each such word]. Every designation-word for an entity denotes an aggregate.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.35]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.35: No, because a single entity is produced from things having many characteristics.

children.text:
'anekavidhalakṣaṇaiḥ' iti madhyamapadalopī
samāsaḥ, gandhādibhiśca guṇairbudhnādibhiścāvayavaiḥ

children.translated_text: And substance is distinct from qualities,
and the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is distinct from its parts.
And both of these have been established by separate reasoning. [End of NyS 4.1.35]

'Having characteristics of many kinds' — this is a compound with ellipsis of the middle term. From qualities such as smell and the rest, and from parts such as the bottom and the rest, a single entity is produced in connection [with them].
[Section: NySBh 4.1.36]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.36: Moreover, precisely because of the determination of the defining characteristic, there is no refutation.

children.translated_text: 'because the word 'entity' is used for an aggregate' — relying on the aggregate, the denial of each individual aggregate-member —
'there is no single entity' — this, being self-contradictory
in both ways, is a worthless argument. [End of NyS 4.1.36]

Moreover, this too has been stated: 'there is no single entity because [there is only] an aggregate.' Because a single [entity] is untenable, the aggregate itself does not exist. 'There is no single entity because the word 'entity' is used for an aggregate' — and because a single [entity] is untenable, the aggregate is untenable, since an aggregate is indeed a collection of single [things].' This is untenable because of self-contradiction — 'there is no single entity.' The very thing whose negation is asserted — 'because the word 'entity' is used for an aggregate' — is itself accepted by the one stating the reason, since an aggregate is indeed a collection of single [things]. And
[Section: NySBh 4.1.37] This is another extreme view —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.37: Everything is non-existence, because of the establishment of mutual non-existence among entities.

children.translated_text: Whatever the class of entities — all of it is non-existence. Why? Because of the establishment of mutual non-existence among entities. 'A cow, being non-existent in the nature of a horse,' 'a cow is a non-horse,' 'a horse, being non-existent in the nature of a cow,' 'a horse is a non-cow' — because the cognition of non-existence and the negation have co-referentiality with the word 'entity,' everything is non-existence.
This is unjustified because of the contradiction in the words of the thesis-statement, and between the thesis and the reason.

children.translated_text: If everything is non-existence,
'because of the establishment of mutual non-existence among entities'

children.text: iti nopapadyate. atha bhāveṣvitaretarābhāvasiddhi ? sarvamabhāva iti nopapadyate // 37 //
children.translated_text: is untenable. But if there is the establishment of mutual non-existence among entities, then 'everything is non-existence' is untenable. [End of NyS 4.1.37]

The meaning of the word 'all' (<s>sarva</s>) is the totality of the manifold, and the meaning of the word 'non-existence' (<s>abhāva</s>) is the negation of existence. The former has designation, the latter is without designation. How can what is being designated be without designation, i.e., non-existence? Non-existence, being without designation, can never be asserted as manifold and total. [Objection:] 'All this is non-existence'? [Reply:] If what you consider to be 'all' is [something] existent — thus? The contradiction is not resolved — the manifold and total cannot be [an object of] the cognition of non-existence. But this cognition exists — 'all.' Therefore it is not non-existence. And there is contradiction between the thesis and the reason — 'everything is non-existence' is the thesis, being the negation of existence. 'Because of the establishment of mutual non-existence among entities' is the reason. Having accepted mutual non-existence among entities, and relying on the establishment of mutual non-existence, it is said 'everything is non-existence.'
[Section: NySBh 4.1.38]
And the connection with a sūtra —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.38: No, because of the self-established nature of entities.

śabde jātiviśiṣṭaṃ dravyaṃ gṛhyate nābhāvamātram.

gośabdena cābhāva ucyeta, yasmāttu gośabdaprayoge
dravyaviśeṣaḥ pratīyate nābhāvastasmādayuktamiti/

"na svabhāvasiddheḥ"
iti 'asan gauraśvātmanā' iti gavātmanā

iti svabhāvasiddhiḥ, 'anaśvo 'śvaḥ' iti vā 'gauragauḥ'

rūpeṇa vidyamānatā dravyasyetivijñāyate|
avyatirekapratiṣedhe
ca bhāvānām asatpratyayasāmānādhikaraṇyam/
saṃyogādisaṃbandho vyatirekaḥ atrāvyatireko 'bhedākhyasaṃbandhaḥ
tatpratiṣedhe cāsatpratyayasāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ
yathā-- 'na santi kuṇḍe badarāṇīti, 'asan
gauraśvātmanā' 'anaśvogauḥ' iti ca gavāśvayoravyatirekaḥ
pratiṣidhyate |
gavāśvayorekatvaṃ nāstīti. tasmin pratiṣidhyamāne
bhāvena gavā sāmādhikaraṇyamasatpratyayasya--
'asan gauraśvātmanā' iti. yathā 'na santi kuṇḍe
badarāṇīti kuṇḍe badarasaṃyoge pratiṣidhyamāne
sadbhirasatpratyayasya sāmādhikaraṇyamiti
// 38 //
children.translated_text: Not everything is non-existence. Why? Because entities exist by their own nature. It is asserted that entities exist by their own property. And what is the own property of entities? For substances, qualities, and actions — the universal beginning with existence (<s>sat</s>). For substances — the particular [property] such as 'possessing action,' and so on. 'Having [qualities] up to touch' for earth, and so on. And for each individually, the distinctions are infinite. And for <s>sāmānya</s> (universals), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularities), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), specific properties are grasped. Since non-existence is without designation, there would be no communicable difference of meaning — but this [difference] does exist; therefore, not everything is non-existence. Or alternatively — 'not, because of the self-established nature of entities' means because of the establishment through their own form. When the word 'cow' is employed, a substance qualified by its universal is grasped, not mere non-existence. And if everything were non-existence, 'cow' would be understood as non-existence, and by the word 'cow' non-existence would be denoted. But since, upon the use of the word 'cow,' a particular substance is cognized and not non-existence — therefore this is unjustified. Or alternatively — 'not, because of self-established nature' — 'a cow, being non-existent in the nature of a horse' — why is it not said 'in the nature of a cow'? Because of the non-saying [of it], there is self-established nature: 'a cow exists in the nature of a cow.' Or why is it not said 'a non-horse is a horse' or 'a non-cow is a cow'? Because of the non-saying [of such things], it is understood that a substance exists by its own form. And when the non-difference [relation] among entities is negated, there is co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence [with the entity]. Conjunction and the like constitute the relation [of difference]; here non-difference is the relation called identity. When that is negated, there is co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence — as in 'there are no jujube fruits in the pot.' 'A cow, being non-existent in the nature of a horse' and 'a cow is a non-horse' — thus the non-difference of a cow and a horse is negated. The identity of a cow and a horse does not exist. When that is being negated, there is co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence with the existent cow — 'a cow, being non-existent in the nature of a horse.' Just as 'there are no jujube fruits in the pot' — when the conjunction of jujube fruits in the pot is being negated, there is co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence with the existent [pot and fruits]. [End of NyS 4.1.38]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.39]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.39: Self-established nature does not [hold], because [things are] relative.

apekṣāsāmarthyāt. tasmānna svabhāvasiddhirbhāvānāmiti
// 39 //
children.translated_text: What is produced by dependence is relative — what is long is so in dependence on the short, and what is short is so in dependence on the long. Nothing is established by its own nature. Why? Because of the power of dependence. Therefore, entities do not have self-established nature.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.40]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.40: Because of self-contradiction, it is unjustified.

children.text:
yadi hrasvāpekṣākṛtaṃ dīrghaṃ kimidānīmapekṣya
'hrasvam' iti gṛhyate ?|
atha dīrghāpekṣākṛtaṃ
hrasvam ? dīrghamanāpekṣikam, evamitaretarāśrayayorekābhāve 'nyatarābhāvādubhayābhāva
ityapekṣāvyavasthānupapannā|
svabhāvasiddhāv asatyāṃ samayoḥ parimaṇḍalayorvā dravyayorāpekṣike dīrghatvahrasvatve kasmānna bhavataḥ ?|
apekṣāyāmanapekṣāyāṃ ca dravyayorabhedaḥ |
yāvatī dravye apekṣamāṇe tāvatī evānapekṣamāṇe nānyataratra bhedaḥ |
āpekṣikatve tu saty anyataratra viśeṣopajanaḥ syāditi|
kimapekṣāsāmarthyamiticet ? dvayorgrahaṇe 'tiśyagrahaṇopapattiḥ|
dve dravye paśyan ekatra vidyamānamatiśayaṃ gṛhṇāti
tad dīrghamiti vyavasyati, yacca hīnaṃ gṛhṇāti
tad hrasvamiti vyavasyatīti, etaccāpekṣāsāmarthyamiti
// 40 //
children.translated_text: If 'long' is produced by reference to the short — then with reference to what is 'short' grasped now? And if 'short' is produced by reference to the long — then 'long' is non-referential. Thus, when one of the two that are mutually dependent is absent, the other is also absent — hence both are absent, and the determination of reference is untenable. If there is no establishment by inherent nature, why do longness and shortness — which are referential — not belong to two equal or spherical substances? Because there is no difference between the substances whether they are in reference or not in reference. The extent of the substance when being referred to is the same as when not being referred to — there is no difference in either case. But if [longness and shortness] are referential, there should be the arising of a distinction in one of them. [Objection:] What is the power of reference? [Reply:] When two [substances] are apprehended, the apprehension of the excess is tenable. Seeing two substances, one grasps the excess present in one and determines 'that is long'; and one grasps what is deficient and determines 'that is short.' And this is the power of reference. [End of NyS 4.1.40]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.41]

children.text:
atheme saṃkhyaikāntāḥ--

children.translated_text: Now these are the numerical absolutists: 'everything is one' — because of the non-differentiation of being; 'everything is twofold' — because of the distinction between eternal and non-eternal; 'everything is threefold' — knower, knowledge, and knowable; 'everything is fourfold' — the cognizer, the means of cognition, the object of cognition, and the resultant cognition; and similarly others as applicable. Regarding these, the examination —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.41: The non-establishment of numerical absolutism, because of the inapplicability and applicability of the reason.
If the object to be established and the means of establishing it are different — the absolutism

children.text: na sidhyati-- vyatirekāt, atha sādhyasādhanayorabhedaḥ ? evamapyekānto na sidhyati-- sādhanābhāvāt,
children.translated_text: is not established, because of the distinction. And if the object to be established and the means of establishing it are identical — even so, absolutism is not established, because of the absence of a means of establishment,
for without it, nothing can be established. [End of NyS 4.1.41]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.42]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.42: No, because the reason is a part of the cause.
There is no non-establishment of the numerical absolutists. Why?

children.text: kāraṇasyāvayavabhāvāt = avayasavaḥ kaścit sādhanabhūta ity avyatirekaḥ/
children.translated_text: Because the reason is a part of the cause — some part serves as the means of establishing, hence there is no distinction.
Similarly for dualism and the rest also. [End of NyS 4.1.42]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.43]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.43: Because of [the whole] being without parts, [the previous sūtra] is not a valid reason.

children.text:
"kāraṇasyāvayavabhāvāt"
ityahetuḥ, kasmāt ? 'sarvamekam' ityanapavargeṇa
pratijñāya kasyacidekatvamucyate tatra vyapavṛkto 'vayavaḥ
sādhanabhūto nopapadyate, evaṃ dvaitādiṣvapīti/

ityevamekāntatvaṃ jahatīti|

children.translated_text: These indeed
are the absolutists examined for the purpose of discriminating true knowledge.
[End of NyS 4.1.43]

'Because the reason is a part of the cause' — this is not a valid reason. Why? Having asserted without exception that 'everything is one,' if oneness is predicated of something, then an excluded part serving as a means of establishing is untenable. Similarly for dualism and the rest. Now, if these numerical absolutists proceed by rejecting the diversity of real distinctions produced by particular [features] — they become speakers of falsehood, due to conflict with perception, inference, and scripture. And if they proceed by accepting [such diversity] — then the grouping of things produced by common properties and the diversity of things produced by particular [features] — thus they abandon absolutism.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.44]
The fruit [of action] is after the state following death. Regarding that —

children.text: NyS_4,1.44: sadyaḥ kālāntare ca phalaniṣpatteḥ saṃśayaḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 4.1.44: Because of the production of fruit both immediately and at another time, there is doubt.

'pacati dogdhīti sadyaḥ phalam
odanapayasī, 'karṣati vapatīti kālāntare
phalaṃ śasyādhigama iti, asti ceyaṃ kriyā--
children.translated_text: 'He cooks,' 'he milks' — the immediate fruit is cooked rice and milk. 'He plows,' 'he sows' — the fruit at another time is the acquisition of grain. And there is this ritual action —
regarding its fruit, there is doubt. [End of NyS 4.1.44]
'One who desires heaven should offer the <s>Agnihotra</s>' —
[Section: NySBh 4.1.45]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.45: Not immediately, because it is to be enjoyed at another time.

children.text: svargaḥ phalaṃ śrūyate tacca bhinne 'smin dehabhedādutpadyate iti na sadyaḥ,

children.translated_text: The fruit of undertaking [is immediate only] for those desiring a village and the like. [End of NyS 4.1.45]
Heaven is declared as the fruit, and that arises in a different [existence] after the separation of the body — hence it is not immediate.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.46]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.46: There is no production at another time, because of the destruction of the cause.

[End of NyS 4.1.46]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.47]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.47: Prior to production, it would be like the fruit of a tree.

children.translated_text: produces the fruit. And this has been stated —
'Because of the connection with the fruit of what was previously done, its arising [occurs]' (3.2.62).
[End of NyS 4.1.47]

Just as one who desires fruit performs the tending such as watering at the root of a tree, and when that [tending] has ceased, the earth-element, combined with the water-element and cooked by the internal fire, produces the juice-substance; that juice, being a substance, following the tree, distinguished by ripening, arranging itself in a particular configuration, produces leaves and fruit — thus the tending such as watering is purposeful, and the production of fruit is not from something destroyed. Similarly, through the activity, an impression characterized as <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) is generated; once generated, aided by other causes, at another time it
[Section: NySBh 4.1.48]
Now, this [effect], prior to its production, while being produced —

children.text: NyS_4,1.48: nāsan na san na sadasat sadasatorvaidharmyāt //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 4.1.48: [The effect prior to its production] is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, because of the dissimilarity of the existent and the non-existent.

children.text:
prāṅniṣpatterniṣpattidharmakaṃ
nāsat-- upādānaniyamāt |
kasyacidutpattaye kiñcidupādeyaṃ na sarvaṃ
sarvasyety asadbhāve niyamo nopapadyate
iti|
na sat-- prāgutpattervidyamānasyotpattiranupapanneti/
na sadasat-- sadasatorvaidharmyāt = 'sat' ityarthābhyanujñā. 'asat' ityarthapratiṣedhaḥ
