// 48 //
children.translated_text: Prior to production, that which has the character of being produced is not non-existent — because of the restriction of the material cause. For the production of something, something specific is to be employed as the material, not everything for everything — and such a restriction is untenable if [the effect] were non-existent. It is not existent — because the arising of what already exists prior to its production is untenable. It is not both existent and non-existent — because of the dissimilarity of the existent and the non-existent. 'Existent' means the acceptance of the thing; 'non-existent' means the denial of the thing. The contradiction between these two is their dissimilarity; because of the contradiction, the non-separation [of both] is untenable. [End of NyS 4.1.48]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.49]

children.text: NyS_4,1.49: prāgutpatterutpattidharmakam asad ity addhā, kasmād utpādavyayadarśanāt //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 4.1.49: Prior to its production, that which has the character of being produced is certainly non-existent — because of the observation of arising and destruction.
What was further stated — 'prior to production, the effect is not non-existent, because of the restriction of the material cause' —
[End of NyS 4.1.49]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.50]

children.text:
idamasyotpattaye samarthaṃ na
sarvamiti prāgutpatterniyatakāraṇaṃ kāryaṃ
buddhyā siddham-- utpattiniyamadarśanāt
tasmādupādānaniyamasyopapattiḥ|
sati tu
kārye prāgutpatterutpattireva nāstīti
// 50 //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 4.1.50: But that non-existence is established by cognition.

'This is capable of producing this, not everything [produces everything]' — thus the effect, prior to production, with a determined cause, is established by cognition — because of the observation of the regularity of production. Therefore the restriction of the material cause is tenable. But if the effect [already] exists, there is simply no arising prior to production. [End of NyS 4.1.50]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.51]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.51: Because of the difference of substrate, 'like the production of the fruit of a tree' is not a valid reason.

children.text: vṛkṣāśrayam. karma ceha śarīre phalaṃ cāmutreti
children.translated_text: The tending at the root and the fruit — both
have the tree as their substrate. But the action [is performed] here in the body, while the fruit [arises] hereafter —
because of the difference of substrate, [the analogy] is not a valid reason. [End of NyS 4.1.51]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.52]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.52: Because pleasure has the self as its substrate, there is no refutation.
Pleasure, being perceptible to the <s>ātman</s>, has the <s>ātman</s> as its substrate; and

<s>karma</s>, designated as <s>dharma</s> (merit), has that same [ātman] as its substrate — because <s>dharma</s> is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>. Therefore the inapplicability of the difference of substrate [is established]. [End of NyS 4.1.52]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.53]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.53: No, because the fruit is specified as sons, cattle, wives, possessions, gold, food, and the like.

children.text:
putrādi phalaṃ nirdiśyate na prītiḥ--
"grāmakāmo yajeta" "putrakāmo yajeta"
iti. tatra yaduktam-- 'prītiḥ phalam' iti etadayuktam
// 53 //
children.translated_text: Sons and the like are specified as the fruit, not pleasure — 'one who desires a village should sacrifice,' 'one who desires a son should sacrifice.' Regarding that, what was said — 'pleasure is the fruit' — that is unjustified. [End of NyS 4.1.53]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.54]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.54: Because the production of the fruit is due to the connection with those, the designation 'fruit' is applied to them figuratively.
the figurative designation 'fruit' [is used], just as food is called <s>prāṇa</s> (life-breath) —
'Food indeed is the life-breaths.'
[End of NyS 4.1.54]
Because of the connection with sons and the like, the fruit characterized as pleasure arises; therefore in sons and the like
[Section: NySBh 4.1.55]

children.text:
phalānantaraṃ duḥkhamuddiṣṭamuktaṃ ca--
"bādhanālakṣaṇaṃ duḥkham 1-1-21"
iti. tat kimidaṃ pratyātmavedanīyasya |
sarvajantupratyakṣasya sukhasya pratyākhyānam ? āhosvidanyaḥ kalpaḥ ? iti, anya ityāha, katham ?, na vai sarvalokasākṣikaṃ sukhaṃ śakyaṃ pratyākhyātum |
ayaṃ tu janmamaraṇaprabandhānubhavanimittād duḥkhād nirviṇṇasya duḥkhaṃ jihāsato duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanopadeśo duḥkhahānārtha iti |
kayā yuktyā ?, sarve khalu sattvanikāyāḥ sarvāṇyutpattisthānāni sarvaḥ punarbhavo bādhanānuṣakto duḥkhasāhacaryāt
"bādhanālakṣaṇaṃ duḥkham 1-1-21"
ityuktam. ṛṣibhirduḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanamupadiśyate,
atra ca heturupādīyate---
children.translated_text: After [discussing] the fruit [of action], suffering has been mentioned. And it was said — 'suffering is characterized by affliction' (1.1.21). Is this a rejection of pleasure, which is experienced by the individual self and is perceptible to all beings? Or is there another interpretation? [Reply:] There is another [interpretation]. How? It is not possible to reject pleasure, which is witnessed by all the world. But this is the teaching of cultivating the notion of suffering, for the sake of abandoning suffering, for one who is disgusted with suffering caused by the experience of the continuum of birth and death and desires to abandon suffering. By what reasoning? Indeed, all classes of beings, all places of birth, every rebirth is attended by affliction; because of the association with suffering, it was said — 'suffering is characterized by affliction' (1.1.21). The sages teach the cultivation of the notion of suffering. And here a reason is adduced —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.55: Because of the connection with various kinds of affliction, birth itself is suffering.

children.text:
janma |
jāyate iti śarīrendriyabuddhayaḥ, śarīrādīnāṃ
saṃsthānaviśiṣṭānāṃ prādurbhāva utpattiḥ,
vividhā ca bādhanā-- hīnā madhyamā utkṛṣṭā
ceti. utkṛṣṭā nārakiṇāṃ. tiraścāṃ tu madhyamā,
manuṣyāpāṃ hīnāḥ. devānāṃ hīnatarā vītarāgāṇāṃ
ca, evaṃ sarvamutpattisthānaṃ vividhabādhanānuṣaktaṃ
paśyataḥ sukhe tatsādhaneṣu ca śarīrendriyabuddhiṣu
duḥkhasaṃjñā vyavatiṣṭhate. duḥkhasaṃjñāvyavasthānāt
sarvalokeṣv anabhiratisaṃjñā bhavati. anabhiratisaṃjñāmupāsīnasya
sarvalokaviṣayātṛṣṇā vicchidyate. tṛṣṇāprahāṇāt
sarvaduḥkhād vimucyate iti, yathā
viṣayogāt payo viṣayamiti budhyamāno
nopādatte. anupādadāno maraṇaduḥkhaṃ nāpnoti
// 55 //
children.translated_text: Birth — 'is born' means the body, sense-organs, and intellect. The manifestation of the body and the rest with their particular configurations is 'arising.' And the affliction is various — low, middling, and extreme. Extreme for the denizens of hell; middling for animals; low for humans. Still lower for the gods and for the dispassionate. Thus, for one who sees that every place of birth is attended by various afflictions, the notion of suffering is established regarding pleasure and regarding the body, sense-organs, and intellect which are its means. Because of the establishment of the notion of suffering, the notion of discontentment regarding all worlds arises. For one who cultivates the notion of discontentment, craving directed toward all worlds is cut off. From the abandonment of craving, one is freed from all suffering. Just as one who, knowing that milk is poisoned due to the mixing of poison, does not take it — and not taking it, does not incur the suffering of death. [End of NyS 4.1.55]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.56]
But the mention of suffering is not a rejection of pleasure. Why? —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.56: Not [a rejection] of pleasure, because it is produced in the intervals [between afflictions].
This mention of suffering is indeed not a rejection of pleasure.
Why? Because pleasure is produced in the intervals [between afflictions].
Pleasure, experienced by the individual self, is indeed produced in the intervals between afflictions
for embodied beings — and that cannot be rejected. [End of NyS 4.1.56]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.57]
And further —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.57: Because of the fault of seeking, there is no refutation [of the teaching], since affliction does not cease for the one who experiences [pleasure].

children.text:
sukhasya duḥkhoddeśeneti prakaraṇāt, paryeṣaṇam |
prārthanā |
viṣayārjanatṛṣṇā. paryeṣaṇasya doṣo yadayaṃ
vedayamānaḥ prārthayate. taccāsya prārthitaṃ na
saṃpadyate. saṃpadya vā vipadyate. nyūnaṃ vā saṃpadyate.
bahupratyanīkaṃ vā saṃpadyate. ityetasmāt
paryeṣaṇadoṣāt nānāvidho mānasaḥ saṃtāpo
bhavati. evaṃ vedayataḥ paryeṣaṇadoṣād bādhanāyā
anavṛttiḥ. bādhanānivṛtterduḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanamuddiśyate.
anena kāraṇena duḥkhaṃ janma na tu sukhasyābhāvāditi/

children.translated_text: And this has been stated in accordance —
'When a desire is fulfilled for one who desires desire,
then another desire quickly afflicts him.'

children.text: "api cedudanemi samantād bhūmimālabhate sagavāśvāṃ na sa tena dhanena dhanaiṣī tṛpyati kiṃ nu sukhaṃ dhanakāme"
children.translated_text: 'Even if one were to gain the entire earth with its cattle and horses, the wealth-seeker would not be satisfied by that wealth — what happiness is there in desiring wealth?'
[End of NyS 4.1.57]

Of pleasure — by the mention of suffering — this is the context. Seeking means craving, the thirst for acquiring sense-objects. The fault of seeking is that this [being], while experiencing [pleasure], craves. And what he craves does not materialize. Or having materialized, it perishes. Or it materializes deficiently. Or it materializes with many adversities. Because of this fault of seeking, various kinds of mental torment arise. Thus, for one who experiences [pleasure], because of the fault of seeking, affliction does not cease. Because affliction does not cease, the cultivation of the notion of suffering is taught. For this reason, birth is suffering — but not because of the absence of pleasure.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.58]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.58: And because of the false notion of pleasure in what is [actually] a variety of suffering.

children.text:
duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanopadeśaḥ
kriyate, ayaṃ khalu sukhasaṃvedane vyavasthitaḥ
sukhaṃ paramapuruṣārthaṃ manyate-- na sukhādanyad
niḥśreyasamasti. sukhe prāpte caritārthaḥ kṛtakaraṇīyo
bhavati. mithyāsaṃkalpāt mukhe tatsādhaneṣu
ca viṣayeṣu saṃrajyate. saṃraktaḥ sukhāya
ghaṭate. ghaṭamānasyāsya janmajarāvyādhiprāyaṇāniṣṭasaṃyogeṣṭaviyogaprārthitānupapattinimittamanekavidhaṃ
yāvad duḥkhamutpadyate taṃ duḥkhavikalpaṃ sukhamityabhimanyate.
sukhāṅgabhūtaṃ duḥkhaṃ-- na duḥkhamanāsādya śakyaṃ
sukhamavāptum. tādarthyāt sukhamevedamiti
sukhasaṃjñopahataprajñaḥ-- 'jāyasya mriyasva saṃghāva'
iti saṃsāraṃ nātivartate. tadasyāḥ sukhasaṃjñānayāḥ
pratipakṣo duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanamupadiśyate. duḥkhānuṣaṅgād
duḥkhaṃ janmeti na sukhasyābhāvāt|
yadyevaṃ kasmāt 'duḥkhaṃ janma' iti nocyate ?. soyamevaṃ
vācye yadevakāha--
"duḥkhameva janma 55"
iti tena sukhābhāvaṃ jñāpayatīti, janmavinigrahārthīyo
vai khalvayamevaśabdaḥ, katham ? na duḥkhaṃ janma
svarūpataḥ kiṃ tu duḥkhopacārāt. evaṃ sukhamapīti
etad anenaiva nivartyate na tu duḥkhameva janmeti
// 58 //
children.translated_text: The teaching of cultivating the notion of suffering is given [for this reason]: this [person], established in the experience of pleasure, considers pleasure to be the supreme human goal — 'there is no highest good other than pleasure.' Having obtained pleasure, he considers his purpose fulfilled and his duty done. From false conception, he becomes attached to pleasure and to the objects that are its means. Being attached, he strives for pleasure. And for this one who strives, manifold suffering arises on account of birth, old age, disease, death, unwanted conjunction, separation from the desired, and the non-attainment of what is sought — and he considers that variety of suffering to be pleasure. 'Suffering is an integral part of pleasure — one cannot obtain pleasure without encountering suffering. Because it serves that purpose, this is indeed pleasure' — thus one whose discernment is impaired by the notion of pleasure — 'be born, die, be gathered together' — does not transcend <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of rebirth). As the antidote to this policy of [false] pleasure-notion, the cultivation of the notion of suffering is taught. Because of the association with suffering, birth is suffering — not because of the absence of pleasure. If so, why is it not said 'birth is suffering'? This is exactly what [the sūtra] says — 'birth itself is suffering [NyS 4.1.55]' — and by that [the word 'eva'] he indicates the absence of pleasure. But this word 'eva' is for the purpose of restricting to birth. How? Birth is not suffering in its own nature, but rather by the figurative attribution of suffering. Similarly, pleasure too — this is negated by this very [word 'eva']; but [the meaning is] not that birth is only suffering. [End of NyS 4.1.58]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.59]
After the teaching of suffering, <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) [is discussed]; that is objected to —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.59: Because of the binding connection with debts, afflictions, and activity, <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) does not exist.

children.text:
ṛṇānubandhānnāstyapavargaḥ = "jāyamāno ha vai brāhmaṇastribhirṛṇairṛṇavān
jāyate-- brahmacaryeṇa ṛṣibhyo yajñena devebhyaḥ prajāyā pitṛbhyaḥ"
iti ṛṇāni. teṣāmanubandhaḥ |
svakarmabhiḥ saṃbandhaḥ-- karmasaṃbandhavacanāt--
children.translated_text: Because of the binding connection with debts, <s>apavarga</s> does not exist — 'Indeed, a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> is born indebted with three debts — by <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibate studentship) to the sages, by sacrifice to the gods, by offspring to the ancestors.' These are the debts. Their binding connection means connection through one's own duties — because of the statement of connection with action —

children.text:
"jarāmarya vā etatsatraṃ yadagnihotraṃ darśapūrṇamāsau
ceti ujarayā ha eṣa tasmāt satrādvimucyate mṛtyunā ha vā"
iti ṛṇānubandhādapavargānuṣṭhānakālo nāstīty apavargābhāvaḥ/
kleśānubandhānnastyapavargaḥ |
kleśānubaddha evāyaṃ mriyate kleśānubaddhaśca
jāyate nāsya kleśānubandhavicchedo gṛhyate/
pravṛttyanubandhānnāstyapavargaḥ |
janmaprabhṛty ayaṃ yāvatprāyaṇaṃ vāgbuddhiśarīrārambheṇāvimukto

children.translated_text: regarding which, what was said —
'From the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, faults, and false knowledge, through the removal of each succeeding one, <s>apavarga</s> [results] [NyS 1.1.2]'
— that is untenable. [End of NyS 4.1.59]

'The <s>Agnihotra</s> and the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> [sacrifices] are a sacrificial session lasting until old age or death; from that session one is released by old age or by death.' Because of the binding connection with debts, there is no time for the practice of <s>apavarga</s> — thus there is no <s>apavarga</s>. Because of the binding connection with afflictions, <s>apavarga</s> does not exist — this [person] dies bound by afflictions and is born bound by afflictions; no cessation of his binding connection with afflictions is apprehended. Because of the binding connection with activity, <s>apavarga</s> does not exist — from birth until death, this [person] is apprehended as unreleased from the initiation of speech, thought, and bodily [action];
[Section: NySBh 4.1.60]
To this it is replied — regarding what was said, 'because of the binding connection with debts': the debts are like debts, not actual debts —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.60: Because the primary meaning of the word is inapplicable, [it is used] in a secondary sense — because the applicability of blame and praise [supports this].

children.text:
"ṛṇaiḥ" iti nāyaṃ pradhānaśabdaḥ, yatra khalvekaḥ pratyādeyaṃ
dadāti dvitīyaśca pratideyaṃ gṛhṇāti tatrāsya
dṛṣṭatvāt pradhānamṛṇaśabdaḥ. na caitadihopapadyate
pradhānaśabdānupapatterguṇaśabdenāyamanuvādaḥ--
ṛṇairiva ṛṇairiti, prayuktopamaṃ caitad
yathā--
"agnirmāṇavakaḥ" iti = anyatra dṛṣṭaścāyamṛṇaśabda iha prayujyate
yathāgniśabdo māṇavake |
kathaṃ guṇaśabdenānuvādaḥ ?, nindāprasaṃsopapatteḥ = karmalope ṛṇīva ṛṇādānād nindyate.
karmānuṣṭhāne ca ṛṇīva ṛṇadānād praśasyate sa evopamārtha iti/
"jāyamānaḥ"
iti guṇaśabdaḥ-- viparyaye 'nadhikārāt = "jāyamāno ha vai brāhmaṇaḥ"
iti ca śabdo gṛhasthaḥ saṃpadyamānaḥ, jāyamāna iti
uyadāyaṃ gṛhastho jāyate tadā karmabhiradhikriyate--
mātṛto jāyamānasyānadhikārāt
uyadā tu mātṛto jāyate kumāro na
tadā karmabhiradhikriyate-- arthinaḥ śaktasya cādhikārāt = arthinaḥ karmabhiradhikāraḥ-- karmavidhau kāmasaṃyogasmṛteḥ--
children.translated_text: 'Debts' — this is not used in the primary sense. Where one person gives something to be repaid and a second person receives what is to be returned — there, because of being observed [in that context], the word 'debt' is primary. But that does not apply here; because of the inapplicability of the primary meaning, this is a restatement in a secondary sense — 'like debts.' And this is a simile employed [figuratively], just as 'fire [applied to] a boy' — the word 'debt,' observed elsewhere, is used here just as the word 'fire' [is used] for a boy. How is [it] a restatement in a secondary sense? Because of the applicability of blame and praise — one who neglects his duties is blamed like a debtor for not repaying a debt; one who performs his duties is praised like a debtor for repaying a debt — that is the meaning of the simile. 'Being born' — this is a secondary expression — because of the contrary [interpretation involving] non-qualification. 'Indeed, a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> being born' — the word [refers to] one becoming a householder; 'being born' means when this [brāhmaṇa] becomes a householder, then he is qualified for [ritual] actions — because a child being born from the mother is not qualified. But when a child is born from the mother, it is not then qualified for [ritual] actions — because qualification belongs to one who desires and is capable. Qualification for actions belongs to one who desires — because of the mention of desire in the injunction of action —

children.text:
"agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāmaḥ"
ityevamādi, śaktasya ca pravṛttisaṃbhavāt
uśaktasya karmabhiradhikāraḥ-- pravṛttisaṃbhavāt
uśaktaḥ khalu vihite karmaṇi pravartate netara
iti|
ubhayābhāvastu pradhānaśabdārthe|
mātṛto
jāyamāne kumāre ubhayam = arthitā śaktiśca na bhavatīti, na bhidyate laukikād
vākyād vaidikaṃ vākyam-- prekṣāpūrvakāripuruṣapraṇītatvena,
tatra laukikastāvadaparīkṣakopi na jātamātraṃ
kumāramevaṃ brūyāt-- 'adhīṣva yajasva brahmacaryaṃ
cara' iti. kuta eṣa ṛṣirupapannānavadyavādī
upadeśārthena prayukta upadiśati ?, na khalu vai
nartakondheṣu pravartate na gāyano badhireṣviti/
upadiṣṭārthavijñānaṃ copadeśaviṣayaḥ |
yaścopadiṣṭamarthaṃ vijānāti taṃ pratyupadeśaḥ
kriyate na caitadasti jāyamānakumārake
iti|
gārhasthyaliṅgaṃ ca mantrabrāhmaṇaṃ karmābhivadati |

children.translated_text: And the <s>mantra</s>s and <s>brāhmaṇa</s>s that enjoin action are consistent with
the marks of the householder's state, such as the connection with a wife and the rest; therefore this
'one being born' refers to the householder.

'One who desires heaven should perform the <s>Agnihotra</s>' — and so forth. And qualification for actions belongs to one who is capable — because of the possibility of undertaking [the action]; one who is capable indeed undertakes the enjoined action, not the other. But both [desire and capability] are absent in the primary meaning [of 'being born']. In a child being born from the mother, both — desire and capability — are absent. The Vedic statement does not differ from a worldly statement — because both are composed by persons who act with deliberation. In the worldly [context], even one who does not examine [carefully] would not say to a just-born child: 'Study, sacrifice, practice <s>brahmacarya</s>.' How much less would this sage, whose speech is well-founded and faultless, employed for the purpose of instruction, teach [thus]? Indeed, a dancer does not perform for the blind, nor a singer for the deaf. And the object of instruction is the comprehension of the meaning instructed — instruction is given to one who comprehends the meaning instructed, and this does not exist in a just-born child. And the <s>mantra</s>s and <s>brāhmaṇa</s>s that enjoin action bear the marks of the householder's state.

children.text:
arthitvasya cāvipariṇāme
jarāmaryavādopapattiḥ|
yāvaccāsya phalenārthitvaṃ
na vipariṇamate |
na nivartate tāvadanena karmānuṣṭheyamityupapadyate
jarāmaryavādastaṃ pratīti.
"jarayā ha vā"
ityāyuṣasturīyasya |
caturthasya pravrajyāyuktasya vacanam--
"jarayā ha vā eṣa etasmādvimucyate"
iti. āyuṣasturīyam |
caturthaṃpravrajyāyuktaṃ jaretyucyate-- tatra
hi pravrajyā vidhīyate, atyantajarāsaṃyoge
children.translated_text: And when the desire for the fruit does not change — as long as his desire for the fruit does not change, does not cease — so long should he perform the [ritual] actions — thus the statement about [the session lasting until] old age or death is applicable to him. 'By old age indeed' — this is a statement regarding the fourth quarter of life, pertaining to one fit for renunciation — 'By old age indeed one is released from that [session].' The fourth [quarter of life], fit for renunciation, is called 'old age' — for there renunciation is enjoined. If there were permanent connection with old age,

children.text:
"jarayā ha vā"
ityanarthakam|
'aśakto vimucyate' ityetadapi
nopapadyate-- svayamaśaktasya bāhyāṃ śaktimāha--
children.translated_text: 'by old age indeed' would be meaningless. And the [argument] that 'one who is incapable is released' is also untenable — [the scripture] states an external capacity for one who is himself incapable —

children.text:
"antevāsī vā juhuyāt brahmaṇā sa parikrītaḥ. kṣīrahotā vā juhuyād dhanena sa parikrītaḥ"
iti athāpi vihitaṃ vānūdyeta ? kāmādvārthaḥ
parikalpyeta ? vihitānuvacanaṃ nyāyyamiti,
ṛṇavānivāsvatantro gṛhyasthaḥ karmasu pravartate
ityupapannaṃ vākyasya sāmarthyam|
phalasya hi sādhanāni prayatnaviṣayo na phalaṃ. tāni saṃpannāni phalāya kalpante|
vihitaṃ ca jāyamānaṃ vidhīyate ca jāyamānaṃ tena yaḥ saṃbadhyate
soyaṃ jāyamāna iti|
pratyakṣavidhānābhāvāditicet ? na-- pratiṣedhasyāpi pratyakṣavidhānābhāvāditi/
pratyakṣato vidhīyate gārhasthyaṃ brāhmaṇena yadi
cāṃśramāntaramabhaviṣyat tadapi vyadhāsyat
pratyakṣataḥ. pratyakṣavidhānābhāvānnāstyāśramāntaramiti,
na-- pratiṣedhasyāpi pratyakṣavidhānābhāvāt = na pratiṣedhopi vai brāhmaṇena pratyakṣato
vidhīyate-- 'na santyāśramāntarāṇi eka eva
gṛhasthāśramaḥ' iti. pratiṣedhasya pratyakṣato 'śravaṇādayuktametaditi
// adhikārācca vidhānaṃ vidyāntaravat //
children.translated_text: 'Let a resident student offer [the oblations], he is purchased by <s>Brahman</s> (sacred knowledge). Or let a hired priest offer, he is purchased by wealth.' But is what is enjoined merely being restated? Or is the meaning to be construed from desire? It is proper that [it is] a restatement of what is enjoined — the householder, being dependent like a debtor, engages in ritual actions — thus the force of the statement is tenable. For the means to the fruit are the object of effort, not the fruit [itself]. When those [means] are accomplished, they conduce to the fruit. And what is enjoined is what is being born [i.e., becoming a householder], and the injunction is for one being born; he who is connected with that is the one 'being born.' [Objection:] Because there is no direct injunction [of other stages of life]? No — because there is no direct injunction of the prohibition either. The householder's state is directly enjoined for the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>; and if there were another stage of life, that too would have been directly enjoined. Because there is no direct injunction, there is no other stage of life — No, because there is no direct injunction of the prohibition either. The prohibition too is not directly enjoined by the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> — 'there are no other stages of life; the householder's stage alone [exists].' Because the prohibition is not heard directly, this is unjustified. And there is injunction based on qualification, just as with other branches of knowledge.

children.text:
yathā śāstrāntarāṇi sve sve 'dhikāre pratyakṣato
vidhāyakāni nārthāntarābhāvād evamidaṃ
brāhmaṇaṃ gṛhasthaśāstraṃ sve 'dhikāre pratyakṣato
vidhāyakaṃ nāśramāntarāṇāmabhāvāditi|
ṛgbrāhmaṇaṃ cāpavargābhidhāyy abhidhīyate |
ṛcaśca brāhmaṇāni cāpavargābhivādīna bhivanti.
ṛvaśca tāvat--
"karmabhirmṛtyumṛṣayo niṣeduḥ prajāvanto draviṇamicchamānāḥ, athāpare
ṛṣayo manīṣiṇaḥ paraṃ karmabhyo 'mṛtatvamānaśuḥ,"
"na karmaṇā na prajayā dhanena tyāgenaike amṛtatvamānaśuḥ"
"pareṇa nākaṃ nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ vibhrājate tad yatayo viśanti"
"vedāhametaṃpuruṣaṃ mahāntamādityavarṇaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt.
tameva viditvātimṛtyumeti nānyaḥ panthā vidyate 'yanāya" |
atha brāhmaṇāni--
"trayo dharmaskandhāḥ-- yajño 'dhyayanaṃ dānamiti prathamastapa
eva dvitīyo brahmacāryācāryakulavāsīti
tṛtīyo 'tyantamātmānamācāryakule 'vasādayan
sarve evaite puṇyalokā bhavanti brahmasaṃstho 'mṛtatvameti"
"etameva pravrājino lokamabhīpsantaḥ pravrajantīti"
"atho khalvāhuḥ-- kāmamaya evāyaṃ puruṣa
iti sa yathākāmo bhavati tathākraturbhavati
yathākraturbhavati tatkarma kurute yatkarma kurute
tadabhisaṃpadyate"
iti karmabhiḥ saṃsaraṇamuktvā prakṛtamanyadupadiśanti--
children.translated_text: Just as other treatises directly enjoin [matters] within their own domain and [this does not imply] the non-existence of other subjects, so too this <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, being a treatise on the householder's [life], directly enjoins within its own domain — [this does not imply] the non-existence of other stages of life. And <s>Ṛc</s>-verses and <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>s that speak of <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) are cited: <s>Ṛc</s>-verses indeed — 'By actions the sages warded off death, desirous of offspring and wealth; but other sages, the wise, attained the supreme immortality beyond actions.' 'Not by action, not by offspring, not by wealth — by renunciation alone some attained immortality.' 'That [which is] established beyond heaven, hidden in the cave — the ascetics enter that which shines forth.' 'I know this great <s>Puruṣa</s>, sun-colored, beyond darkness. Only by knowing him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for going.' And <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>s — 'There are three branches of <s>dharma</s>: sacrifice, study, and charity are the first; austerity is the second; a <s>brahmacārin</s> dwelling in the teacher's house is the third — one who permanently establishes himself in the teacher's house. All these indeed attain meritorious worlds; one who is established in <s>Brahman</s> attains immortality.' 'Desiring this very world, wandering ascetics renounce [the world].' 'Now they say: this person is indeed made of desire. As his desire is, so is his resolve; as his resolve is, so is the action he performs; as the action he performs, so does he attain.' Having spoken of transmigration through actions, they teach something else as the topic —

children.text:
"iti tu kāmayamāno 'thākāmayamāno yo 'kāmo
niṣkām ātmakāma āptakāmo bhavati na tasya
prāṇā utkrāmanti ihaiva samavalīyante brahmaiva
san brahmāpyeti"
iti, tatra yaduktam-- 'ṛṇānubandhādapavargābhāvaḥ'
iti etadayuktamiti/
"yecatvāraḥ pathayo devayānāḥ"
iti ca cātugaśramyaśruteraikāśramyānupapattiḥ/
phalārthinaścedaṃ brāhmaṇam--
"jarāmaryaṃ vā etatsatraṃ yadagrihotraṃ darśapūrṇamāsau ca" iti
// 60 //
children.translated_text: 'Thus, the one who desires, and then the one who is without desire — he who is free from desire, whose desires are fulfilled, whose desire is the self, whose desires are attained — his vital breaths do not depart; right here they merge; being <s>Brahman</s>, he goes to <s>Brahman</s>.' Regarding this, what was said — 'because of the binding connection with debts, <s>apavarga</s> does not exist' — this is unjustified. And from the <s>śruti</s>: 'those four divine paths' — from the Vedic statement about the four stages of life, the [doctrine of] a single stage of life is untenable. And this <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> is for those who desire the fruit — 'the <s>Agnihotra</s> and the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> [sacrifices] are a sacrificial session lasting until old age or death.' [End of NyS 4.1.60]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.61] How?
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.61: Because of the [ritual of] placing [the fires] upon oneself, there is no preclusion for the self.

children.text:
"prājāpattyāmiṣṭiṃ nirupya nasyāṃ sarvavedasaṃ hutvā ātmanyagnīn samāropya brāhmaṇaḥ pravrajet"
iti śrūyate tena vijānīmaḥ-- prajāvittalokaiṣaṇābhyo
vyutthitasya nivṛtte phalārthitve samāropaṇaṃ
vidhīyate iti, evaṃ ca brāhmaṇāni--
"so 'nyad vratamupākariṣyamāṇo yājñavalkyo maitreyīmitihovāca--
pravrajiṣyan vā are ahamasmāt sthānādasmi
hanta te 'nayā kātyāyanyā sahāntaṃ karavāṇīti.
athāpyuktānuśāsanāsi maitreyi etāvadare
khalvamṛtatvamiti hoktvā yājñavalkyaḥ pravavrāja"
iti// 61 //
children.translated_text: 'Having offered the <s>Prājāpatya Iṣṭi</s> (sacrifice to <s>Prajāpati</s>), having offered [an oblation] with all the <s>Veda</s>s in it, having placed the [sacrificial] fires upon the self, a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should renounce' — thus it is heard. By that we understand: for one who has arisen from the desires for offspring, wealth, and worlds — when the desire for the fruit has ceased — the [ritual of] placing [the fires] is enjoined. And thus [it is stated in] <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>s — '<s>Yājñavalkya</s>, being about to undertake another observance, said to <s>Maitreyī</s>: "I am about to renounce from this station; come, let me make a settlement between you and <s>Kātyāyanī</s>." And having also given the teaching to [her], "This much indeed, dear, is immortality" — having said this, <s>Yājñavalkya</s> renounced.' [End of NyS 4.1.61]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.62]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.62: And because of the non-tenability of [the cycle ending with] the exhaustion of the succession of recipients, there is no fruit.

children.text:
jarāmarye ca karmaṇy aviśeṣeṇa
kalpyamāne sarvasya pātracayāntāni karmāṇīti
prasajyate tatraiṣaṇāvyutthānaṃ na śrūyeta--
"etaddha sma vai tatpūrve brāhmaṇā anūcānā vidvāṃsaḥ
prajāṃ na kāmayante kiṃ prajayā kariṣyāmo
yeṣāṃ noyamātmāyaṃ loka iti. te ha
sma putraiṣaṇāyāśca vittaiṣaṇāyāśca lokaiṣaṇāyāśca
vyutthāyātha bhikṣācaryaṃ caranti"
iti, eṣaṇābhyaśca vyutthitasya pātracayāntāni
karmāṇi nopapadyante iti nāviśeṣeṇa kartuḥ
prayojakaṃ phalaṃ bhavatīti|
cāturāśramyavidhānāccetihāsapurāṇadharmaśāstreṣvaikāśramyānupapattiḥ/
tadapramāṇamiticet ? na-- pramāṇena prāmāṇyābhyanujñānāt/
pramāṇena khalu brāhmaṇenetihāsapurāṇasya
prāmāṇyamabhyanujñāyate--
"te vā khalvete atharvāṅgirasa etaditihāsapurāṇamabhyavadan
itihāsapurāṇaṃ pañcamaṃ vedānāṃ vedaḥ"
iti. tasmād ayuktametat-- aprāmāṇyamiti/
aprāmāṇye ca dharmaśāstrasya prāṇabhṛtāṃ
vyavahāralopāt lokocchedaprasaṅgaḥ,
draṣṭṛpravaktṛsāmānyāccāprāmāṇyānupapattiḥ = ye eva mantrabrāhmaṇasya draṣṭāraḥ pravaktāraśca
te khalvitihāsapurāṇasya dharmaśāstrasya
ceti|
viṣayavyavasthānācca yathāviṣayaṃ prāmāṇyam = anyo mantrabrāhmaṇasya viṣayo 'nyaścetihāsapurāṇadharmaśāstraṇāmiti |
yajño mantrabrāhmaṇasya. lokavṛttamitihāsapurāṇasaya.
lokavyavahāravyavasthānaṃ dharmaśāstrasya
viṣayaḥ, tatraikena na sarvaṃ vyavasthāpyate
iti yathāviṣayametāni pramāṇānīndriyādivaditi
// 62 //
children.translated_text: And if death and old age are indiscriminately assigned as <s>karma</s>, the consequence would be that the actions of everyone end with the accumulation of a begging bowl — then the rising above desires (<s>eṣaṇāvyutthāna</s>) would not be heard [in scripture]: 'Those ancient <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, learned and well-versed, did not desire progeny — what shall we do with progeny, we whose self is this world? They, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then practiced mendicancy.' And for one who has risen above desires, actions ending with the accumulation of a begging bowl are untenable. Therefore, the fruit does not indiscriminately motivate the agent. And because of the injunction of the four stages of life (<s>cāturāśramya</s>) in the <s>itihāsas</s>, <s>purāṇas</s>, and <s>dharmaśāstras</s>, a single stage of life (<s>aikāśramya</s>) is untenable. If [one says] 'those are not authoritative' — no, because their authority is acknowledged by authoritative means. For by an authoritative <s>brāhmaṇa</s> text, the authority of <s>itihāsa</s> and <s>purāṇa</s> is acknowledged: 'They — those very <s>Atharvāṅgirasas</s> — declared this <s>itihāsa-purāṇa</s>: the <s>itihāsa-purāṇa</s> is the fifth <s>Veda</s> among the <s>Vedas</s>.' Therefore it is inappropriate [to say] they are not authoritative. And if the <s>dharmaśāstra</s> were not authoritative, because of the loss of the practical conduct of living beings, the destruction of the world would follow. And because of the commonality of seers and promulgators, non-authority is untenable — for those who are the seers and promulgators of the <s>mantra-brāhmaṇa</s> texts are also [the seers and promulgators] of the <s>itihāsa-purāṇa</s> and <s>dharmaśāstra</s>. And because of the differentiation of subject-matter, the authority [of each] is according to its subject-matter — the subject-matter of the <s>mantra-brāhmaṇa</s> is different, and that of the <s>itihāsa-purāṇa</s> and <s>dharmaśāstra</s> is different. Sacrifice is the subject-matter of the <s>mantra-brāhmaṇa</s>; the conduct of the world is [that] of the <s>itihāsa-purāṇa</s>; the establishment of worldly transactions is the subject-matter of the <s>dharmaśāstra</s>. There, one [authority] does not establish everything — thus these are authoritative each in its own domain, like the sense-organs and the rest. [End of NyS 4.1.62]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.63]
Now, regarding what was said — 'because of the non-cessation of the continuity of afflictions' —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.63: [As in] the non-seeing of dreams by one who is deeply asleep, liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) [is tenable] because of the absence of afflictions.
the continuity of attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and the continuity of pleasure and pain are severed —
so too in liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). And this is cited as the form of the liberated self
by the knowers of <s>Brahman</s>. [End of NyS 4.1.63]
Just as for one deeply asleep, in the non-seeing of dreams,
[Section: NySBh 4.1.64]
And regarding what was said about the continuity of activity —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.64: There is no activity for the purpose of reconnection [with rebirth] for one whose afflictions are diminished.

children.text:
prakṣīṇeṣu rāgadveṣāmoheṣu
pravṛttirna pratisaṃdhānāya, pratisaṃdhistu pūrvajanmanivṛttau
punarjanma taccādṛṣṭakāritaṃ tasyāṃ prahīṇāyāṃ
janmāntarābhāvaḥ |
apratisaṃdhānam |
apavargaḥ|
karmavaiphalyaprasaṅga iticet ? na--
karmavipākapratisaṃvedanasyāpratyākhyānāt/
pūrvajanmanivṛttau punarjanma na bhavatītyucyate

children.translated_text: but the experiencing of the ripening of <s>karma</s> is not denied.
For all previous <s>karmas</s> ripen in the final birth.
[End of NyS 4.1.64]

When attachment (<s>rāga</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>) are exhausted, there is no activity for the purpose of reconnection. Reconnection means rebirth after the cessation of the previous life, and that is caused by the unseen [karmic force] (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>). When that [karmic force] is exhausted, there is no further birth — no reconnection — [that is] liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). If [one objects:] 'there would be the undesirable consequence of the fruitlessness of <s>karma</s>' — no, because the experiencing of the ripening of <s>karma</s> (<s>karmavipākapratisaṃvedana</s>) is not denied. It is said that when the previous life-activity ceases, rebirth does not occur —
[Section: NySBh 4.1.65]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.65: [Objection:] Because of the natural character of the continuity of afflictions, [their cessation is] not [possible].
The cessation of the continuity of afflictions is not tenable.

children.text: kasmāt ?, kleśasaṃtateḥ svābhāvikatvāt = anādiriyaṃ kleśasaṃtatiḥ na cānādiḥ
children.translated_text: Why? Because the continuity of afflictions is natural. This continuity of afflictions is beginningless, and what is beginningless
cannot be cut off. [End of NyS 4.1.65]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.66]
Here, someone offers a solution —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.66: Just as the non-existence prior to production is non-eternal [though beginningless], so too there is non-eternality even in what is natural.
Just as the non-existence prior to production, which is beginningless, is removed by the produced entity — so too the natural continuity of afflictions is non-eternal. [End of NyS 4.1.66]
[Section: NySBh 4.1.67]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.67: Indeed, like the non-eternality of the blackness of an atom.
Another says — just as the blackness of an atom, though beginningless, is nevertheless non-eternal through conjunction with fire, so too the continuity of afflictions. [End of NyS 4.1.67]

children.text:
sataḥ khalu dharmo nityatvamanityatvaṃ ca
tattvaṃ bhāve 'bhāve bhāktamiti|
'anādiraṇuśyāmatā'
iti hetvabhāvādayuktam|
anutpattidharmakamanityamiti
nātra heturastīti/
children.translated_text: The eternality and non-eternality of an existent property is real with respect to existence and non-existence [respectively], and figurative [otherwise]. 'The beginningless blackness of an atom' — this is unjustified because there is no valid reason. [The claim that] what has the character of non-production is non-eternal — there is no reason for this.
[Section: NySBh 4.1.68]
But here is the [correct] solution —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.68: And because attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and the rest are caused by false conception (<s>saṃkalpa</s>), [their cessation is possible].

children.text:
'karmanimittatvāditaretaranimittatvācca'
iti samuccayaḥ, mithyāsaṃkalpebhyo rañjanīyakopanīyamohanīyebhyo
rāgadveṣamohā utpadyante, karma ca kattvanikāyanirvartakaṃ
naiyamikān rāgadveṣamohān nirvartayati--
niyamadarśanāt |
dṛśyate hi kaścitsattvanikāyo rāgabahulaḥ
kaścid dveṣabahulaḥ kaścid
mohabahulaḥ iti, itaretaranimittā ca
rāgādīnāmutpattiḥ
umūḍho rajyati mūḍhaḥ kupyati. rakto muhyati.
kupito muhyati|
sarvamithyāsaṃkalpānāṃ
tattvajñānādanutpattiḥ kāraṇānutpattau ca kāryānutpatteriti
rāgādīnāmatyantamanutpattiriti|
'anādiśca kleśasaṃtatiḥ' ity ayuktam-- sarve ime khalvādhyātmikā
bhāvā anādinā prabandhena pravartante śarīrādayo.
na jātvatra kaścidanutpannapūrvaḥ prathamata utpadyate 'nyatra
tattvajñānāt|
na caivaṃ saty anutpattidharmakaṃ
kiñcid vyayadharmakaṃ pratijñāyate iti/
karma ca sattvanikāyanirvartakaṃ tattvajñānakṛtād
mithyāsaṃkalpavighātānna rāgādyutpattinimittaṃ
bhavati sukhaduḥkhasaṃvittiphalaṃ tu bhavatīti
// 68 //
children.translated_text: 'Because of being caused by <s>karma</s>, and because of mutual causation' — this is a conjunction [of reasons]. From false conceptions (<s>mithyāsaṃkalpa</s>) — those that excite, anger, and delude — attachment, aversion, and delusion arise. And <s>karma</s>, which produces classes of beings, produces fixed types of attachment, aversion, and delusion — because of the observation of a fixed rule. For it is observed that some class of beings is predominantly attached, some predominantly averse, some predominantly deluded. And the arising of attachment and the rest is from mutual causation — the deluded one becomes attached, the deluded one becomes angry; the attached one becomes deluded; the angry one becomes deluded. From the knowledge of truth (<s>tattvajñāna</s>), all false conceptions do not arise; and when the cause does not arise, the effect does not arise — therefore there is the absolute non-arising of attachment and the rest. And 'the continuity of afflictions is beginningless' is unjustified — for all these internal states continue in a beginningless series, beginning with the body and the rest. Never here does something that has not previously arisen arise for the first time, except through the knowledge of truth. And this being so, nothing is asserted to have the character of non-production and the character of destruction. And <s>karma</s>, which produces classes of beings, because of the destruction of false conceptions accomplished by the knowledge of truth, does not become the cause of the arising of attachment and the rest; but it does become [the cause] of the fruit that is the experience of pleasure and pain. [End of NyS 4.1.68]

children.text: // iti vātsyāyanaviracite nyāyabhāṣye caturthādhyāyasya prathamamāhnikaṃ samāptam /
children.translated_text: Thus ends the first section of the fourth chapter of the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> composed by <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
Now the second section of the fourth chapter of the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s>.

children.text:
kiṃ nu khalu bho yāvanto viṣayāstāvatsu pratyekaṃ tattvajñānamutpadyate ? atha kvacidutpadyate ? iti|
kaścātra viśeṣaḥ ?, na tāvadekaikatra |
yāvadviṣayamutpadyate-- jñeyānāmānantyāt, nāpi kvacidutpadyate-- tatra notpadyate tatrānivṛtto moha iti mohaśeṣaprasaṅgaḥ-- na cānyaviṣayeṇa tattvajñānenānyaviṣayo mohaḥ śakyaḥ pratiṣeddhumiti|
mithyājñānaṃ vai khalu moho na tattvajñānasyānutpattimātraṃ tacca mithyājñānaṃ yatra viṣaye pravartamānaṃ saṃsārabījaṃ bhavati sa viṣayastattvato jñeya iti|
kiṃ punastanmithyājñānam ?, anātmanyātmagrahaḥ |
ahamasmīti moho 'haṅkāra iti. anātmānaṃ khalvahamasmīti paśyato dṛṣṭirahaṅkāra iti|
kiṃ punastadarthajātaṃ yadviṣayo 'haṅkāraḥ ?, śarīrendriyamanovedanābuddhayaḥ|
kathaṃ tadviṣayo 'haṅkāraḥ saṃsārabījaṃ bhavati ?, ayaṃ khalu śarīrādyarthajātam ahamasmīti vyavasitaḥ taducchedenātmocchedaṃ manyamāno 'nucchedatṛṣṇāpariplutaḥ punaḥ punastadupādatte tadupādadāno janmamaraṇāya yatate tenāviyogād nātyantaṃ duḥkhādvimucyate iti|
yastu duḥkhaṃ duḥkhāyatanaṃ duḥkhānuṣaktaṃ sukhaṃ ca sarvamidaṃ duḥkhamiti paśyati sa duḥkhaṃ parijānāti parijñātaṃ ca duḥkhaṃ prahīṇaṃ bhavati-- anupādānāt saviṣānnavat, evaṃ doṣān karma ca duḥkhaheturiti paśyati|
na cāprahīṇeṣu doṣeṣu duḥkhaprabandhocchedena śakyaṃ bhavitumiti doṣān jahāti. prahīṇeṣu ca doṣeṣu na pravṛttiḥ pratisaṃdhānāyetyuktam, pretyabhāvaphaladuḥkhāni ca jñeyāni vyavasthāpayati karma ca doṣāṃśca praheyān, apavargo 'dhigantavyastasyādhigamopāyastattvajñānam. evaṃ catasṛbhirvidhābhiḥ prameyaṃ vibhaktamāsevamānasya |

children.translated_text: practices [it],
and develops [it] — right vision (<s>samyagdarśana</s>),
the understanding of things as they really are,
the knowledge of truth arises.

Now then, does the knowledge of truth arise regarding each and every object, or does it arise regarding some? And what is the distinction here? Firstly, it does not arise regarding each — because of the infinity of knowable things. Nor does it arise regarding just some — because where it does not arise, delusion is not removed there, and the consequence of residual delusion [would follow] — for delusion regarding one object cannot be negated by the knowledge of truth regarding another object. False knowledge is indeed delusion, not merely the non-arising of true knowledge. And that false knowledge, operating regarding which object becomes the seed of <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) — that object is to be known in truth. What then is that false knowledge? The apprehension of self in what is not-self — 'I am' — this is delusion, egoism (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>). One who sees the not-self as 'I am' — that seeing is egoism. What then is that class of things that is the object of egoism? Body, sense-organs, mind, feeling, and cognitions. How does egoism regarding these become the seed of <s>saṃsāra</s>? This [being], having determined the class of things beginning with the body as 'I am,' thinking that the destruction of those is the destruction of the self, overwhelmed by the craving for non-destruction, repeatedly takes up those [body, etc.], and taking them up, strives toward birth and death — because of non-separation from that, one is not absolutely freed from suffering. But one who sees suffering, the abode of suffering, pleasure associated with suffering — all this as suffering — that one comprehends suffering. And suffering that is comprehended becomes abandoned — because of non-grasping, like poisoned food. Similarly, one sees faults and <s>karma</s> as the cause of suffering. And without the abandonment of faults, it is not possible for the continuity of suffering to be cut off — therefore one abandons the faults. And when the faults are abandoned, 'there is no activity for reconnection' — this has been stated. And one establishes the sufferings that are the fruits of the hereafter as things to be known, and <s>karma</s> and faults as things to be abandoned; liberation is to be attained, and the means to its attainment is the knowledge of truth. Thus, for one who, having divided the knowable into four categories, cultivates [this knowledge],
[Section: NySBh 4.2.1]
And thus —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.1: From the knowledge of truth regarding [things] caused by faults, there is the cessation of egoism (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>).

children.text: śarīrādi duḥkhāntaṃ prameyaṃ doṣanimittam, tadviṣayatvānmithyājñānasya tadidaṃ tattvajñānaṃ tadviṣayamutpannam ahaṅkāraṃ nivartayati-- samānaviṣaye tayorvirodhāt. evaṃ tattvajñānāt"
children.translated_text: The knowable, from the body to suffering, is caused by faults. Because false knowledge has that as its object, this knowledge of truth, having arisen regarding that same object, removes egoism — because of the contradiction of the two regarding the same object. Thus, from the knowledge of truth —

'from the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, faults, and false knowledge, because of the absence of the immediately preceding [cause], there is liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) [NyS 1.1.2].'

children.text: iti, sa cāyaṃ śāstrārthasaṃgraho 'nūdyate nāpūrvo vidhīyate iti // 1 //
children.translated_text: And this is a summary of the teaching of the śāstra that is recapitulated, not a new injunction. [End of NyS 4.2.1]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.2]
But in the order of contemplation (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>) —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.2: Form and the rest, which are objects caused by faults, are produced by [false] conception.

children.text: kāmaviṣayā indriyārthā iti rūpādaya ucyante. te mityā saṃkalpyamānā rāgadveṣamohān pravartayanti tān pūrvaṃ prasaṃcakṣīta, tāṃśca prasaṃcakṣāṇasya rūpādiviṣayo mithyāsaṃkalpo nivartate, tannivṛttau adhyātmaṃ śarīrādi prasaṃcakṣīta, tatprasaṃkhyānādadhyātmaviṣayo 'haṅkāro nivartate. soyamadhyātmaṃ bahiśca viviktacitto viharan mukta ityucyate // 2 //
children.translated_text: Objects of desire — the objects of the sense-organs — are called form and the rest. When falsely conceived, they set in motion attachment, aversion, and delusion. One should first contemplate those. And for one contemplating those, the false conception regarding the objects of form and the rest ceases. Upon its cessation, one should contemplate internally the body and the rest. From that contemplation, the egoism directed toward internal [objects] ceases. One who thus dwells with a mind discerning both internally and externally is called 'liberated.' [End of NyS 4.2.2]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.3]

children.text: ataḥ paraṃ kācit saṃjñā heyā kācid bhāvayitavyetyupadiśyate, nārthanirākaraṇamarthopādānaṃ vā, kathamiti---
children.translated_text: Hereafter, it is taught that a certain notion is to be abandoned and a certain [notion] is to be cultivated — it is not the rejection or acceptance of [external] objects. How? —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.3: But caused by those [faults] is the false attribution of wholeness (<s>avayavyabhimāna</s>).

children.text:
teṣām |
doṣāṇāṃ nimittaṃ tv avayavyabhimānaḥ, sā ca khalu strīsaṃjñā sapariṣkārā puruṣasya puruṣasaṃjñā ca striyāḥ, pariṣkāraśca |
nimittasaṃjñā anuvyañjanasaṃjñā ca, nimittasaṃjñā |
rasanāśrotraṃ dantoṣṭhaṃ cakṣurnāsikam, anuvyañjanasaṃjñā |
itthaṃ dantau itthamoṣṭhāviti, seyaṃ saṃjñā kāmaṃ vardhayati tadanuṣaktāṃśca doṣān vivarjanīyān|
children.translated_text: tongue, ear, teeth, lips, eye, nose. The notion of secondary marks — 'such teeth, such lips' — this notion increases desire, and the faults associated with it are to be abandoned.
But the abandonment of this [notion] is through the differentiated notion of parts (<s>avayavasaṃjñā</s>).

children.text: keśalomamāṃsaśoṇitāsthisnāyuśirākaphapittoccārādisaṃjñā tāmaśubhasaṃjñetyācakṣate. tāmasya bhāvayataḥ kāmarāgaḥ prahīyate. satyeva ca dvividhe viṣaye kācit saṃjñā bhāvanīyā kācit parivarjanīyetyupadiśyate yathā viṣasaṃpṛkte 'nne annasaṃjñopādānāyā viṣasaṃjñā prahāṇāyeti // 3 //
children.translated_text: The notion of hair, body-hair, flesh, blood, bone, sinew, vein, phlegm, bile, excrement, and the rest — this they call the notion of the impure (<s>aśubhasaṃjñā</s>). For one who cultivates that, sensual desire (<s>kāmarāga</s>) is abandoned. And when there is indeed a twofold object, it is taught that a certain notion is to be cultivated and a certain [notion] is to be abandoned — just as, regarding food mixed with poison, the notion of food is for acceptance, and the notion of poison is for abandonment. [End of NyS 4.2.3]

Of those — faults — the cause is the false attribution of wholeness. And that is: the notion 'woman' with her adornments, for a man; and the notion 'man' for a woman, and the adornments. And the notion of marks and the notion of secondary marks. The notion of marks —
[Section: NySBh 4.2.4] Now, for one who wishes to reject the [external] objects, the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is established —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.4: The doubt [arises] from the twofold [nature of] knowledge and ignorance (<s>vidyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s>).

children.text: sadasatorupalambhād vidyā dvividhā. sadasatoranupalambhād avidyapi dvividhā, upalabhyamāne 'vayavini vidyādvaividhyāt saṃśayaḥ. anupalabhyamāne cāvidyādvaividhyāt saṃśayaḥ, so 'yam avayavī yadyupalabhyate athāpi nopalabhyate na kathañcana saṃśayād mucyate iti // 4 //
children.translated_text: Because what exists and what does not exist are both apprehended, knowledge is twofold. Because what exists and what does not exist are both not apprehended, ignorance too is twofold. When the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is apprehended, there is doubt because of the twofold nature of knowledge. And when it is not apprehended, there is doubt because of the twofold nature of ignorance. Thus, whether the composite whole is apprehended or not apprehended, one is in no way freed from doubt. [End of NyS 4.2.4]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.5]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.5: There is no doubt regarding that, because of the established validity of the previously stated reasons.

children.text: tasminn anupapannaḥ saṃśayaḥ, kasmāt ?, pūrvoktahetūnāmapratiṣedhādasti dravyāntarārambha iti // 5 //
children.translated_text: Doubt regarding that is untenable. Why? Because the previously stated reasons have not been refuted — the origination of a different substance is established. [End of NyS 4.2.5]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.6]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.6: Then, because of the untenability of [the composite's] occurrence, there should be no doubt either.
Then, because of the untenability of occurrence too, there should be no doubt — [i.e.,] the composite whole does not exist. [End of NyS 4.2.6]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.7]
That [the opponent] elaborates —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.7: Because the parts do not occur in the whole or in a part [of the whole], the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) does not exist.

children.text: ekaiko 'vayavo na tāvat kṛtsne 'vayavinirvatate-- tayoḥ parimāṇabhedād avayavāntarasaṃbandhābhāvaprasaṅgācca, nāpyavayavyekadeśe-- na hyasyānye avayavā ekadeśabhūtāḥ santīti // 7 //
children.translated_text: A single part does not occur in the entire composite whole — because of the difference in magnitude between them, and because the consequence of the absence of connection with other parts would follow. Nor [does a part occur] in a part of the composite whole — for it has no other parts that constitute a part [of the whole]. [End of NyS 4.2.7]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.8] But does the composite whole occur in the parts? —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.8: And because of non-occurrence in them [the parts], the composite whole does not exist.

children.text: na tāvat pratyavayavaṃ vartate-- tayoḥ parimāṇabhedād dravyasya. caikadravyatvaprasaṅgāt, nāpyekadeśe-- sarveṣvanyāvayavābhāvāt, tadevaṃ na yuktaḥ saṃśayaḥ-- nāstyavayavīti // 8 //
children.translated_text: It does not occur in each individual part — because of the difference in magnitude between the substance [and the part], and because the consequence of the substance being a single substance [identical with each part] would follow. Nor [does it occur] in a part [of the whole] — because of the absence of other parts in all [individual parts]. Thus doubt is not justified — the composite whole does not exist. [End of NyS 4.2.8]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.9]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.9: And because of non-occurrence separately from the parts.
And separately from the parts —
because the property is not grasped apart from its substrates — the reasoning is the same. [End of NyS 4.2.9]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.10]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.10: And the parts are not [identical with] the composite whole.
[Section: NySBh 4.2.11]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.11: Because in a single [whole] there is no division, the use of words implying division is untenable — hence there is no [valid] question.

children.text: kiṃ pratyavayavaṃ kṛtsno 'vayavī vartate athaikadeśeneti nopapadyate praśnaḥ, kasmāt ?, ekasmin bhedābhāvād bhedaśabdaprayogānupapatteḥ |
children.translated_text: The question 'Does the composite whole occur in each part as a whole or by a portion?' is untenable. Why? Because in a single [whole] there is no division, the use of words implying division is untenable.

children.text: 'kṛtsnam' ityanekasyāśeṣābhidhānam. 'ekadeśaḥ' iti nānātve kasyacidabhidhānam, tāvimau kṛsnaikadeśaśabdau bhedaviṣayau naikasminn avayavinyupapadyete-- bhedābhāvāditi // 11 //
children.translated_text: 'Whole' (<s>kṛtsna</s>) is the designation of many without remainder. 'Part' (<s>ekadeśa</s>) is the designation of some among many. These two words 'whole' and 'part,' which pertain to division, are not applicable to the single composite whole — because there is no division [in it]. [End of NyS 4.2.11]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.12]
That 'the [composite whole] does not occur by a portion because of the absence of other parts' is not a [valid] reason —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.12: Even given the existence of other parts, because of non-occurrence [of the composite in them], the reason is not valid.

children.text:
avayavāntarābhāvāditi, yadyapyekadeśo 'vayavāntarabhūtaḥ syāt tathāpyavayave 'vayavāntaraṃ varteta nāvayavīti-- anyo 'vayavīti|
anyāvayavabhāvepyavṛtteḥ-- 'avayavino naikadeśena vṛttiḥ-- anyāvayavābhāvāt' ityahetuḥ|
vṛttiḥ kathamiticet ? ekasyānekatrāśrayāśritasaṃbandhalakṣaṇā prāptiḥ|
āśrayāśritabhāvaḥ kathamiticet ? yasya yato 'nyatrātmalābhānupapattiḥ sa āśrayaḥ na kāraṇadravyebhyo 'nyatra kāryadravyamātmānaṃ labhate. viparyayastu kāraṇadravyeṣviti|

children.translated_text: If [one asks] how this [applies] to eternal [substances]? It is established by observation in non-eternal [substances].

children.text: nityeṣu dravyeṣu kathamāśrayāśrayibhāva iticet ? anityeṣu dravyaguṇeṣu darśanādāśrayāśrayibhāvasya nityeṣu siddhiriti|
children.translated_text: If [one asks] how the relation of substrate and supported [applies] to eternal substances? Because of its being observed in non-eternal substances and qualities, the relation of substrate and supported is established for eternal [substances] also.

children.text: tasmādavayavyabhimānaḥ pratiṣidhyate niḥśreyasakāmasya. nāvayavī. yathā rūpādiṣu mityāsaṃkalpo na rūpādaya iti // 12 //
children.translated_text: Therefore the notion of the composite whole is to be negated by one who desires the highest good. The composite whole does not exist. Just as the false conception regarding form and the rest [is to be negated] — [it is not that] form and the rest do not exist. [End of NyS 4.2.12]

'Because of the absence of other parts' — even if a portion existed as another part, still in the part, another part would occur, not the composite whole — [for] the composite whole is different. Even given the existence of other parts, because of non-occurrence — 'the composite whole does not occur by a portion because of the absence of other parts' is not a valid reason. How then does occurrence [work]? The relation defined as one [thing] being the substrate and the supported in many [substrates] is contact (<s>prāpti</s>). How does the relation of substrate and supported [work]? That without which a thing cannot obtain its existence elsewhere is the substrate — the product-substance does not obtain its existence apart from the causal substances. The reverse [holds] for causal substances.
[Section: NySBh 4.2.13] Even though he maintains 'the non-apprehension of everything is because of the non-establishment of the composite whole [NyS 2.1.34],' [the opponent] says this —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.13: That apprehension is like the perception of a mass of hair by one with an eye-disease (<s>taimirika</s>).

children.text: yathaikaikaḥ keśastaimirikeṇa nopalabhyate keśasamūhastūpalabhyate tathaikaiko 'ṇurnopalabhyate aṇusaṃcayastūpalabhyate tadidamaṇusamūhaviṣayaṃ grahaṇamiti // 13 //
children.translated_text: Just as a person with an eye-disease does not perceive each individual hair but perceives a mass of hair, so too each individual atom is not perceived but an aggregate of atoms is perceived — this apprehension has an aggregate of atoms as its object. [End of NyS 4.2.13]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.14]

children.text: NyS_4,2.14: svaviṣayānatikrameṇendriyasya paṭumandabhāvād viṣayagrahaṇasya tathābhāvo nāviṣaye pravṛttiḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 4.2.14: Because of the keen and dull states of the sense-organs without exceeding their own domain, there are such states of object-apprehension — there is no operation in what is not its domain.

children.text:
yathāviṣayamindriyāṇāṃ paṭumandabhāvād viṣayagrahaṇānāṃ paṭumandabhāvo bhavati |
cakṣuḥ khalu prakṛṣyamāṇaṃ nāviṣayaṃ gandhaṃ gṛhṇāti. nikṛṣyamāṇaṃ ca na svaviṣayāt pracyavate, soyaṃ taimirikaḥ kaściccakṣurviṣayaṃ keśaṃ na gṛhṇāti gṛhṇāti ca keśasamūham. ubhayaṃ hy ataimirikeṇa cakṣuṣā gṛhyate, paramāṇavastv atīndriyāḥ |
indriyāviṣayabhūtā kenacidindriyeṇa gṛhyante samuditāstu gṛhyante ityaviṣaye pravṛttirindriyasya prasajyeta-- na jātvarthāntaramaṇubhyo gṛhyate iti. te khalvime paramāṇavaḥ saṃhatā gṛhyamāṇā atīndriyatvaṃ jahati viyuktāścāgṛhyamāṇā indriyaviṣayatvaṃ na labhante iti soyaṃ dravyāntarānutpattāvatimahān vyāghāta ityupapadyate dravyāntaraṃ yad grahaṇasya viṣaya iti|
saṃcayamātraṃ viṣaya iticet ? na-- saṃcayasya saṃyogabhāvāttasya cātīndriyasyāgrahaṇādayuktam|
children.translated_text: If [one says] the mere aggregate is the object? No — because the aggregate consists of conjunction, and that [conjunction], being beyond the senses, is not grasped — this is unjustified.

children.text: saṃcayaḥ khalvanekasya saṃyogaḥ sa ca gahyamāṇāśrayo gṛhyate nātīndriyāśrayaḥ. bhavati hīdamanena saṃyuktam' iti. tasmādayuktametaditi|
children.translated_text: An aggregate is the conjunction of many, and that is grasped when its substrates are grasped, not when its substrates are beyond the senses. For [one says] 'this is conjoined with that.' Therefore this is unjustified.

And for an object that is grasped by the sense-organs, obstruction and the like are apprehended as causes of non-apprehension. Therefore the non-apprehension of atoms is not due to the weakness of the sense-organs — just as the non-apprehension of smell and the like by the eye is not due to the weakness of the sense-organ. [End of NyS 4.2.14]

Because of the keen and dull states of the sense-organs with respect to their respective domains, there are keen and dull states of object-apprehension. The eye, even when intensified, does not grasp smell, which is not its domain. And when weakened, it does not deviate from its own domain. Now this person with an eye-disease does not grasp a single hair which is an object of the eye, yet grasps a mass of hair. Both are grasped by the eye of a person without eye-disease. But atoms are beyond the senses. Being objects not within the domain of any sense-organ, [yet claiming that] when accumulated they are grasped — this would entail the sense-organ's operation in what is not its domain, since no other substance beyond atoms is ever grasped [on that view]. For these atoms, when conjoined and being grasped, would lose their being-beyond-the-senses, and when separated and not being grasped, would not obtain the status of being objects of the senses — and this is a very great contradiction if no different substance is produced. Thus it is justified that a different substance is the object of apprehension.
[Section: NySBh 4.2.15]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.15: And in this way, there would be the consequence of the parts of the parts [regressing] until dissolution.

children.text: yaḥ khalvavayavino 'vayaveṣu vṛttipratiṣedhādabhāvaḥ soyamavayavasyāvayaveṣu prasajyamānaḥ sarvapralayāya vā kalpeta niravayavādvā nivarteta. ubhayathā copalabdhiviṣayasyābhāvaḥ tadabhāvādupalabdhyabhāvaḥ, upalabdhyāśrayaścāyaṃ vṛttipratiṣedhaḥ sa āśrayaṃ vyāghnan ātmaghātāya kalpate iti // 15 //
children.translated_text: The non-existence of the composite whole due to the denial of its occurrence in parts — this [denial], when applied to the parts of the parts, would tend either toward universal dissolution or would stop at what is partless. In both cases, the object of apprehension would not exist; from its non-existence, there would be non-apprehension. And this denial of occurrence is based on apprehension — so it, destroying its own basis, tends toward self-destruction. [End of NyS 4.2.15]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.16]
And moreover —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.16: There is no [universal] dissolution, because of the existence of atoms.

children.text: avayavavibhāgamāśritya vṛttipratiṣedhādabhāvaḥ prasajyamāno niravayavāt paramāṇornivartate na sarvapralayāya kalpate|

children.translated_text: The partlessness of the atom [is established] because there is no consequence of something smaller [than it] from divisions, since nothing smaller subsists therein.

children.text: loṣṭasya khalu pravibhajyamānāvayavasyālpataramalpatamamuttaramuttaraṃ bhavati sa cācamalpataraprasaṅgaḥ yasmānnalpataramasti |
children.translated_text: For a clod being divided into parts, each successive [part] becomes smaller and smallest — and that process of becoming smaller stops where there is nothing smaller.

children.text: yaḥ paramo 'lpastatra nivartate. yataśca nālpīyosti taṃ pṛramāṇuṃ pracakṣmahe iti // 16 //
children.translated_text: What is the ultimate smallest — the process stops there. And that from which there is nothing smaller — we call that the <s>paramāṇu</s> (atom). [End of NyS 4.2.16]
The non-existence consequent upon the denial of occurrence, when applied through the division of parts, stops at the partless atom and does not tend toward universal dissolution.
[Section: NySBh 4.2.17]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.17: Or what is beyond cutting (<s>truṭi</s>).
Because the division of parts has no [further] standing, and because of the innumerability of substances — the cessation of cutting [is established]. [End of NyS 4.2.17]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.18]
Now one who holds the doctrine of non-apprehension, thinking 'nothing at all exists,' says —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.18: Because of the pervasion of space (<s>ākāśa</s>), that [atom] is untenable.
The atom — partless and eternal — is untenable. Why? Because of the pervasion of space.
The atom is permeated by space both inside and outside.
Being permeated, because of permeation, it has parts; because of having parts, it is non-eternal. [End of NyS 4.2.18]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.19]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.19: Or [there would follow] the non-omnipresence of space.
But if this is not accepted —
that there is no space inside the atom? — then the consequence of non-omnipresence [of space] would follow. [End of NyS 4.2.19]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.20]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.20: 'Inside' and 'outside' are said of a product-substance in reference to intervening causes; in a non-product, there is no such [distinction].

children.text: 'antaḥ' iti pihitaṃ kāraṇāntaraiḥ kāraṇamucyate, 'bahiḥ' iti ca vyavadhāyakamavyavahitaṃ kāraṇamevocyate. tadetat kāryadravyasya saṃbhavati. nāṇoḥ-- akāryatvāt |
children.translated_text: 'Inside' refers to a cause that is covered by other causes; 'outside' refers to a cause that is the intervening [or outermost] unobstructed cause. This applies to product-substances, not to the atom — because it is not a product.

children.text: akārye hi paramāṇāv antarbahirityasyābhāvaḥ, yatra cāsya bhāvo 'ṇukāryaṃ tat na paramāṇuḥ, yato hi nālpataramasti sa paramāṇuriti // 20 //
children.translated_text: For in the atom, which is a non-product, the [distinction of] 'inside' and 'outside' does not apply. And where this [distinction] does apply — that is a product of atoms, not the atom itself; for what has nothing smaller than it — that is the atom. [End of NyS 4.2.20]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.21]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.21: And [space is] omnipresent, because of the pervasion of all conjunctions, sounds, and [their] manifestation.
Sounds produced anywhere pervade space;

children.text: tadāśrayā bhavanti. manobhiḥ paramāṇubhistatkāryaiśca saṃyogā bhavantyākāśe. nāsaṃyuktamākāśena kiñcinmūrtadravyamupalabhyate tasmānnāsarvagatamiti // 21 //
children.translated_text: they have [space] as their substrate. Conjunctions occur in space — of minds, atoms, and their products. No corporeal substance is apprehended that is not conjoined with space; therefore [space] is not non-omnipresent. [End of NyS 4.2.21]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.22]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.22: And non-displacement, non-obstruction, and all-pervasiveness are properties of space (<s>ākāśa</s>).

children.text: saṃsapatā pratighātinā dravyeṇa na vyūhyate tathā kāṣṭhenodakam, kasmāt ?, niravayavatvārt, sapacca pratighāti dravyaṃ na viṣṭabhnāti |
children.translated_text: It is not displaced by a substance that is moving and capable of resistance, in the way water [is displaced] by wood. Why? Because it is partless. And a substance capable of resistance does not obstruct it —

children.text: nāsya kriyāhetuṃ guṇaṃ pratibadhnāti, kasmāt ? asparśatvāt viparyaye hi viṣṭambho dṛṣṭa iti, sāvayave sparśavati dravye dṛṣṭaṃ dharmaṃ viparīte nāśaṅkitumarhati //
children.translated_text: it does not obstruct its quality that is the cause of activity. Why? Because [space] is without touch. For in the contrary case, obstruction is observed — in a substance that has parts and has touch. One should not suspect a property observed in the opposite [kind of substance] to apply to [space, which is] the contrary. The negation of atomic products from the consequence of a sub-atomic part being smaller than the atom —

children.text: sāvayavatve cāṇoraṇvavayavo 'ṇutara iti prasajyate, kasmāt ?, kāryakāraṇadravyayoḥ parimāṇabhedadarśanāt. tasmādaṇvavayavasyāṇutaratvam, yastu sāvayavaḥ aṇukāryaṃ taditi. tasmādaṇukāryamidaṃ pratiṣidhyate iti|
children.translated_text: And if the atom had parts, a sub-atomic part would be smaller — this would follow. Why? Because of the observation of a difference in magnitude between cause-substance and product-substance. Therefore the sub-atomic part would be smaller; but what has parts is a product of atoms. Therefore this atomic product is negated.
And the non-eternality of the product is due to the separation of its causes, not due to the pervasion of space.
The non-eternality of a clod is due to the separation of its parts, not due to the entry of space [into it]. [End of NyS 4.2.22]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.23]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.23: And because of the tenability of shape for corporeal [substances], the existence of parts [is established].

children.text: paricchinnānāṃ hi sparśavatāṃ saṃsthānaṃ trikoṇaṃ caturasraṃ samaṃ parimaṇḍalamityupapadyate yattat saṃsthānaṃ so 'vayavasaṃniveśaḥ parimaṇḍalāścāṇavastasmāt sāvayavā iti // 23 //
children.translated_text: For delimited substances that possess touch, shapes such as triangular, quadrilateral, even, and spherical are tenable. That shape is an arrangement of parts. And atoms are spherical; therefore they have parts. [End of NyS 4.2.23]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.24]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.24: And because of the tenability of conjunction.

children.text: madhye sann aṇuḥ pūrvāparābhyāmaṇubhyāṃ saṃyuktastayorvyavadhānaṃ kurute. vyavadhānenānunamīyate-- pūrvabhāgena pūrveṇāṇunā saṃyujyate parabhāgena pareṇāṇunā saṃyujyate. yau tau pūrvāparau bhāgau tāv asyāvayavau. evaṃ sarvataḥ saṃyujyamānasya sarvato bhāgā avayavā iti // 24 //
children.translated_text: An atom, being in the middle, conjoined with the preceding and following atoms, creates an interposition between them. By the interposition, [parts] are inferred — it conjoins with the preceding atom by its anterior part and with the following atom by its posterior part. Those anterior and posterior parts are its parts. Thus, for [an atom] that is conjoined on all sides, parts exist on all sides as parts. [End of NyS 4.2.24]

children.text:
yattāvat--
"mūrtimatāṃ saṃsthānopapatteravayavasadbhāvaḥ 23"
iti. atroktam|
kimuktam ?, 'vibhāgālpataraprasaṅgasya
yato nālpīyastatra nivṛtteḥ, aṇvavayavasya
cāṇutaratvaprasaṅgādaṇukāryapratiṣedhaḥ'
iti|
yatpunaretat--
"saṃyogopapatteśca"
iti ?, sparśavattvād vyavadhānam. āśrayasya
cāvyāptyā bhāgabhaktiḥ uktaṃ cātra-- sparśavānaṇuḥ
sparśavatoraṇvoḥ pratighātāt vyavadhāyako
na sāvayavatvāt, sparśavattvācca vyavadhāne
saty aṇusaṃyogo nāśrayaṃ vyāpnotīti
bhāgabhaktirbhavati |
bhāgavānivāyamiti, uktaṃ nātra-- 'vibhāge ālpataraprasaṅgasya

children.translated_text: since there is no cessation at what is smaller;
and because of the consequence of the part of an atom being smaller than the atom, the effect of the atom is precluded.'

As for the [argument] — 'because of the tenability of configuration in corporeal [things], the existence of parts [is established]' (4.2.23) — regarding this it has been said. What was said? 'Because of the consequence of smallerness through division, since there is no cessation at what is smaller, and because of the consequence of the atom's part being smaller than the atom, the effect of the atom is precluded.' And as for this — 'and because of the tenability of conjunction' — interposition [occurs] because of possessing tangibility. And through the non-pervasion of the substrate, there is attribution of parts. And it has been said regarding this — the atom, possessing tangibility, creates an interposition through the mutual resistance of two tangible atoms, not because of having parts. And because of its tangibility, when there is interposition, the conjunction of atoms does not pervade the substrate — hence there is attribution of parts. [One says:] 'it is as though it has parts.' [But] it has been said — this is not [so] here — 'because of the consequence of smallerness through division,
[Section: NySBh 4.2.25]

children.text:
mūrtimatāṃ ca saṃsthānopapatteḥ
saṃyogopapatteśca paramāṇūnāṃ
sāvayavattvamitihetvoḥ---
children.translated_text: The two reasons for the atoms having parts — configuration of corporeal things and tenability of conjunction —
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.25: Because of producing infinite regress and because infinite regress is untenable, there is no refutation.

children.text:
yāvad mūrtimad yāvacca saṃyujyate tat sarvaṃ sāvayavamityanavasthākāriṇāvimau hetū.
sācānavasthā nopapadyate.
satyāmanavasthāyāṃ satyau hetū syātāṃ.
tasmādapratiṣedhoyaṃ niravayavatvasyeti|
vibhāgaśca vibhajyamānahānernopapadyate tasmāt pralayāntatā nopapadyate iti|
anavasthāyāṃ capratyadhikaraṇaṃ dravyāvayavānāmānantyāt
parimāṇabhedānāṃ gurutvasya cāgrahaṇaṃ samānaparimāṇatvaṃ
cāvayavāvayavinoḥ paramāṇvavayavavibhāgādūrdhvamiti
// 25 //
children.translated_text: Whatever is corporeal and whatever conjoins — all of that has parts — these two reasons produce infinite regress. And that infinite regress is untenable. If there were an infinite regress, the two reasons would hold. Therefore, there is no refutation of partlessness. And division too is untenable because of the diminution of what is being divided — therefore the conclusion of dissolution [of everything into nothing] is untenable. And in the [hypothetical] infinite regress, because of the infinity of substance-parts at each substrate, the distinctions of size and gravity would not be apprehended, and there would be equality of size between the part and the whole — [which obtains] beyond the division of the atom's parts. [End of NyS 4.2.25]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.26]

children.text:
yadidaṃ bhavān buddhirāśritya 'buddhiviṣayāḥ
santīti manyate mithyābuddhaya etāḥ, yadi
hi tattvabuddhayaḥ syurbuddhyā vivecane
kriyamāṇe yathātmyaṃ buddhiviṣayāṇāmupalabhyeta---
children.translated_text: Now, you rely on cognition and think 'the objects of cognition exist.' [But] these are false cognitions. For if they were true cognitions, then when discrimination is being performed by cognition, the true nature of the objects of cognition would be apprehended —

children.text: NyS_4,2.26: buddhyā vivecanāttu bhāvānāṃ yāthātmyānupalabdhistantvapakarṣaṇe paṭasadbhāvānupalabdhivattadanupalabdhiḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 4.2.26: But because of the non-apprehension of the true nature of things through discrimination by cognition, [it is] like the non-apprehension of the existence of a cloth when the threads are separated — that non-apprehension [follows].

children.text:
yathā 'ayaṃ tanturayaṃ tantuḥ' iti pratyekaṃ
tantuṣu vivicyamāneṣu nārthāntaraṃ kiñcidupalabhyate

children.translated_text: that could be the object of the cognition of 'cloth' — because of the non-apprehension of its true nature.
The cognition of 'cloth,' arising when the object does not exist, is a false cognition.
So it is everywhere. [End of NyS 4.2.26]
Just as when the threads are being discriminated one by one — 'this is a thread, this is a thread' — nothing else is apprehended
[Section: NySBh 4.2.27]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.27: Because of self-contradiction, [this] is not a valid reason.

children.text:
yadi buddhyā vivecanaṃ bhāvānām ? na sarvabhāvānāṃ
yāthātmyānupalabdhiḥ, atha sarvabhāvānāṃ yāthātmyānupalabdhiḥ ? na buddhyā vivecanaṃ bhāvānām, buddhyā
vivecanaṃ ca yāthātmyānupalabdhiśceti vyāhanyate. taduktam---
"avayavāvayavaprasaṅgaścaivam āpralayāt 15" iti
// 27 //
children.translated_text: If there is discrimination of things by cognition — then there is no non-apprehension of the true nature of all things. And if there is non-apprehension of the true nature of all things — then there is no discrimination of things by cognition. 'Discrimination by cognition' and 'non-apprehension of the true nature' are mutually contradictory. Thus it has been said — 'and the consequence of [infinite division of] parts of parts, up to dissolution' (4.2.15). [End of NyS 4.2.27]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.28]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.28: Because of being its substrate, there is non-separate apprehension.

children.text:
kāryadravyaṃ kāraṇadravyāśritaṃ tatkāraṇebhyaḥ
pṛthaṅ nopalabhyate. viparyaye pṛthak grahaṇāt
yatrāśrayāśritabhāvo nāsti tatra pṛthag

children.translated_text: apprehension. But through discrimination by cognition of things,
there is separate apprehension.
In the case of atoms, which are beyond the senses — what is grasped by the senses, when being discriminated by this
cognition, is [recognized as] something different. [End of NyS 4.2.28]

The effect-substance depends on the cause-substance as its substrate; it is not apprehended separately from those causes. In the contrary case, there is separate apprehension; where the relation of substrate and what depends on it does not obtain, there is separate
[Section: NySBh 4.2.29]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.29: And because of the ascertainment of meaning from the means of valid knowledge.

children.text:
buddhyā vivecanād bhāvānāṃ yāthātmyopalabdhiḥ |
yadasti yathā ca yannāsti yathā ca tatsarvaṃ pramāṇata
upalabdhyā sidhyati, yā ca pramāṇata upalabdhistad
buddhyā vivecanaṃ bhāvānāṃ tena sarvaśāstrāṇi
sarvakarmāṇi sarve ca śarīriṇāṃ
vyavahārā vyāptāḥ-- parīkṣamāṇo hi buddhyādhyavasyati--
'idamasti idaṃ nāstīti. tatra ca na sarvabhāvānupapattiḥ
// 29 //
children.translated_text: Through the discrimination of things by cognition, the true nature [of things] is apprehended. Whatever exists, and how it exists, and whatever does not exist, and how — all of that is established through apprehension by the means of valid knowledge. And the apprehension through the means of valid knowledge is the discrimination of things by cognition. By that, all sciences, all actions, and all activities of embodied beings are pervaded — for one who examines determines by cognition — 'this exists, this does not exist.' And in that case, the non-existence of all things does not follow. [End of NyS 4.2.29]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.30]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.30: Because of the inapplicability and applicability of the means of valid knowledge.

children.text:
evaṃ ca sati sarvaṃ nāstīti nopapadyate,
kasmāt ?. pramāṇānupapattyupapattibhyām |

children.translated_text: If the means of valid knowledge is applicable [to the thesis that] 'everything is non-existent' — then 'everything

children.text: nāstītyetad vyāhanyate, atha pramāṇaṃ nopapadyate ? sarvaṃ nāstītyasya kathaṃ siddhiḥ ?, atha pramāṇamantareṇa
children.translated_text: is non-existent' is self-contradictory. And if the means of valid knowledge is inapplicable — how is 'everything is non-existent' established? And if it is established without
a means of valid knowledge — then how is 'everything exists' not established [in the same way]? [End of NyS 4.2.30]
This being so, 'everything is non-existent' is untenable. Why? Because of the inapplicability and applicability of the means of valid knowledge.
[Section: NySBh 4.2.31]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.31: This notion of valid knowledge and objects of knowledge is like the notion of objects in a dream.

children.text: yathā svapne na viṣayāḥ santi atha cābhimāno bhavati. evaṃ
children.translated_text: Just as in a dream, the objects do not exist, yet the notion [of them] occurs — so too,

children.text: na pramāṇāni prameyāṇi ca santi atha ca pramāṇaprameyābhimāno
children.translated_text: the means of valid knowledge and the objects of knowledge do not exist, yet the notion of valid knowledge and objects of knowledge
occurs. [End of NyS 4.2.31]
[Section: NySBh 4.2.32]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.32: Or like illusion (<s>māyā</s>), a city of the <s>Gandharvas</s>, or a mirage.
[Section: NySBh 4.2.33]
<s>NyS</s> 4.2.33: Because of the absence of a reason, [this is] not established.
there is no reason here. Because of the absence of a reason, [the thesis is] not established.
And [the claim that] objects that do not exist are apprehended at the end of a dream — here too
there is an absence of a reason.
'Like the notion of objects at the end of a dream — so the notion of valid knowledge and objects of knowledge. But not like the apprehension of objects at the end of waking' —

santīti ? tarhi ye ime pratibuddhena
viṣayā upalabhyante (te) upalambhāt santīti--
viparyaye hi hetusāmarthyam |
upalambhābhāve sati anupalambhādabhāvaḥ
sidhyati, ubhayathā tvabhāve nānupalambhasya
sāmarthyamasti. yathā pradīpasyābhāvād rūpasyādarśanamiti,
tatra bhāvenābhāvaḥ samarthyate iti|
svapnāntavikalpe ca hetuvacanam/
"svapnaviṣayābhimānavat"
iti bruvatā svapnāntavikalpe heturvācyaḥ,
kaścitsvapno bhayopasaṃhitaḥ kaścit pramodopasaṃhitaḥ

children.translated_text: some are the opposite of both; and sometimes one
does not dream at all. For the notion of dream-objects, which has a cause,
the distinction [in content] is tenable because of the distinction in causes. [End of NyS 4.2.33]

[Objection:] Because of non-apprehension upon awakening? [Reply:] Because of the apprehension of objects upon awakening, there is no refutation.
