children.text: ityanena tṛtīyapakṣo yujyate tadā viśeṣahetuvacanāt prayatnānantaramāramalābhaḥ śabdasya nābhivyaktiriti siddhaḥ prathamapakṣo na ṣaṭpakṣī pravartate iti // 43 //
children.translated_text: — by this, the third position is justified, then because of the statement of a specific reason, the first position is established — that sound attains existence immediately after effort, not manifestation — and the six-position [schema] does not proceed. [End of NyS 5.1.43]

Depending on the establishment, the fault 'because of the multiplicity of the products of effort' [raised by] the refutation-reason proponent pertains to the characteristic of his own position. Why? Because it arises from his own position. This one, depending on the fault pertaining to the characteristic of his own position, without extracting [and refuting] it, having conceded [it], applies the tenable fault — 'in the refutation too, the same fault [NyS 5.1.39]' — to the opposing position, and thus indicates the reason — 'thus the refutation is non-conclusive.' There, when the indication of the reason and the summation of the applicable fault depend on the characteristic of one's own position, the opposing position is accepted by this [person]. How so? The fault of non-conclusiveness stated by the opponent through 'because of the multiplicity of the products of effort' and the like — without extracting that, he says 'in the refutation too, the same fault [NyS 5.1.39].' Thus, having accepted the establishment as faulty, for one who implies the same fault even in the refutation, the same fault arises from the acceptance of the opposing position. Just as for the opponent, having accepted the refutation as faulty, in the counter-refutation too the implication of the same fault becomes a concession of position — so too for this one, having accepted the establishment as faulty, for one who implies the same fault in the refutation, a concession of position follows. This indeed is the sixth position. In this [schema], the proponent of the establishment-reason has the first, third, and fifth positions; the proponent of the refutation-reason has the second, fourth, and sixth positions. When examining their correctness and incorrectness — the fourth and sixth involve the fault of repetition because of non-distinction. In the fourth position, it is said to the opponent 'the same fault' — 'in the counter-refutation of the refutation, the fault is like the fault of the refutation [NyS 5.1.41]'; in the sixth too, 'from the acceptance of the opposing position, the same fault' — only the same fault is stated, with no difference of meaning. Similarly, the third and fifth involve the fault of repetition. In the third position too, sameness is accepted — 'in the refutation too, the same fault [NyS 5.1.39]'; in the fifth position too, the implication of the same fault in the counter-refutation is accepted — with no difference of meaning stated. There, because of the non-distinction of the fifth and sixth positions, there is the fault of repetition; in the third and fourth, there is concession of position; in the first and second, there is the absence of a specific reason — thus in the six-position [schema], non-establishment for both [sides]. When does the six-position [schema arise]? When

children.text: // iti vātsyāyanaviracite nyāyabhāṣye pañcamādhyāyasya prathamamāhnikaṃ samāptam //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the first section of the fifth chapter of the <s>Nyāya Bhāṣya</s> composed by <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
Now the second section of the fifth chapter of the <s>Nyāya Bhāṣya</s>.
[Section: NySBh 5.2.1]

children.text:
vipratipattyapratipattyorvikalpānnigrahasthānabahutvamiti saṃkṣepeṇoktaṃ tadidānīṃ virbhajanīyam|
nigrahasthānāni khalu parājayavastūny aparādhādhikaraṇāni prāyeṇa pratijñādyavayavāśrayāṇi tattvavādinam atattvavādinaṃ cābhisaṃplavante, teṣāṃ vibhāgaḥ---
children.translated_text: Because of the varieties of misunderstanding and non-understanding, there is a multiplicity of points of defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>) — this was stated in summary; now it is to be divided. The points of defeat are indeed grounds for defeat, loci of error, generally based on the components [of reasoning] such as the thesis and the rest; they apply to the one who speaks the truth and the one who does not speak the truth. Their classification —

children.text: NyS_5,2.1: pratijñāhāniḥ pratijñāntaraṃ pratijñāvirodhaḥ pratijñāsaṃnyāso hetvantaramarthāntaraṃ nirarthakam avijñātārtham apārthakam aprāptakālaṃ nyūnamadhikaṃ punaruktam ananubhāṣaṇam ajñānam apratibhā vikṣepo matānujñā paryanuyojyopekṣaṇaṃ niranuyojyānuyogopasiddhānto hetvābhāsāśca nigrahasthānāni //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5.2.1: Abandonment of the thesis, shifting to another thesis, contradiction of the thesis, renunciation of the thesis, shifting to another reason, shifting to another meaning, meaninglessness, unintelligibility, incoherence, untimeliness, deficiency, excess, repetition, non-response, ignorance, lack of ready wit, evasion, concession of position, overlooking what is to be questioned, questioning what is not to be questioned, an established conclusion [used against oneself], and pseudo-reasons — these are the points of defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>).
These are divided into twenty-two types and defined. [End of NyS 5.2.1]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.2]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.2: The acceptance of a property [shown] in the counter-example in one's own example is the abandonment of the thesis.

children.text: sādhyadharmapratyanīkena dharmeṇa pratyavasthite pratidṛṣṭāntadharmaṃ svadṛṣṭānte 'bhyanujānan pratijñāṃ jahātīti pratijñāhāniḥ, nidarśanam-- 'aindriyakatvādanityaḥ śabdo ghaṭavat' itikṛte. apara āha-- 'dṛṣṭamaindriyakatvaṃ sāmānye nitye kasmānna tathā śabdaḥ ?' iti. ( evam ) pratyavasthite. idamāha-- 'yadyaindriyakaṃ sāmānyaṃ nityam ? kāmaṃ ghaṭo nityostu' iti, sa khalvayaṃ sādhakasya dṛṣṭāntasya nityatvaṃ prasañjayan nigamanāntameva pakṣaṃ jahāti. pakṣaṃ jahat pratijñā jahātītyucyate-- pratijñāśrayatvāt pakṣasyeti // 2 //
children.translated_text: When [the opponent] is confronted with a property that is the opposite of the property to be proved, one who concedes the property of the counter-example in his own example abandons the proposition — this is <s>pratijñāhāni</s> (abandonment of the proposition). An illustration: when it is stated 'sound is non-eternal because of being perceptible, like a pot,' another says — 'perceptibility is observed in the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), which is eternal; why should sound not be likewise?' Thus being confronted, [the proponent] says — 'If the universal, being perceptible, is eternal, then let the pot too be eternal.' This proponent, by entailing the eternality of his own example, abandons the very position up to and including the conclusion. One who abandons the position is said to abandon the proposition — because the position is the basis of the proposition. [End of NyS 5.2.2]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.3]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.3: When the proposition's meaning is refuted, the statement of a different meaning through a difference in properties is <s>pratijñāntara</s> (a different proposition).

children.text:
pratijñātārthaḥ-- 'anityaḥ śabda aindriyakatvād ghaṭavat' ityukte yo 'sya pratiṣedhaḥ |
pratidṛṣṭāntena hetuvyabhicāraḥ-- 'sāmānyamaindriyakaṃ nityam' iti tasmiṃśca pratijñātārthapratiṣedhe dharmavikalpāditi |
dṛṣṭāntapratidṛṣṭāntayoḥ sādharmyayoge dharmabhedāt |
sāmānyamaindriyakaṃ sarvagatam aindriyakastv asarvagato ghaṭa iti dharmavikalpāt. tadarthaṃ nirdeśa iti sādhyasiddhyartham|
children.translated_text: the universal is perceptible and omnipresent, but the pot, though perceptible, is not omnipresent — because of this difference in properties, the statement for the purpose of that [new argument] is for the purpose of establishing the thesis.

children.text: katham ? yathā ghaṭo 'sarvagata evaṃ śabdopyasarvagato ghaṭavadevānitya iti, tatra-- 'anityaḥ śabdaḥ' iti pūrvā pratijñā. 'asarvagataḥ' iti dvitīyā pratijñā pratijñāntaram|
children.translated_text: How? 'Just as the pot is non-omnipresent, so too sound is non-omnipresent and non-eternal, like the pot.' Therein, 'sound is non-eternal' is the first proposition. 'It is non-omnipresent' is a second proposition — a different proposition.

children.text: tat kathaṃ nigrahasthānamiti ?, na pratijñāyāḥ sādhanaṃ pratijñāntaraṃ kiṃ tu hetudṛṣṭāntau sādhanaṃ pratijñāyāḥ, tadetad asādhanopādānam anarthakamiti. ānarthakyānnigrahasthānamiti // 3 //
children.translated_text: How is this a point of defeat? A different proposition is not the means of establishing the [original] proposition; rather, the reason and example are the means of establishing the proposition. This [different proposition] is the adoption of a non-establishing [element] — it is purposeless. Because of its purposelessness, it is a point of defeat. [End of NyS 5.2.3]

The meaning of the proposition is: when it is stated 'sound is non-eternal because of being perceptible, like a pot,' its refutation [comes through] a counter-example showing the deviation of the reason — 'the universal is perceptible and eternal.' When the meaning of the proposition is thus refuted through a difference in properties —
[Section: NySBh 5.2.4]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.4: The contradiction of the proposition and the reason is <s>pratijñāvirodha</s> (contradiction of the proposition).

children.text: 'guṇavyatiriktaṃ dravyam' iti pratijñā. 'rūpādito 'rthāntarasyānupalabdheḥ' iti hetuḥ. soyaṃ pratijñāhetvorvirodhaḥ|
children.translated_text: 'Substance is different from qualities' — this is the proposition. 'Because nothing other than form and the rest is apprehended' — this is the reason. This is the contradiction of the proposition and the reason.

children.text: katham ?, yadi guṇavyatiriktaṃ dravyam ? rūpādibhyo 'rthāntarasyānupalabdheḥ ( iti ) nopapadyate, atha rūpādibhyorthāntarasyānupalabdhiḥ ? guṇavyatiriktaṃ dravyamiti, nopapadyate, guṇavyatiriktaṃ ca dravyaṃ rūpādibhyorthāntarasyānupalabdhiriti virudhyate |
children.translated_text: How? If substance is different from qualities — then 'because nothing other than form and the rest is apprehended' is untenable. If nothing other than form and the rest is apprehended — then 'substance is different from qualities' is untenable. That substance is different from qualities and that nothing other than form and the rest is apprehended — these are contradictory.
They are mutually destructive.
They are not possible [together]. [End of NyS 5.2.4]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.5]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.5: When the thesis is refuted, the denial of the meaning of the proposition is <s>pratijñāsaṃnyāsa</s> (renunciation of the proposition).

children.text: 'anityaḥ śabda aindriyakatvāt' ityukte paro brūyāt-- 'sāmānyamaindriyakaṃ na cānityamevaṃ śabdopyaindriyako na cānityaḥ' iti. evaṃ pratiṣiddhe pakṣe yadi brūyāt-- 'kaḥ punarāha anityaḥ śabdaḥ (iti) ?' iti. soyaṃ pratijñātārthanihnavaḥ pratijñāsaṃnyāsa iti // 5 //
children.translated_text: When it is stated 'sound is non-eternal because of being perceptible,' the opponent says — 'the universal is perceptible and not non-eternal; so too sound, though perceptible, is not non-eternal.' When the thesis is thus refuted, if one says — 'But who says that sound is non-eternal?' — this denial of the meaning of the proposition is the renunciation of the proposition. [End of NyS 5.2.5]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.6]

children.text: NyS_5,2.6: aviśeṣokte hetau pratiṣiddhe viśeṣamicchato hetvantaram //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5.2.6: When a reason stated without specification is refuted, [the introduction of] a different reason by one who desires specification is <s>hetvantara</s> (a different reason).

children.text: nidarśanam-- 'ekaprakṛtīdaṃ vyaktam' iti pratijñā. kasmād hetoḥ ? 'ekaprakṛtīnāṃ vikārāṇāṃ parimāṇāt' 'mṛtpūrvakāṇāṃ śarāvādīnāṃ dṛṣṭaṃ parimāṇaṃ yāvān prakṛtervyūho bhavati tāvān vikāraḥ' iti. dṛṣṭaṃ ca prativikāraṃ parimāṇam. asti cedaṃ parimāṇaṃ prativyaktam, tadekaprakṛtīnāṃ vikārāṇāṃ parimāṇāt paśyāmo vyaktamidamekaprakṛtīti|
asya vyabhicāreṇa pratyavasthānam-- nānāprakṛtīnāmekaprakṛtīnāṃ ca vikārāṇāṃ dṛṣṭaṃ parimāṇamiti|
children.translated_text: The counter-position through deviation from this: 'Measure is observed in modifications of many sources as well as of a single source.'

children.text: evaṃ pratayavasthite āha-- ekaprakṛtisamanvaye sati śarāvādivikārāṇāṃ parimāṇadarśanāt. sukhaduḥkhamohasamanvitaṃ hīdaṃ vyaktaṃ parimitaṃ gṛhyate. tatra prakṛtyantararūpasamanvayābhāve satyekaprakṛtitvamiti|
children.translated_text: When thus confronted, [the proponent] says — 'Because of the observation of the measure of modifications like pots and the like when there is a connection with a single source. For this manifest [world] is grasped as measured, endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion. Therein, in the absence of a connection with the form of another source, it is of a single source.'

children.text: tadidamaviśeṣokte hetau pratiṣiddhe viśeṣaṃ bruvato hetvantaraṃ bhavati, sati ca hetvantarabhāve pūrvasya hetorasādhakatvānnigahasthānam, hetvantara vacane sati yadi hetvarthanidarśano dṛṣṭānta upādīyate ? nedaṃ vyaktamekaprakṛti bhavati-- prakṛtyantaropādānāt, atha nopādīyate ?. dṛṣṭānte hetvarthasyānidarśitasya sādhakabhāvānupapatteḥ ānarthakyād hetoranivṛttaṃ nigrahasthānamiti // 6 //
children.translated_text: This is the introduction of a different reason by one who desires specification when a reason stated without specification has been refuted. And when there is a different reason, because the previous reason fails to establish [the thesis], it is a point of defeat. When a different reason is stated, if an example illustrating the meaning of the reason is adopted — 'this manifest [world] is not of a single source, because of the employment of another source' — then [the argument proceeds]. But if [an example] is not adopted — then because of the inability of the reason to establish [the thesis] when its meaning is not illustrated in an example, due to the purposelessness of the reason, the point of defeat is not averted. [End of NyS 5.2.6]

An illustration: 'The manifest [world] is of a single source (<s>prakṛti</s>)' — this is the proposition. From what reason? 'Because of the measure of modifications that are of a single source' — 'as is observed in pots and the like which are preceded by clay, the extent of the arrangement of the source is the extent of the modification.' And measure is observed for each modification. And this measure exists for each manifest [thing]. Therefore, 'from the measure of modifications that are of a single source, we see that this manifest [world] is of a single source.'
[Section: NySBh 5.2.7]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.7: [A statement of] meaning unconnected with the subject under discussion is <s>arthāntara</s> (an irrelevant statement).

children.text: yathoktalakṣaṇe pakṣapratipakṣaparigrahe hetutaḥ sādhyasiddhau prakṛtāyāṃ brūyāt-- 'nityaḥ śabdaḥ asparśatvāditi hetuḥ' heturnāma hinoterdhātostuni pratyaye kṛdantapadam. padaṃ ca-- nāmākhyātopasarganipātāḥ, abhidheyasya kriyāntarayogād viśiṣyamāṇarūpaḥ śabdo nāma, kriyākārakasamudāyaḥ. kārakasaṃkhyāviśiṣṭakriyākālayogābhidhāyi ākhyātam. dhātvarthamātraṃ ca kālābhidhānaviśiṣṭam, prayogeṣvarthādabhidyamānarūpā nipātāḥ, upasṛjyamānāḥ kriyāvadyotakā upasargāḥ, ityevamādi. tadarthāntaraṃ veditavyam // 7 //
children.translated_text: When the thesis and counter-thesis have been taken up as described, and the establishment of the thesis through the reason is under discussion, one says — 'Sound is eternal, because of being intangible — this is the reason.' 'Reason' (<s>hetu</s>) is a word derived by the <s>kṛt</s> suffix <s>tun</s> from the root <s>hi</s>. A word is either a noun, a verb, a prefix, or a particle. A noun is sound whose form is specified by a connection with another action and the referent — a combination of action and agent. A verb denotes the connection of action with time specified by the number of agents. It denotes only the meaning of the root, specified by the designation of time. Particles are [words] whose form is understood from context in usage. Prefixes illuminate action and are employed [with verbs]. And so forth. This should be understood as an irrelevant statement. [End of NyS 5.2.7]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.8]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.8: [A statement] like the enumeration of the sequence of letters is <s>nirarthaka</s> (meaningless).

children.text: yathānityaḥ śabdaḥ kacaṭatapānāṃ jabagaḍadaśatvāt jhabhañghaḍhadhaṣavat' iti, evaṃprakāraṃ nirarthakam-- abhidhānābhidheyabhāvānupapattau arthagaterabhāvād varṇāḥ krameṇa nirdiśyante iti // 8 //
children.translated_text: [A statement such as] 'sound is non-eternal because of the eight-ness of ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa, like jha-bha-ña-gha-ḍha-dha-ṣa-va' — such a statement is meaningless, because when the relation of signifier and signified is untenable, there is no comprehension of meaning. The letters are merely enumerated in sequence. [End of NyS 5.2.8]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.9]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.9: What is not understood even after being stated three times to the assembly and opponent is <s>avijñātārtha</s> (of unknown meaning).

children.text: yad vākyaṃ pariṣadā prativādinā ca trirabhihitamapi na vijñāyate śliṣṭaśabdam apratītaprayogam atidrutoccāritamityevamādinā kāraṇena tadavijñātārtham, avijñātārtham asāmarthyasaṃvaraṇāya prayuktamiti nigrahasthānamiti // 9 //
children.translated_text: A statement that is not understood even after being stated three times to the assembly and the opponent — because of ambiguous words, unfamiliar usage, excessively rapid pronunciation, and such reasons — that is of unknown meaning. [A statement] of unknown meaning, employed to conceal one's incapacity, is a point of defeat. [End of NyS 5.2.9]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.10]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.10: What has an unconnected meaning due to the impossibility of sequential connection is <s>apārthaka</s> (incoherent).

children.text: yatrānekasya padasya vākyasya vā paurvāpayeṇānvayayogo nāsti ity asaṃbaddhārthatvaṃ gṛhyate tatsamudāyārthasyāpāyādapārthakaṃ yathā-- 'daśa dāḍimāni. ṣaḍapūpāḥ. kuṇḍamajājinam. palalapiṇḍaḥ. adharaurukametat. kumāryāḥ prāyyaṃ tasyāḥ pitā apratiśīnaḥ' iti // 10 //
children.translated_text: Where the sequential connection of many words or sentences is not possible, the unconnected meaning is grasped; because the collective meaning is lost, it is incoherent. For example: 'Ten pomegranates. Six cakes. A pot and a goatskin. A lump of chaff. The thigh-gourd is this. The maiden's [property] belongs to her father who is unconcerned.' [End of NyS 5.2.10]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.11]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.11: A statement with the members [of the syllogism] in the wrong order is <s>aprāptakāla</s> (untimely).

children.text: pratijñādīnāmakyavānāṃ yathālakṣaṇamarthavaśāt kramaḥ tatrāvayavaviparyāsena vacanam aprāptakālam asaṃbaddhārthaṃ nigrahasthānamiti // 11 //
children.translated_text: The sequence of the members — proposition and the rest — follows from their definitions and the requirements of meaning. A statement with the members in the wrong order is untimely, of unconnected meaning, and a point of defeat. [End of NyS 5.2.11]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.12]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.12: [An argument] deficient by even a single member among [the members beginning with] the proposition is <s>nyūna</s> (deficient).

[An argument] deficient by even a single member among the members — proposition and the rest — is deficient, a point of defeat — because in the absence of a means of proof, the thesis is not established. [End of NyS 5.2.12]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.13]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.13: [An argument] excessive in reason and example is <s>adhika</s> (redundant).
Because one [of the pair] accomplishes [the task], the other is purposeless — this should be understood in the case of accepting a restriction [that only one is needed]. [End of NyS 5.2.13]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.14]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.14: The repetition of words or meanings is <s>punarukta</s> (tautology), except in the case of restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>).

children.text: anyatrānuvādāt śabdapunaruktam arthapunaruktaṃ vā-- 'nityaḥ śabdaḥ nityaḥ śabdaḥ' iti śabdapunaruktam. arthapunaruktam-- 'anityaḥ śabdaḥ. nirodhadharmako dhvānaḥ' iti|

children.translated_text: But in the case of restatement, it is not tautology — because a specific meaning is justified by the repetition of the word. As —
'The restatement of the proposition with the citation of the reason is the conclusion [NyS 1.1.39].'
[End of NyS 5.2.14]

Except in the case of restatement, there is tautology of words or of meaning — 'sound is eternal, sound is eternal' is tautology of words. Tautology of meaning: 'sound is non-eternal; the resonance has the property of cessation.'
[Section: NySBh 5.2.15]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.15: Restating in one's own words what is already implied by the meaning [is also tautology].

children.text:
punaruktamiti prakṛtam, nidarśanam-- 'utpattidharmakatvādanityam'
ityaktvā arthādāpannasya yo 'bhidhāyakaḥ śabdastena
svaśabdena brūyāt-- 'anutpattidharmakaṃ nityam'
iti tacca punaruktaṃ veditavyam-- arthasaṃpratyayārthe
śabdaprayoge pratītaḥ so 'rtho 'rthāpattyeti
// 15 //
children.translated_text: Tautology is the subject. An illustration: having said 'that which has the property of origination is non-eternal,' restating what is already implied by the meaning in one's own words — 'that which does not have the property of origination is eternal' — this too should be understood as tautology, because the meaning comprehended through the use of the word for the purpose of conveying meaning is [already obtained by] implication (<s>arthāpatti</s>). [End of NyS 5.2.15]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.16]

children.text: NyS_5,2.16: vijñātasya pariṣadā trirabhihitasyāpy apratyuccāraṇam ananubhāṣaṇam //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5.2.16: Not responding to what has been understood by the assembly even after being stated three times is <s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s> (non-response).
not responding to what has been stated three times is
<s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s> (non-response) — a point of defeat. For one who does not respond, on what basis
would he state a refutation of the opponent's position? [End of NyS 5.2.16]
When the meaning of a statement has been understood by the assembly and the opponent,
[Section: NySBh 5.2.17]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.17: And not understanding [what has been stated] is <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance).
When the meaning of what has been understood by the assembly and stated three times by the opponent
is not understood — that ignorance is a point of defeat. For one who does not understand,
whose [position] would he refute? [End of NyS 5.2.17]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.18]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.18: Not conceiving a reply is <s>apratibhā</s> (lack of ready wit).

children.text: parapakṣapratiṣedhaḥ uttaraṃ tad yadā na pratipadyate ? tadā nigṛhīto bhavati // 18 //
children.translated_text: The refutation of the opponent's position is the reply. When one does not conceive it, then one is defeated. [End of NyS 5.2.18]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.19]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.19: Interruption of the discussion due to an obligation to perform a task is <s>vikṣepa</s> (evasion).

children.text:
yatra kartavyaṃ vyāsajya kathāṃ vyavacchinatti--
'idaṃ me karaṇīyaṃ vidyate tasminn avasite paścāt kathayiṣyāmīti (tat) vikṣepo nāma nigrahasthānam|
ekanigrahāvasānāyāṃ kathāyāṃ svayameva kathāntaraṃ pratipadyate iti
// 19 //
children.translated_text: When one, having become engaged in a task to be done, interrupts the discussion — 'I have something that needs to be done; when that is completed, I shall discuss afterwards' — that evasion is a point of defeat. When the discussion is meant to end with the defeat of one [party], one voluntarily takes up another discussion. [End of NyS 5.2.19]
[Section: NySBh 5.2.20]

children.text: NyS_5,2.20: svapakṣe doṣābhyupagamāt parapakṣe doṣaprasaṅgo matānujñā //
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5.2.20: Admitting a fault in one's own position and pointing out the same fault in the opponent's position is <s>matānujñā</s> (admission of the opponent's view).

children.text:
yaḥ pareṇa coditaṃ doṣaṃ svapakṣe 'bhyupagamya |
anuddhṛtya vadati-- 'bhavatpakṣepi samāno doṣaḥ'

children.translated_text: without removing it, says — 'the same fault exists in your position too' —
he, by admitting the fault in his own position and pointing out the fault in the opponent's position, concedes the opponent's view.
incurs the ground of defeat of accepting what is approved [by the opponent]. [End of NyS 5.2.20]
One who, having acknowledged the fault pointed out by the opponent in one's own position,
[Section: NySBh 5.2.21]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.21: The non-censure of one who has reached a ground of defeat, [and] the overlooking of one who should be challenged — [this is a ground of defeat].

children.text: paryanuyojyo nāma nigrahopapattyā codanīyaḥ. tasyopekṣaṇam = 'nigrahasthānaṃ prāpto 'sīty ananuyogaḥ/

children.translated_text: And this should be said by the assembly, when not asked

children.text: vacanīyam-- na khalu nigrahaṃ prāptaḥ svakaupīnaṃ
children.translated_text: 'whose is the defeat?' — for indeed, one who has reached a [point of] defeat would not
expose his own loincloth. [End of NyS 5.2.21]

'One who should be challenged' means one who ought to be censured because a ground of defeat has obtained for him. The overlooking of such a person means the failure to challenge [him by saying] 'you have reached a ground of defeat.'
[Section: NySBh 5.2.22]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.22: The charge of a ground of defeat where there is no ground of defeat is the censure of one who should not be censured.
one who says to the other 'you are defeated' — through the censure of one who should not be censured —
should be understood as himself defeated
through [the ground of defeat called] the censure of one who should not be censured. [End of NyS 5.2.22]
Due to a false determination of the definition of a ground of defeat, at a point where there is no ground of defeat,
[Section: NySBh 5.2.23]

<s>NyS</s> 5.2.23: Having accepted a <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine), [if] due to lack of restriction, one opens up an [unwanted] discussion — [this is] <s>apasiddhānta</s> (deviation from the established doctrine).

children.text:
kasyacidarthasya tathābhāvaṃ pratijñāya pratijñātārthaviparyayāt |
aniyamāt kathāṃ prasañjayato 'pasiddhānto
veditavyo yathā-- 'na sad ātmānaṃ jahāti |
na sato vināśaḥ, nāsad ātmānaṃ labhate = nāsadutpadyate' iti siddhāntamabhyupetya
svapakṣaṃ vyavasthāpayati--ekaprakṛtīdaṃ vyaktam--
vikārāṇāmanvayadarśanāt. mṛdanvitānāṃ
śarāvādīnāṃ dṛṣṭamekaprakṛtitvaṃ tathā cāyaṃ
vyaktabhedaḥ sukhaduḥkhamohasamanvito dṛśyate
tasmāt samanvayadarśanāt sukhādibhirekaprakṛtīdaṃ viśvamiti|
evamuktavān anuyujyate-- atha prakṛtirvikāra
iti kathaṃ lakṣitavyam ? iti, yasyāvasthitasya
dharmāntaranivṛttau dharmāntaraṃ pravartate sā
prakṛtiḥ. yacca dharmāntaraṃ pravartate sa vikāra
iti|
so 'yaṃ pratijñātārthaviparyayāt |
aniyamāt kathāṃ prasañjayati |
pratijñātaṃ khalvanena-- nāsadāvirbhavati na
sattiro bhavatīti|
sadasatośca tirobhāvāvirbhāvam antareṇa
na kasyacit pravṛttiḥ pravṛttyuparamaśca bhavati,

children.text: na syāt, evaṃ pratyavasthito yadi sataścātmahānam asataścātmalābhamabhyupaiti ? tadasyāpasiddhānto nigrahasthānaṃ bhavati,
children.translated_text: If, when thus challenged, he accepts the loss of being of the existent and the acquisition of being of the non-existent, then this <s>apasiddhānta</s> becomes his ground of defeat.
But if he does not accept it, then his thesis is not established. [End of NyS 5.2.23]

Having asserted the nature of some thing, due to the contradiction with the asserted meaning, one who, because of lack of restriction, opens up a [further] discussion — this should be understood as <s>apasiddhānta</s>. For example: having accepted the <s>siddhānta</s> — 'the existent does not abandon its own nature; the existent is not destroyed; the non-existent does not acquire its own nature; the non-existent does not arise' — one establishes one's own thesis: 'this manifest [world] has a single material cause — because of the observation of continuity among modifications. The single material cause of pots and the like, which are pervaded by clay, is observed; similarly, this diversity of the manifest [world] is observed to be pervaded by pleasure, pain, and delusion; therefore, because of the observation of continuity with pleasure and the rest, this universe has a single material cause.' When one has thus stated, one is challenged: 'Now, how is the material cause to be distinguished from the modification?' [One replies:] 'When, in something that persists, one property ceases and another property arises — that is the material cause. And the other property that arises — that is the modification.' This person, due to the contradiction with the asserted meaning, because of lack of restriction, opens up a [further] discussion. For this person has asserted — 'the non-existent does not come into being, and the existent does not disappear.' But without the disappearing and appearing of the existent and the non-existent, there is no arising of activity or cessation of activity for anything. When clay persists, the property characterized as pot and the like — 'it will come into being' — this is activity; 'it existed [before]' —
